Left side charge is −1 + 4 = +3 and the right side is 0, so 3 electrons are required. This matches N changing from +5 to +2.
Determine the oxidation number of sulfur in each of H₂S, S₈, SO₂ and SO₄²⁻. (4 marks)
H₂S: S = −2 as each H is +1 [1]. S₈: S = 0 as it is an uncombined element [1]. SO₂: S = +4 as each O is −2 [1]. SO₄²⁻: S = +6 since S + 4(−2) = −2 [1].

Sulfur dioxide is oxidised to sulfate ions by acidified permanganate ions, which are reduced to Mn²⁺. Write the balanced half-equation for the oxidation of SO₂ in acidic solution and combine it with the reduction half-equation to give the overall equation. (4 marks)

Oxidation: SO₂(g) + 2H₂O(l) → SO₄²⁻(aq) + 4H⁺(aq) + 2e⁻ [1]. Reduction: MnO₄⁻(aq) + 8H⁺(aq) + 5e⁻ → Mn²⁺(aq) + 4H₂O(l) [1]. Multiply oxidation by 5 and reduction by 2 so 10 electrons cancel [1]. Overall: 5SO₂(g) + 2MnO₄⁻(aq) + 2H₂O(l) → 5SO₄²⁻(aq) + 2Mn²⁺(aq) + 4H⁺(aq) [1].
Magnesium ribbon reacts with dilute hydrochloric acid and bubbles of gas form. Write the oxidation and reduction half-equations, the overall ionic equation, and name the species oxidised. (4 marks)
Oxidation: Mg(s) → Mg²⁺(aq) + 2e⁻ [1]. Reduction: 2H⁺(aq) + 2e⁻ → H₂(g) [1]. Overall: Mg(s) + 2H⁺(aq) → Mg²⁺(aq) + H₂(g) [1]. Mg is the species oxidised (0 to +2) [1].
Use oxidation numbers to show that Fe₂O₃(s) + 2Al(s) → Al₂O₃(s) + 2Fe(s) is a redox reaction, and identify the oxidising agent and the reducing agent. (4 marks)
Fe changes from +3 to 0, so it is reduced [1]. Al changes from 0 to +3, so it is oxidised [1]. Oxidising agent is Fe₂O₃ [1]. Reducing agent is Al [1].
Explain, using oxidation numbers, why Zn(s) + 2HCl(aq) → ZnCl₂(aq) + H₂(g) is a redox reaction whereas NaOH(aq) + HCl(aq) → NaCl(aq) + H₂O(l) is not. (2 marks)

In the zinc reaction Zn changes from 0 to +2 and H changes from +1 to 0, so oxidation numbers change and it is redox [1]. In the NaOH and HCl reaction every element keeps its oxidation number (Na +1, O −2, H +1, Cl −1), so it is not redox [1].

A 0.486 g strip of magnesium reacts completely with excess copper(II) sulfate solution: Mg(s) + Cu²⁺(aq) → Mg²⁺(aq) + Cu(s). Calculate the mass of copper deposited. M(Mg) = 24.3 g mol⁻¹, M(Cu) = 63.5 g mol⁻¹. (3 marks)
Explain why oxidation and reduction must always occur together in a redox reaction. (2 marks)

Electrons lost in oxidation cannot exist freely in solution, so they must be gained by another species in reduction [1]. The number of electrons lost by the reducing agent equals the number gained by the oxidising agent [1].
vce-chem12-reactivity-series-and-metal-d: chem12a3-rs-9
Which of these metals reacts with cold water to produce hydrogen gas and a metal hydroxide solution?
Sodium
Iron
Copper
Lead
Sodium is a very strong reducing agent and reduces water: 2Na + 2H₂O → 2Na⁺ + 2OH⁻ + H₂. Iron reacts only very slowly with water (as rusting), and copper and lead do not react.
chem12a3-rs-10
A silver wire is placed in copper(II) sulfate solution. Which statement is correct?
Copper metal deposits on the wire and the solution becomes colourless
Hydrogen gas bubbles form on the wire
No reaction occurs, because Ag is a weaker reducing agent than Cu
The wire dissolves and the solution turns blue

Ag(s) is a weaker reductant than Cu(s), so it cannot reduce Cu²⁺ and there is no reaction. Copper deposition would require silver to be the more reactive metal, which is the reverse of the actual order.
chem12a3-rs-11
A clean iron nail is placed in blue copper(II) sulfate solution. Which observation is expected after some time?
No change, as iron is less reactive than copper
Silver crystals form on the nail and the solution turns colourless
The nail dissolves completely and the solution turns brown
A reddish-brown coating forms on the nail and the blue colour fades to a pale green
Fe(s) + Cu²⁺(aq) → Fe²⁺(aq) + Cu(s): copper deposits as a reddish-brown layer and the blue Cu²⁺ is replaced by pale green Fe²⁺. 'No change' is wrong because iron is the stronger reductant.
chem12a3-rs-12
In the reaction Zn(s) + Cu²⁺(aq) → Zn²⁺(aq) + Cu(s), which species is the oxidising agent?
Cu²⁺(aq)
Zn(s)
Zn²⁺(aq)
Cu(s)
Cu²⁺ gains electrons (is reduced), so it is the oxidising agent. Zn(s) is oxidised and so is the reducing agent.
chem12a3-rs-13
Which of the following combinations will result in a displacement reaction?
Copper metal in zinc sulfate solution
Silver metal in lead(II) nitrate solution
Lead metal in silver nitrate solution
Iron metal in magnesium chloride solution
Pb is a stronger reducing agent than Ag, so Pb(s) + 2Ag⁺(aq) → Pb²⁺(aq) + 2Ag(s). In each other option the metal is less reactive than the metal ion's parent metal, so there is no reaction.
chem12a3-rs-14
An iron nail is left in excess copper(II) sulfate solution until 0.100 mol of copper has deposited. What mass of iron has dissolved? (Fe = 55.8)
Fe + Cu²⁺ → Fe²⁺ + Cu is a 1 : 1 ratio, so n(Fe) = 0.100 mol and m = 0.100 × 55.8 = 5.58 g. 6.35 g is the mass of copper formed, not iron dissolved.
chem12a3-rs-15
Metal M displaces copper from copper(II) sulfate solution but does not react with zinc sulfate solution. M is best placed:
between zinc and copper in the reactivity series
above zinc in the reactivity series
below copper in the reactivity series
at the same position as zinc
M reduces Cu²⁺, so it is more reactive than copper. It cannot reduce Zn²⁺, so it is less reactive than zinc. Hence it lies between zinc and copper.
chem12a3-rs-16
Which of these metals will NOT produce hydrogen gas when added to dilute hydrochloric acid?
Magnesium
Iron
Copper
Zinc
Cu²⁺/Cu (+0.34 V) lies above H⁺/H₂ (0.00 V), so Cu is a weaker reductant than H₂ and cannot reduce H⁺. Mg, Zn and Fe all lie below hydrogen and react.
chem12a3-rs-17
Aluminium is more reactive than zinc, yet aluminium cookware does not visibly react with water. The best explanation is that aluminium:
is a weaker reducing agent than zinc
has a thin, unreactive coating of aluminium oxide that protects the metal beneath
does not lose electrons to form ions
reacts with water to form a gas that blocks the surface
A tightly adhering Al₂O₃ layer forms on the surface and prevents contact with water and oxygen. The reactivity series is unchanged, so aluminium is still the stronger reductant than zinc.
chem12a3-rs-18
A copper wire is placed in excess silver nitrate solution and 0.0500 mol of copper reacts. What mass of silver is deposited? (Ag = 107.9)
Cu + 2Ag⁺ → Cu²⁺ + 2Ag, so n(Ag) = 2 × 0.0500 = 0.100 mol and m = 0.100 × 107.9 = 10.8 g. 5.40 g comes from ignoring the 1 : 2 mole ratio.
chem12a3-rs-19
In a metal displacement reaction, a more reactive metal atom displaces a less reactive metal ion from solution because the more reactive metal:
gains electrons more readily than the less reactive metal ion
has a larger atomic mass than the metal ion
loses electrons to the less reactive metal ion, which is reduced to metal
is always a solid while the other metal is always a liquid

The more reactive metal is the stronger reductant, so it transfers electrons to the ion, which is reduced to the solid metal. Gaining electrons more readily describes the weaker reductant's ion, not the reactive metal.
chem12a3-rs-20
A piece of magnesium ribbon is placed in copper(II) sulfate solution. Describe two observations and write the balanced ionic equation with states. (3 marks)
A reddish-brown solid (copper) deposits on the magnesium [1]; the blue colour of the solution fades [1]; Mg(s) + Cu²⁺(aq) → Mg²⁺(aq) + Cu(s) [1].
chem12a3-rs-21
Describe an experiment, using only strips of Zn, Pb, Cu and Ag and solutions of their nitrates, to determine the order of reactivity of these four metals. State the expected order. (4 marks)

Place a strip of each metal into a solution of each of the other metals' nitrates (or a systematic set of pairs) and observe for deposits of metal [1]; a reaction (metal deposit on the strip) shows the strip is more reactive than the metal in solution [1]; zinc displaces all three others, silver displaces none [1]; order from most to least reactive: Zn > Pb > Cu > Ag [1].
chem12a3-rs-22
Aluminium foil is placed in copper(II) chloride solution. Write the oxidation half-equation, the reduction half-equation and the overall balanced ionic equation. (3 marks)
Oxidation: Al(s) → Al³⁺(aq) + 3e⁻ [1]; reduction: Cu²⁺(aq) + 2e⁻ → Cu(s) [1]; overall: 2Al(s) + 3Cu²⁺(aq) → 2Al³⁺(aq) + 3Cu(s) [1].
chem12a3-rs-23
A 3.27 g piece of zinc (Zn = 65.4) is added to excess copper(II) sulfate solution and all of the zinc reacts. Calculate the mass of copper formed. (Cu = 63.5) (3 marks)
chem12a3-rs-24
Explain why zinc reacts with dilute hydrochloric acid to produce hydrogen gas, but copper does not. (2 marks)

Zinc lies below hydrogen in the reactivity series, so Zn is a stronger reducing agent than H₂ and can reduce H⁺ to H₂ [1]; copper lies above hydrogen, so it is a weaker reducing agent than H₂ and cannot reduce H⁺ [1].
chem12a3-rs-25
Explain why an iron nail placed in magnesium sulfate solution shows no change. Refer to reducing agents in your answer. (2 marks)
Iron is a weaker reducing agent than magnesium (Fe²⁺/Fe lies above Mg²⁺/Mg in the electrochemical series) [1]; so Fe(s) cannot transfer electrons to Mg²⁺ and no displacement occurs [1].
chem12a3-rs-26
Define a metal displacement reaction in terms of electron transfer, and give one example with a balanced ionic equation. (2 marks)

A reaction in which a more reactive metal transfers electrons to the ion of a less reactive metal, so the more reactive metal is oxidised and the ion is reduced to the metal [1]; e.g. Mg(s) + 2Ag⁺(aq) → Mg²⁺(aq) + 2Ag(s) [1].
vce-chem12-concentration-units-and-dilut: A water sample contains 25 µg L⁻¹ of lead ions. What is this concentration in ppb?
1 ppb is 1 µg per litre (1 µg per kg of dilute aqueous solution), so 25 µg L⁻¹ is 25 ppb. 25 000 ppb would be 25 mg L⁻¹ (25 ppm).
4.00 g of sodium hydroxide (M = 40.0 g mol⁻¹) is dissolved in water to make 500.0 mL of solution. What is the concentration of the solution?
n = 4.00 ÷ 40.0 = 0.100 mol; c = 0.100 ÷ 0.5000 L = 0.200 mol L⁻¹. 2.00 mol L⁻¹ results from using 50.0 mL instead of 500.0 mL.
50.0 mL of 0.800 mol L⁻¹ KNO₃ solution is diluted with water to a total volume of 200.0 mL. What is the concentration of the diluted solution?
c₂ = 0.800 × 50.0 ÷ 200.0 = 0.200 mol L⁻¹, since the volume has increased four-fold. 3.20 mol L⁻¹ comes from multiplying by the dilution factor instead of dividing.
What is the concentration of chloride ions in a 0.150 mol L⁻¹ solution of calcium chloride, CaCl₂?
CaCl₂ → Ca²⁺ + 2Cl⁻, so [Cl⁻] = 2 × 0.150 = 0.300 mol L⁻¹. 0.150 mol L⁻¹ is the Ca²⁺ concentration.
20.0 mL of 1.00 mol L⁻¹ HCl is to be diluted to 0.250 mol L⁻¹. Assuming volumes are additive, what volume of water must be added?
V₂ = 1.00 × 20.0 ÷ 0.250 = 80.0 mL final volume, so 80.0 − 20.0 = 60.0 mL of water is added. 80.0 mL is the final volume, not the volume of water added.
Which piece of glassware is most suitable for making up a standard solution to an accurately known final volume?
A volumetric flask is calibrated to contain one precise volume when filled to its mark. A measuring cylinder is graduated but much less accurate.
What mass of anhydrous sodium carbonate, Na₂CO₃ (M = 106.0 g mol⁻¹), is needed to prepare 250.0 mL of a 0.100 mol L⁻¹ solution?
n = 0.100 × 0.2500 = 0.0250 mol; m = 0.0250 × 106.0 = 2.65 g. 10.6 g is the mass in one litre of 0.100 mol L⁻¹ solution, ignoring the actual volume.
15.0 mL of ethanol is mixed with water to make 250.0 mL of solution. What is the concentration in % (v/v)?
10.0 mL of a stock solution is diluted to a final volume of 250.0 mL. What is the dilution factor?
Dilution factor = V₂ ÷ V₁ = 250.0 ÷ 10.0 = 25.0, so the concentration falls to one twenty-fifth of the original. 0.0400 is the inverse, the fraction of the original concentration remaining.
A water supply contains 2.0 ppm fluoride. What mass of fluoride is present in 5.0 L of this water (assume density 1.00 g mL⁻¹)?
2.0 ppm = 2.0 mg L⁻¹, so 5.0 L contains 2.0 × 5.0 = 10 mg. 10 g confuses mg with g.
What is the concentration, in g L⁻¹, of a 0.0500 mol L⁻¹ solution of potassium permanganate, KMnO₄ (M = 158.0 g mol⁻¹)?
Mass concentration = c × M = 0.0500 × 158.0 = 7.90 g L⁻¹. 3.16 × 10⁻⁴ results from dividing by the molar mass instead of multiplying.
When a solution is diluted by adding water, which quantity remains unchanged?
The amount of solute, in mol
Adding solvent does not add or remove solute particles, so n(solute) is constant, which is why c₁V₁ = c₂V₂. Concentration and volume both change.
100.0 mL of 0.200 mol L⁻¹ NaCl is mixed with 100.0 mL of 0.300 mol L⁻¹ NaCl. Assuming volumes are additive, what is the final concentration of NaCl?
n = 0.0200 + 0.0300 = 0.0500 mol in 0.2000 L, so c = 0.250 mol L⁻¹. 0.500 mol L⁻¹ simply adds the two concentrations without accounting for the larger volume.
A solution of sodium hydroxide (M = 40.0 g mol⁻¹) has a concentration of 0.0400 g L⁻¹. What is its concentration in mol L⁻¹?
c = 0.0400 g L⁻¹ ÷ 40.0 g mol⁻¹ = 1.00 × 10⁻³ mol L⁻¹. 1.60 mol L⁻¹ results from multiplying by the molar mass instead of dividing.
What volume of 12.0 mol L⁻¹ stock hydrochloric acid is required to prepare 500.0 mL of 0.600 mol L⁻¹ HCl?
V₁ = c₂V₂ ÷ c₁ = 0.600 × 500.0 ÷ 12.0 = 25.0 mL. 250 mL is out by a factor of ten from a decimal slip.
Calculate the mass of potassium chloride, KCl (M = 74.6 g mol⁻¹), required to prepare 500.0 mL of a 0.100 mol L⁻¹ solution. (2 marks)
The chloride concentration in a sample of river water is 2.50 × 10⁻⁴ mol L⁻¹. Calculate this concentration in ppm (mg L⁻¹). The molar mass of chlorine is 35.5 g mol⁻¹. (2 marks)
Mass concentration = 2.50 × 10⁻⁴ mol L⁻¹ × 35.5 g mol⁻¹ = 8.875 × 10⁻³ g L⁻¹ [1]; = 8.88 mg L⁻¹ = 8.88 ppm (assuming density 1.00 g mL⁻¹) [1].
A 0.250 mol L⁻¹ solution of sodium phosphate, Na₃PO₄, is prepared. Write the equation for its dissociation in water and determine the concentration of each ion in the solution. (3 marks)
20.0 mL of 0.600 mol L⁻¹ nitric acid is mixed with 30.0 mL of water. Assuming volumes are additive, calculate the concentration of the diluted acid. (3 marks)
Explain why a volumetric flask, rather than a beaker, is used to prepare a standard solution, and why the solvent is added in two stages (dissolving, then making up to the mark). (2 marks)

A volumetric flask is calibrated to hold one precise volume when filled to its mark, whereas a beaker's graduations are only approximate [1]; the solute is first dissolved in less water and then made up to the mark so that the total final volume of solution (not the volume of water added) is accurately known, giving an accurate concentration [1].
A stock solution contains 1000 ppm of copper(II) ions. Calculate the volume of stock needed to prepare 100.0 mL of a 25.0 ppm solution, and describe how the dilution is carried out. (3 marks)

Use c₁V₁ = c₂V₂ (concentration in ppm is directly proportional to the amount of solute per volume) [1]; V₁ = 25.0 × 100.0 ÷ 1000 = 2.50 mL [1]; pipette 2.50 mL of stock into a 100.0 mL volumetric flask, then add deionised water to the mark and mix by inverting [1].
50.0 mL of 0.400 mol L⁻¹ magnesium chloride, MgCl₂, solution is diluted to 200.0 mL with water. Calculate the concentration of Mg²⁺ and of Cl⁻ in the diluted solution. (3 marks)
vce-chem12-stoichiometry-and-limiting-re: Ammonia is made by N₂(g) + 3H₂(g) → 2NH₃(g). What amount of NH₃ can be made from 1.5 mol of H₂ with excess N₂?
n(NH₃) = 2/3 × n(H₂) = 2/3 × 1.5 = 1.0 mol. 2.25 mol comes from using the ratio upside down (3/2).
Magnesium burns in oxygen: 2Mg(s) + O₂(g) → 2MgO(s). What mass of MgO (M = 40.3 g mol⁻¹) forms when 4.86 g of Mg (M = 24.3 g mol⁻¹) burns completely?
n(Mg) = 4.86 ÷ 24.3 = 0.200 mol; the ratio Mg:MgO is 1:1, so m(MgO) = 0.200 × 40.3 = 8.06 g. 4.03 g wrongly halves the amount using the coefficient of O₂.
Hydrogen peroxide decomposes: 2H₂O₂(aq) → 2H₂O(l) + O₂(g). What volume of O₂ forms at SLC (molar volume 24.8 L mol⁻¹) from 0.200 mol of H₂O₂?
n(O₂) = ½ × 0.200 = 0.100 mol; V = 0.100 × 24.8 = 2.48 L. 4.96 L assumes a 1:1 ratio between H₂O₂ and O₂.
Which statement best describes the limiting reactant in a reaction?
The reactant with the smaller mass at the start
The reactant with the smaller coefficient in the balanced equation
The reactant with the lower molar mass
The reactant that is completely used up first, so no more product can form

The limiting reactant is the one fully consumed first, and it sets the maximum amount of product. Initial mass or coefficient alone does not identify it, because the amounts in mol and the ratio must be compared.
The theoretical yield of a salt is 25.0 g. If the percentage yield of the experiment is 84.0 %, what mass of salt is actually obtained?
Actual = 84.0 ÷ 100 × 25.0 = 21.0 g. 29.8 g comes from dividing by 0.840 instead of multiplying, which would give more than the theoretical maximum.
0.30 mol of Al reacts with 0.30 mol of Cl₂: 2Al(s) + 3Cl₂(g) → 2AlCl₃(s). What amount of AlCl₃ forms?
0.30 mol Al needs 0.45 mol Cl₂, but only 0.30 mol is present, so Cl₂ is limiting: n(AlCl₃) = 2/3 × 0.30 = 0.20 mol. 0.30 mol wrongly takes Al as limiting.
2.0 mol of Mg and 0.50 mol of O₂ react completely: 2Mg(s) + O₂(g) → 2MgO(s). What amount of the excess reactant remains?
O₂ is limiting and uses 2 × 0.50 = 1.0 mol of Mg, leaving 2.0 − 1.0 = 1.0 mol Mg. 1.5 mol results from subtracting 0.50 mol directly, ignoring the 2:1 ratio.
What volume of 0.250 mol L⁻¹ NaOH is needed to react completely with 20.0 mL of 0.200 mol L⁻¹ H₂SO₄? H₂SO₄(aq) + 2NaOH(aq) → Na₂SO₄(aq) + 2H₂O(l)
Excess Na₂SO₄ solution is added to a solution containing 0.0200 mol of BaCl₂. What mass of BaSO₄ (M = 233.4 g mol⁻¹) precipitates?
Ba²⁺(aq) + SO₄²⁻(aq) → BaSO₄(s) is a 1:1 ratio, so n(BaSO₄) = 0.0200 mol and m = 0.0200 × 233.4 = 4.67 g. 9.34 g wrongly doubles the amount.
Propane burns: C₃H₈(g) + 5O₂(g) → 3CO₂(g) + 4H₂O(g). At the same temperature and pressure, what volume of O₂ is needed to burn 10 L of propane completely?
Equal volumes of gases at the same temperature and pressure contain equal amounts, so volume ratios match mole ratios: 10 × 5 = 50 L. 30 L uses the coefficient of CO₂ instead of O₂.
A student calculates a percentage yield of 108 % for a precipitate. Which is the most likely explanation?
The reaction did not go to completion
Some precipitate was lost during filtration
The precipitate was not fully dried and still contained water or impurities
A side reaction consumed some of the reactants
A yield above 100 % means more mass was measured than is theoretically possible, which happens when the product is wet or impure. The other options would all lower the measured mass.
In a balanced chemical equation, the coefficients represent the ratio of which quantity?
Amounts in moles of reactants and products
Volumes of all reactants and products, whatever their states
Numbers of atoms of each element in one formula unit
Coefficients give the mole ratio in which substances react and form. They do not give mass ratios, because molar masses differ.
1.215 g of Mg (M = 24.3 g mol⁻¹) reacts with excess HCl: Mg(s) + 2HCl(aq) → MgCl₂(aq) + H₂(g). What volume of H₂ forms at SLC (24.8 L mol⁻¹)?
n(Mg) = 0.0500 mol; the Mg:H₂ ratio is 1:1, so V = 0.0500 × 24.8 = 1.24 L. 2.48 L wrongly doubles the amount using the coefficient of HCl.
Explain why the limiting reactant determines the maximum amount of product formed in a reaction. (2 marks)

The limiting reactant is the reactant that is completely consumed first [1]; once it is used up the reaction stops, so no more product can form regardless of how much of the other reactants (in excess) remains [1].
Aluminium burns in oxygen: 4Al(s) + 3O₂(g) → 2Al₂O₃(s). Calculate the mass of Al₂O₃ (M = 102.0 g mol⁻¹) formed when 5.40 g of Al (M = 27.0 g mol⁻¹) burns completely in excess oxygen. (3 marks)

0.540 g of aluminium (M = 27.0 g mol⁻¹) is added to 50.0 mL of 1.00 mol L⁻¹ HCl: 2Al(s) + 6HCl(aq) → 2AlCl₃(aq) + 3H₂(g). Identify the limiting reactant and calculate the volume of H₂ produced at SLC (molar volume 24.8 L mol⁻¹). (4 marks)

20.0 mL of 0.500 mol L⁻¹ CuSO₄ is mixed with excess NaOH solution: CuSO₄(aq) + 2NaOH(aq) → Cu(OH)₂(s) + Na₂SO₄(aq). After filtering and drying, 0.850 g of Cu(OH)₂ (M = 97.5 g mol⁻¹) is collected. Calculate the percentage yield. (3 marks)
A student has 10 g of substance X and 20 g of substance Y and states that X must be the limiting reactant because it has the smaller mass. Explain why this reasoning is flawed. (2 marks)

The limiting reactant depends on the amounts in mol available compared with the mole ratio in the balanced equation, not on mass [1]; substances have different molar masses and coefficients, so each mass must be converted to moles and compared with the stoichiometric ratio [1].
Ethanol burns completely: C₂H₅OH(l) + 3O₂(g) → 2CO₂(g) + 3H₂O(l). Calculate the volume of O₂ at SLC (molar volume 24.8 L mol⁻¹) required to burn 2.30 g of ethanol (M = 46.0 g mol⁻¹). (3 marks)

25.0 mL of 0.400 mol L⁻¹ Pb(NO₃)₂ is mixed with 25.0 mL of 0.600 mol L⁻¹ KI: Pb²⁺(aq) + 2I⁻(aq) → PbI₂(s). Determine the limiting reactant, calculate the mass of PbI₂ (M = 461.0 g mol⁻¹) formed, and find the concentration of Pb²⁺ remaining in the final solution (assume volumes are additive). (4 marks)
Limestone is heated: CaCO₃(s) → CaO(s) + CO₂(g). The percentage yield of CaO is 80.0 %. Calculate the mass of CaCO₃ (M = 100.1 g mol⁻¹) required to obtain 5.61 g of CaO (M = 56.1 g mol⁻¹). (3 marks)

4.60 g of sodium (M = 23.0 g mol⁻¹) reacts with 0.150 mol of chlorine gas: 2Na(s) + Cl₂(g) → 2NaCl(s). Identify the limiting reactant and calculate the mass of NaCl (M = 58.5 g mol⁻¹) formed. (3 marks)
n(Na) = 4.60 ÷ 23.0 = 0.200 mol, which needs only 0.100 mol Cl₂ [1]; Cl₂ (0.150 mol) is in excess, so Na is the limiting reactant [1]; n(NaCl) = 0.200 mol, m = 0.200 × 58.5 = 11.7 g [1].
vce-chem12-gas-laws-and-molar-volume: What amount of nitrogen gas is present in 12.4 L of N₂ at SLC (25 °C and 100 kPa)?
n = V ÷ Vm = 12.4 ÷ 24.8 = 0.500 mol. 0.554 mol comes from using 22.4 L mol⁻¹, the molar volume at STP, instead of the SLC value.
What volume does 2.00 mol of methane gas occupy at STP (0 °C and 101.3 kPa)? (Vm = 22.4 L mol⁻¹)
V = n × Vm = 2.00 × 22.4 = 44.8 L. 49.6 L uses the SLC molar volume of 24.8 L mol⁻¹, and 11.2 L divides instead of multiplying.
A 300 mL sample of gas at 27 °C is cooled to −73 °C at constant pressure. What is its new volume?
Charles' law with kelvin temperatures: V₂ = 300 × 200 K ÷ 300 K = 200 mL. Using Celsius values gives a meaningless negative volume, and 450 mL inverts the temperature ratio.
A gas occupies 4.0 L at 100 kPa and 300 K. Its pressure is doubled to 200 kPa and its temperature is doubled to 600 K. What is the new volume?
V₂ = V₁ × (P₁ ÷ P₂) × (T₂ ÷ T₁) = 4.0 × ½ × 2 = 4.0 L. The halving from doubled pressure is cancelled by the doubling from doubled temperature.
What is the mass of 5.60 L of helium gas at STP? (Vm = 22.4 L mol⁻¹)
n = 5.60 ÷ 22.4 = 0.250 mol, so m = 0.250 × 4.00 = 1.00 g. 0.903 g comes from using 24.8 L mol⁻¹, which applies at SLC rather than STP.
What is the density of oxygen gas (O₂) at SLC, in g L⁻¹?
Density = M ÷ Vm = 32.0 ÷ 24.8 = 1.29 g L⁻¹. 0.775 g L⁻¹ inverts the ratio, and 32.0 is the molar mass, not a density.
In the reaction 2H₂(g) + O₂(g) → 2H₂O(g), what volume of oxygen reacts completely with 10 L of hydrogen, with all gases measured at the same temperature and pressure?
At the same T and P, gas volumes are in the same ratio as the mole ratio, so V(O₂) = ½ × 10 = 5.0 L. Assuming equal volumes (10 L) ignores the 2 : 1 coefficients.
A 500 mL flask holds a gas at 100 kPa and 300 K. Using R = 8.31 J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹ and kPa and L as pressure and volume units, what amount of gas is present?
Convert 500 mL to 0.500 L: n = PV ÷ RT = (100 × 0.500) ÷ (8.31 × 300) = 0.0201 mol. Using 500 directly for the volume gives 20.1 mol, which is 1000 times too large.
For a fixed amount of gas at constant temperature, which graph is a straight line passing through the origin?
Boyle's law gives PV = constant, so V is directly proportional to 1 ÷ P. A plot of P against V is a curve (hyperbola), not a straight line.
Why is the molar volume of a gas at SLC (24.8 L mol⁻¹) greater than at STP (22.4 L mol⁻¹)?
The gas molecules are larger at SLC
The gas has a greater number of molecules at SLC
The gas particles have a greater mass at SLC
The temperature is higher, so the gas particles move faster and spread further apart

A higher temperature (25 °C rather than 0 °C) gives more energetic collisions, so a mole of gas occupies a larger volume. A mole always contains the same number of particles, and particle size and mass do not change with temperature.
What volume of carbon dioxide at SLC is produced when 10.0 g of calcium carbonate reacts completely with excess hydrochloric acid? CaCO₃(s) + 2HCl(aq) → CaCl₂(aq) + H₂O(l) + CO₂(g)
n(CaCO₃) = 10.0 ÷ 100.1 = 0.0999 mol, equal to n(CO₂) (1 : 1), so V = 0.0999 × 24.8 = 2.48 L. 2.24 L results from using the STP molar volume.
Four gas samples are at the same temperature and pressure. Which contains the greatest number of molecules?

By Avogadro's hypothesis, the number of molecules is proportional to volume at the same T and P, so the largest volume (3.0 L) has the most. The identity, mass or molecular size of the gas does not matter.
A sealed rigid container of gas at 300 K has its pressure doubled by heating. What is the final temperature?
At constant volume P ∝ T (in kelvin), so doubling P gives T = 600 K = 327 °C. 600 °C wrongly doubles a Celsius value.
Calculate the volume occupied by 8.00 g of methane, CH₄, at SLC. (2 marks)
A 3.0 L sample of gas at 150 kPa is compressed at constant temperature to 1.2 L. Calculate the final pressure. (2 marks)
Boyle's law: P₁V₁ = P₂V₂ [1]; P₂ = 150 × 3.0 ÷ 1.2 = 375 kPa [1].
A 250 mL syringe of air at 15 °C is warmed to 45 °C at constant pressure. Calculate the final volume. (2 marks)
Temperatures in kelvin: T₁ = 288 K and T₂ = 318 K [1]; V₂ = 250 × 318 ÷ 288 = 276 mL [1].
A gas occupies 2.50 L at 27 °C and 200 kPa. Calculate its volume at 127 °C and 100 kPa. (3 marks)
Convert to kelvin: T₁ = 300 K, T₂ = 400 K [1]; combined gas law: P₁V₁ ÷ T₁ = P₂V₂ ÷ T₂ [1]; V₂ = 2.50 × (200 ÷ 100) × (400 ÷ 300) = 6.67 L [1].
Magnesium reacts with hydrochloric acid: Mg(s) + 2HCl(aq) → MgCl₂(aq) + H₂(g). Calculate the mass of magnesium needed to produce 2.48 L of hydrogen gas at SLC. (3 marks)
A sample of unknown gas has a mass of 1.50 g and occupies 1.00 L at 27 °C and 100 kPa. Calculate the molar mass of the gas. (R = 8.31 J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹) (3 marks)
Use the kinetic molecular theory to explain why the pressure of a fixed amount of gas increases when its volume is decreased at constant temperature. (2 marks)

With a smaller volume, the gas particles strike the container walls more frequently, as they have less distance to travel between collisions [1]; the average kinetic energy is unchanged (constant temperature), so the greater collision rate per unit area increases the pressure [1].
Explain why 1.0 L of hydrogen and 1.0 L of carbon dioxide at the same temperature and pressure contain the same number of molecules, even though CO₂ molecules are larger and heavier. (2 marks)

Gas particles are very far apart, so the volume of the gas is mostly empty space and the size of individual particles is negligible [1]; the volume of a gas therefore depends only on the number of particles (at fixed T and P), not on their identity (Avogadro's hypothesis) [1].

Propane burns according to: C₃H₈(g) + 5O₂(g) → 3CO₂(g) + 4H₂O(g). If 4.0 L of propane is burned completely, all gases being measured at the same temperature and pressure, calculate the volume of oxygen consumed and the volume of carbon dioxide produced. (3 marks)
At the same T and P, gas volumes are in the same ratio as the coefficients, so C₃H₈ : O₂ : CO₂ = 1 : 5 : 3 [1]; V(O₂) = 5 × 4.0 = 20 L [1]; V(CO₂) = 3 × 4.0 = 12 L [1].
vce-chem12-volumetric-analysis-and-titra: chem12a3-vt-9
What is a standard solution in volumetric analysis?
A solution whose concentration is accurately known
A solution that has been made up to exactly 1.00 L
A solution of a primary standard only
A solution with a pH of exactly 7

A standard solution has an accurately known concentration, so it can be used to determine the concentration of an unknown. It can be prepared from a primary standard or standardised against one, and it need not be neutral or 1.00 L.
chem12a3-vt-10
How should the volume be read from a burette containing a colourless solution?
At the top of the meniscus, with the eye above the liquid
At the bottom of the meniscus, with the eye level with the meniscus
At the bottom of the meniscus, with the eye looking down from above
At the top of the meniscus, with the eye level with the meniscus
The reading is taken at the bottom of the meniscus with the eye at the same level, which avoids parallax error. Reading from above or below makes the reading appear higher or lower than it really is.
chem12a3-vt-11
What is the difference between the end point and the equivalence point of a titration?
They are always the same point by definition
The end point is where the reactants are in exact stoichiometric ratio; the equivalence point is where the indicator changes colour
The equivalence point is where the reactants are in exact stoichiometric ratio; the end point is where the indicator changes colour
The end point occurs before the first drop of titrant is added

The equivalence point is the stoichiometric point calculated from the equation, while the end point is the observed colour change of the indicator. A good indicator makes the two very close, but they are not defined as identical.
chem12a3-vt-12
A 25.00 mL aliquot of HCl is titrated with 0.0800 mol L⁻¹ NaOH. The mean titre is 20.50 mL. What is the concentration of the HCl?
0.0328 mol L⁻¹
0.0976 mol L⁻¹
0.131 mol L⁻¹
0.0656 mol L⁻¹
n(NaOH) = 0.0800 × 0.02050 = 1.64 × 10⁻³ mol = n(HCl) (1:1); c(HCl) = 1.64 × 10⁻³ ÷ 0.02500 = 0.0656 mol L⁻¹. 0.0976 mol L⁻¹ comes from dividing by the titre instead of the aliquot volume.
chem12a3-vt-13
Just before a titration, a student rinses the conical flask with deionised water and leaves some water in it. What effect does this have on the calculated concentration of the analyte?
No effect, because the amount of analyte in the flask is unchanged
The concentration will be too high, because the titre is larger
The concentration will be too low, because the analyte is diluted
The concentration will be too low, because the titre is smaller

The extra water does not change the number of moles of analyte in the aliquot, so the same volume of titrant is needed to reach the end point. Dilution in the flask therefore does not affect the result.
chem12a3-vt-14
A student rinses the pipette with deionised water, not with the analyte solution, before measuring the aliquot. The calculated analyte concentration will be:
too high, because the titre is larger
too low, because the aliquot contains fewer moles of analyte
unchanged, because the pipette volume is fixed
too high, because the water adds to the moles of analyte
Residual water dilutes the aliquot, so it contains fewer moles of analyte than expected and the titre is smaller. The calculation assumes the original aliquot concentration, so the result is too low.
chem12a3-vt-15
An air bubble is trapped in the tip of a burette at the start of a titration and is dislodged and escapes during the titration. How is the calculated analyte concentration affected?
Too low, because less titrant was delivered than was read
Unchanged, because air has no mass
Too high, because the measured titre is larger than the volume of titrant actually delivered
Too low, because the titre is smaller than expected

Some of the volume read off the burette was air, so the recorded titre is larger than the volume of liquid delivered. This overestimates the moles of titrant and gives an analyte concentration that is too high.
chem12a3-vt-16
A 20.00 mL aliquot of Na₂CO₃ solution is titrated with 0.100 mol L⁻¹ HCl: Na₂CO₃(aq) + 2HCl(aq) → 2NaCl(aq) + H₂O(l) + CO₂(g). The mean titre is 24.00 mL. What is the concentration of the Na₂CO₃?
0.120 mol L⁻¹
0.0480 mol L⁻¹
0.0300 mol L⁻¹
0.0600 mol L⁻¹
chem12a3-vt-17
Which substance is the most suitable primary standard for making up a standard acid solution?
Anhydrous sodium carbonate
Solid sodium hydroxide
Concentrated hydrochloric acid
Potassium permanganate

Anhydrous sodium carbonate is pure, stable, non-hygroscopic and has a known formula. Sodium hydroxide absorbs water and CO₂, and concentrated hydrochloric acid loses HCl gas, so neither has a reliably known amount.
chem12a3-vt-18
1.325 g of anhydrous Na₂CO₃ (M = 106.0 g mol⁻¹) is dissolved in water and made up to 250.0 mL in a volumetric flask. What is the concentration of the solution?
0.0125 mol L⁻¹
0.0500 mol L⁻¹
0.0100 mol L⁻¹
n = 1.325 ÷ 106.0 = 0.0125 mol; c = 0.0125 ÷ 0.2500 = 0.0500 mol L⁻¹. 0.0125 is the number of moles, not the concentration, because the volume was not used.
chem12a3-vt-19
Ammonia solution is titrated with hydrochloric acid. Which indicator is more suitable, and why?
Phenolphthalein, because its colour change is at pH 8.3–10.0
Either indicator, because the equivalence point is at pH 7
Phenolphthalein, because ammonia is a base
Methyl orange, because the solution at equivalence contains NH₄⁺ and is acidic

At equivalence the solution contains NH₄⁺, a weak acid, so the pH is below 7 and methyl orange (pH 3.1–4.4) changes colour in the steep region. Phenolphthalein would change colour well before the equivalence point is reached.
chem12a3-vt-20
Four titres are recorded: 23.60 mL, 22.45 mL, 22.40 mL and 22.50 mL. The first is a rough titre. What mean titre should be used in the calculation?
The rough titre is discarded and the concordant titres (22.45, 22.40, 22.50 mL, all within 0.10 mL) are averaged to give 22.45 mL. 22.74 mL results from including the rough titre.
chem12a3-vt-21
A 20.00 mL aliquot of KOH solution is titrated with 0.0500 mol L⁻¹ H₂SO₄. The mean titre is 15.60 mL. What is the concentration of the KOH? (H₂SO₄(aq) + 2KOH(aq) → K₂SO₄(aq) + 2H₂O(l))
0.0390 mol L⁻¹
0.0780 mol L⁻¹
0.156 mol L⁻¹
0.0641 mol L⁻¹
chem12a3-vt-22
Why should only a few drops of indicator be added to the analyte in the conical flask?
More indicator makes the colour change impossible to see
Indicators only work in very small amounts of water
Indicators are weak acids or bases, so a larger amount would react with the titrant and alter the titre
The indicator would otherwise change the concentration of the standard solution
Most indicators are themselves weak acids or bases, so excess indicator consumes some titrant and gives a titre that is too large. The amount is kept small to make this effect negligible.
chem12a3-vt-23
Describe how the burette, the pipette and the conical flask should each be rinsed before a titration, and justify the choice for the conical flask. (3 marks)

Burette is rinsed with a small amount of the titrant (standard solution) [1]; pipette is rinsed with a small amount of the analyte solution it will measure [1]; conical flask is rinsed with deionised water only, because the water does not change the moles of analyte in the aliquot, whereas rinsing with analyte would add extra moles and make the titre too large [1].
chem12a3-vt-24
Explain why a rough titration is carried out first and why further titres must be concordant. (2 marks)

The rough titre gives an approximate end point so that later titrations can add titrant dropwise near the end point for accuracy [1]; concordant titres (within 0.10 mL) show that the results are reproducible and that random errors are small, so the mean is reliable [1].
chem12a3-vt-25
Distinguish between the accuracy and the precision of a titration result, and explain how a titration could be precise but not accurate. (3 marks)

Accuracy is how close the result is to the true value [1]; precision is how close repeated measurements (titres) are to each other [1]; a systematic error, such as a burette not rinsed with titrant or a consistently misread meniscus, shifts all titres the same way so they are concordant (precise) but the result is wrong (inaccurate) [1].
chem12a3-vt-26

10.00 mL of household ammonia (NH₃) cleaner is diluted to 500.0 mL in a volumetric flask. 25.00 mL aliquots of the diluted solution are titrated with 0.0950 mol L⁻¹ HCl, giving a mean titre of 21.30 mL. NH₃(aq) + HCl(aq) → NH₄Cl(aq). Calculate the concentration of NH₃ in the original cleaner in mol L⁻¹ and g L⁻¹ (M(NH₃) = 17.0 g mol⁻¹). (4 marks)
chem12a3-vt-27

Explain why bromothymol blue (colour change pH 6.0–7.6) is suitable for the titration of hydrochloric acid with sodium hydroxide, and why the choice of indicator is less critical for this titration than for ethanoic acid with sodium hydroxide. (3 marks)

The equivalence point of a strong acid with a strong base is at pH 7, which lies within the range of bromothymol blue [1]; the pH changes very steeply (from about 3 to 11) near equivalence, so a drop of titrant moves the pH through the whole range of the indicator [1]; therefore several indicators (such as phenolphthalein or methyl orange) give a nearly identical titre, whereas a weak acid has a smaller, higher-pH steep region so only some indicators are suitable [1].
chem12a3-vt-28

0.6300 g of oxalic acid dihydrate, H₂C₂O₄·2H₂O (M = 126.0 g mol⁻¹), is dissolved and made up to 100.0 mL. A 20.00 mL aliquot is titrated with NaOH solution and the mean titre is 19.40 mL. H₂C₂O₄(aq) + 2NaOH(aq) → Na₂C₂O₄(aq) + 2H₂O(l). Calculate the concentration of the NaOH. (4 marks)
chem12a3-vt-29
Outline the steps for preparing 250.0 mL of a standard solution from a solid primary standard using a volumetric flask. (4 marks)

Accurately weigh the required mass of the primary standard (for example by difference) [1]; dissolve it in a beaker with deionised water, then transfer the solution to the volumetric flask, rinsing the beaker and funnel into the flask [1]; add deionised water until the bottom of the meniscus sits on the calibration mark at eye level [1]; stopper and invert the flask several times to mix thoroughly [1].
vce-chem12-gravimetric-analysis: chem12a3-ga-9
Gravimetric analysis determines the amount of an analyte by:
measuring the volume of a standard solution needed to react with it
converting it to a pure solid of known formula and measuring its mass
measuring the intensity of light absorbed by its solution
measuring the electrical conductivity of its solution

In gravimetric analysis the analyte is isolated as a pure, stable solid and weighed, and its amount is calculated from that mass. Measuring a volume of reagent describes titration, not gravimetric analysis.
chem12a3-ga-10
Which solution could be added to a water sample to precipitate sulfate ions for gravimetric analysis?
sodium nitrate
potassium chloride
barium chloride
hydrochloric acid
Ba²⁺ forms insoluble BaSO₄ with sulfate ions. Sodium nitrate, potassium chloride and hydrochloric acid contain no cation that forms an insoluble sulfate.
chem12a3-ga-11
In a gravimetric analysis, the clear liquid that passes through the filter paper is called the:
residue
precipitate
supernatant solid
filtrate
The filtrate is the liquid that passes through the filter paper. The precipitate (residue) is the solid that is retained on the paper.
chem12a3-ga-12
Excess sodium carbonate solution is added to a solution of calcium chloride and 0.250 g of dry CaCO₃ (M = 100.1 g mol⁻¹) is collected. What mass of calcium (M = 40.1 g mol⁻¹) was in the solution?
n(CaCO₃) = 0.250 ÷ 100.1 = 2.50 × 10⁻³ mol = n(Ca²⁺); m(Ca) = 2.50 × 10⁻³ × 40.1 = 0.100 g. 0.250 g is the mass of the whole precipitate, which includes carbonate.
chem12a3-ga-13

A sample containing sodium chloride is dissolved in water and treated with excess silver nitrate, giving 1.434 g of dry AgCl (M = 143.4 g mol⁻¹). What mass of NaCl (M = 58.5 g mol⁻¹) was in the sample?
n(AgCl) = 1.434 ÷ 143.4 = 0.0100 mol = n(NaCl); m(NaCl) = 0.0100 × 58.5 = 0.585 g. 0.355 g is the mass of chloride only, not NaCl.
chem12a3-ga-14
Which of the following is NOT a requirement for a precipitate used in gravimetric analysis?
It has a very low solubility in the solution
It has a known, fixed formula
It is stable when dried
It is soluble in water so that it is easy to wash
The precipitate must be insoluble so that essentially none is lost in the filtrate or during washing. Being soluble in water would make it unsuitable.
chem12a3-ga-15
A crucible is heated, cooled and weighed repeatedly until its mass is constant before it is used to collect a precipitate. This is done so that:
the crucible mass does not change during the experiment
the crucible becomes coated with a layer of precipitate
the precipitate dissolves more easily
the crucible reacts with the analyte

A crucible at constant mass will not gain or lose mass (for example, by losing moisture) during heating, so any later mass change comes from the precipitate. It has nothing to do with dissolving the precipitate.
chem12a3-ga-16
During transfer, some of the precipitate is left behind in the beaker and is not collected on the filter paper. The calculated percentage of the analyte in the sample will be:
too high, because the filtrate contains extra solid
unaffected, because the precipitate is still produced
too high, because the beaker adds mass
too low, because the measured mass of precipitate is less than the actual mass
Lost precipitate means a smaller mass is weighed, so the calculated amount of analyte is too low. The reaction still produced the full amount, but it was not all weighed.
chem12a3-ga-17

A 0.500 g sample containing barium is dissolved and excess sulfate ions are added. The dried BaSO₄ (M = 233.4 g mol⁻¹) has a mass of 0.2334 g. What is the percentage by mass of barium (M = 137.3 g mol⁻¹) in the sample?
n(BaSO₄) = 0.2334 ÷ 233.4 = 1.000 × 10⁻³ mol = n(Ba); m(Ba) = 0.1373 g; % = 0.1373 ÷ 0.500 × 100 = 27.5 %. 58.8 % is the percentage of barium in pure BaSO₄, not in the sample.
chem12a3-ga-18
After filtering a BaSO₄ precipitate, a student wants to check that all the sulfate has been precipitated. The best test is to:
add a few more drops of barium chloride to the filtrate and see whether more precipitate forms
heat the filtrate until it boils dry
add sodium hydroxide to the filtrate
weigh the filtrate
If no further precipitate forms when more Ba²⁺ is added to the filtrate, no sulfate remains and precipitation was complete. Weighing or boiling the filtrate does not show whether sulfate ions remain.
chem12a3-ga-19
Excess potassium iodide is added to 50.0 mL of lead(II) nitrate solution, producing 0.461 g of dry PbI₂ (M = 461.0 g mol⁻¹). What was the concentration of Pb²⁺ in the original solution?
0.0100 mol L⁻¹
0.0200 mol L⁻¹
0.0400 mol L⁻¹
n(PbI₂) = 0.461 ÷ 461.0 = 1.00 × 10⁻³ mol = n(Pb²⁺); c = 1.00 × 10⁻³ ÷ 0.0500 = 0.0200 mol L⁻¹. Doubling the answer wrongly applies a 2:1 ratio, but Pb²⁺ and PbI₂ are in a 1:1 ratio.
chem12a3-ga-20
A precipitate is dried, cooled and weighed repeatedly, giving masses of 0.512 g, 0.498 g, 0.497 g and 0.497 g. Which statement is correct?
The precipitate has reached constant mass and 0.497 g should be used
The precipitate should be dried until the mass reaches 0.512 g
The precipitate has not reached constant mass because the values are not all the same
The average of all four masses should be used

The last two masses agree, which shows all the water has been removed, so 0.497 g is the dry mass. Averaging includes the earlier masses of a still-damp precipitate and gives a value that is too high.
chem12a3-ga-21
A 5.00 g sample of a hydrated salt is heated to constant mass, leaving 4.10 g of anhydrous solid. What is the percentage by mass of water in the hydrated salt?
Mass of water lost = 5.00 − 4.10 = 0.90 g; % = 0.90 ÷ 5.00 × 100 = 18.0 %. 22.0 % divides by the mass of the anhydrous solid instead of the original hydrated sample.
chem12a3-ga-22
Explain why a precipitate is washed with distilled water before it is dried and weighed in a gravimetric analysis. (2 marks)

Washing removes soluble impurities (such as excess precipitating reagent or spectator ions) that are stuck to the surface of the precipitate [1]; if left, these would dry onto the precipitate, adding mass and making the calculated amount of analyte too high [1].
chem12a3-ga-23
Outline the main steps in a gravimetric analysis to determine the percentage of chloride in a solid salt sample. (4 marks)

Accurately weigh the sample and dissolve it in distilled water [1]; add excess silver nitrate solution so that all chloride ions precipitate as AgCl [1]; filter the mixture and wash the precipitate with distilled water [1]; dry the precipitate to constant mass, weigh it and use the mole ratio n(Cl⁻) = n(AgCl) to calculate the percentage of chloride [1].
chem12a3-ga-24

A 1.250 g sample of a salt mixture containing sodium chloride is dissolved in water and excess silver nitrate solution is added. The dried precipitate of AgCl has a mass of 2.868 g. Calculate the percentage by mass of NaCl in the sample. (M(AgCl) = 143.4 g mol⁻¹; M(NaCl) = 58.5 g mol⁻¹) (4 marks)
chem12a3-ga-25

Excess sodium carbonate solution is added to a 25.0 mL sample of calcium chloride solution. The dried CaCO₃ precipitate has a mass of 0.350 g. Calculate the concentration of Ca²⁺ in the original solution in mol L⁻¹. (M(CaCO₃) = 100.1 g mol⁻¹) (3 marks)
chem12a3-ga-26
4.92 g of hydrated magnesium sulfate, MgSO₄·xH₂O, is heated to constant mass, leaving 2.40 g of anhydrous MgSO₄ (M = 120.4 g mol⁻¹). Determine the value of x. (M(H₂O) = 18.0 g mol⁻¹) (3 marks)
chem12a3-ga-27
A student adds too little precipitating agent to a sample solution in a gravimetric analysis. Explain the effect on the calculated mass of analyte in the sample. (2 marks)

Not all of the analyte ions are precipitated, because the precipitating agent is the limiting reactant [1]; the mass of precipitate is lower than it should be, so the calculated mass of analyte is too low [1].
chem12a3-ga-28

A student heats a precipitate in a crucible and records masses of 18.642 g, then 18.615 g, then 18.598 g after successive heating and cooling. Explain what these results show and describe what the student should do next. (3 marks)

The mass is still decreasing, so the precipitate has not reached constant mass and still contains water [1]; the student should reheat the precipitate and cool it in a desiccator to prevent water being reabsorbed [1]; then reweigh, repeating until two successive masses agree [1].
chem12a3-ga-29
State two properties that a precipitate must have to be suitable for gravimetric analysis and explain why each is needed. (2 marks)

It must be very insoluble, so that almost none is lost in the filtrate or during washing [1]; it must have a known formula (composition), so that the amount of analyte can be calculated from its mass [1].
chem12a3-ga-30

Excess silver nitrate solution is added to a 250.0 mL sample of river water. The washed and dried AgCl precipitate has a mass of 0.0287 g. Calculate the concentration of chloride ions in the river water in mg L⁻¹. (M(AgCl) = 143.4 g mol⁻¹; M(Cl) = 35.5 g mol⁻¹) (4 marks)
vce-chem12-colorimetry-and-uv-visible-sp: chem12a3-cu-9
Which range of wavelengths corresponds to visible light?
Visible light spans roughly 400–700 nm. Wavelengths below 400 nm are ultraviolet, and those above 700 nm are infrared.
chem12a3-cu-10
A dye solution within the linear range of a spectrophotometer has an absorbance of 0.80. A 10.0 mL portion is diluted to 20.0 mL with water. What absorbance is expected for the diluted solution?
Diluting by a factor of 2 halves the concentration, and absorbance is proportional to concentration, so A = 0.40. 1.6 comes from multiplying instead of dividing by the dilution factor.
chem12a3-cu-11
What are the units of absorbance?
mol L⁻¹
nm
It has no units
cm⁻¹
Absorbance is a logarithm of a ratio of light intensities, so it is dimensionless. Wavelength is measured in nm, which is a different quantity.
chem12a3-cu-12
Why is a quartz cuvette, rather than a glass or plastic one, required for measurements in the ultraviolet region?
Quartz is cheaper and easier to clean
Quartz scatters light, which increases sensitivity
Quartz absorbs visible light, which removes interference
Quartz is transparent to UV radiation, whereas glass and most plastics absorb it
Glass and most plastics absorb UV radiation, so they would block the beam and give false absorbances. Quartz transmits UV and visible light.
chem12a3-cu-13
Which statement correctly distinguishes a UV-visible spectrophotometer from a simple colorimeter?
A colorimeter measures emitted light, whereas a spectrophotometer measures absorbed light
A colorimeter works only on colourless solutions
A spectrophotometer cannot be used with a calibration curve
A spectrophotometer can select any wavelength across the UV and visible range, whereas a colorimeter uses a few fixed filters in the visible range

A spectrophotometer uses a monochromator to select any wavelength, including UV, while a colorimeter typically uses filters or LEDs for a few visible wavelengths. Both measure absorbance and both use calibration curves.
chem12a3-cu-14
When a calibration curve is plotted for a colorimetric analysis, which choice is standard?
Concentration on the y-axis and absorbance on the x-axis
Absorbance on the y-axis and concentration of the standards on the x-axis
Absorbance on the y-axis and wavelength on the x-axis
Transmittance on the y-axis and time on the x-axis
Absorbance (measured response) is plotted against the known concentration of the standards. Absorbance against wavelength is an absorption spectrum, not a calibration curve.
chem12a3-cu-15
Which of the following ions in aqueous solution could NOT be determined directly by visible colorimetry, without first reacting it to form a coloured species?
Cu²⁺ (blue)
MnO₄⁻ (purple)
Zn²⁺ (colourless)
Cr₂O₇²⁻ (orange)
Zn²⁺(aq) does not absorb visible light, so a reagent must be added to make a coloured complex. The other ions already absorb strongly in the visible region.
chem12a3-cu-16
A solution is measured and found to have an absorbance of 0 at the chosen wavelength, relative to a blank. This means that:
the sample absorbs no more light at that wavelength than the blank does
the sample absorbs all of the light at that wavelength
the concentration of the sample is 1.0 mol L⁻¹
the instrument has failed
An absorbance of 0 means the same intensity is transmitted as for the blank, so the analyte absorbs no measurable light. Total absorption would give a very large absorbance, not zero.
chem12a3-cu-17
What is plotted on the axes of a UV-visible absorption spectrum?
Concentration against absorbance
Absorbance against time
Wavelength against concentration
Absorbance against wavelength
An absorption spectrum shows how absorbance varies with wavelength, and the peak gives λmax. Absorbance against concentration is a calibration curve.
chem12a3-cu-18
Another species in a water sample absorbs light at the same wavelength as the analyte being measured. How will this affect the calculated concentration of the analyte?
It will be too low, because less analyte absorbs light
It will be too high, because the measured absorbance includes the other species
It will be unaffected, because only the analyte is coloured
It will be zero
Absorbances from different species at the same wavelength add together, so the reading is higher than the analyte alone would give. This overestimates the concentration.
chem12a3-cu-19
A student prepares standards and measures them in 1.0 cm cuvettes, but measures the sample in a 2.0 cm cuvette. The sample concentration read from the calibration curve will be:
half the true value
unchanged, since concentration does not depend on cuvette
about double the true value
zero, as the beam cannot pass through
Absorbance is proportional to path length, so doubling the path doubles the absorbance and the concentration read from the curve. Halving would occur only if the path were shorter.
chem12a3-cu-20
Why should a cuvette be held only by its frosted (non-optical) sides?
Fingerprints on the clear faces absorb and scatter light, giving a falsely high absorbance
The frosted sides contain the sample
Oil from fingers reacts with the analyte to change its colour
The frosted sides are the only ones that are sterile
Marks, smudges and fingerprints on the clear faces scatter and absorb the beam, adding to the absorbance. They do not change the chemistry of the analyte.
chem12a3-cu-21
Compared with visible light, ultraviolet radiation has:
longer wavelength and higher energy per photon
longer wavelength and lower energy per photon
the same energy but a lower frequency
shorter wavelength and higher energy per photon

UV radiation has wavelengths below about 400 nm, and energy is inversely related to wavelength, so each photon carries more energy. Higher energy is why UV can excite electrons in many colourless compounds.
chem12a3-cu-22
Describe how a student could prepare 100.0 mL of a 20 mg L⁻¹ standard solution from a 100 mg L⁻¹ stock solution. Include the volume of stock required. (3 marks)

Use c₁V₁ = c₂V₂: V₁ = 20 × 100.0 ÷ 100 = 20 mL of stock required [1]. Measure 20.0 mL of the stock accurately using a pipette (or burette) and transfer it to a 100.0 mL volumetric flask [1]. Add deionised water up to the mark, stopper and invert several times to mix thoroughly [1].
chem12a3-cu-23

Standard solutions of 0.50, 1.0, 1.5 and 2.0 mmol L⁻¹ of a coloured complex give absorbances of 0.12, 0.24, 0.36 and 0.48 respectively. A 25.0 mL sample gives an absorbance of 0.30. Calculate the amount, in mol, of the complex in the 25.0 mL sample. (3 marks)
The calibration is linear through the origin with a slope of 0.24 per mmol L⁻¹ (0.12 ÷ 0.50) [1]. c = 0.30 ÷ 0.24 = 1.25 mmol L⁻¹ [1]. n = 1.25 × 10⁻³ mol L⁻¹ × 0.0250 L = 3.1 × 10⁻⁵ mol [1].
chem12a3-cu-24
A colourless analyte is to be determined by visible colorimetry. Explain why it is first reacted with a reagent, and why the amount of reagent is controlled. (2 marks)

The reagent reacts with the analyte to form a coloured species that absorbs in the visible region, so absorbance can be measured [1]. The reagent is added in excess/fixed amounts so that all the analyte reacts and the colour intensity (absorbance) is proportional to the analyte concentration [1].
chem12a3-cu-25

A calibration graph of absorbance against concentration curves towards the horizontal axis at high concentrations. Explain why this limits the analysis and state what should be done with a sample of high concentration. (2 marks)

The absorbance is no longer proportional to concentration at high concentrations, so the calibration is unreliable beyond the linear range and concentrations cannot be read accurately [1]. The sample should be diluted by a known factor so that its absorbance falls within the linear range, then the dilution factor is applied to the result [1].
chem12a3-cu-26

A 0.500 g sample of brass is dissolved and made up to 250.0 mL. A 1.00 mL aliquot is diluted to 100.0 mL and its copper concentration is determined by colorimetry. A calibration line through the origin has a slope of 0.040 absorbance units per mg L⁻¹, and the diluted solution has an absorbance of 0.48. Calculate the percentage of copper by mass in the brass. (4 marks)

Concentration of diluted solution = 0.48 ÷ 0.040 = 12 mg L⁻¹ [1]. Dilution factor = 100.0 ÷ 1.00 = 100, so the 250.0 mL solution is 1200 mg L⁻¹ [1]. Mass of Cu = 1200 mg L⁻¹ × 0.2500 L = 300 mg [1]. % Cu = 300 ÷ 500 × 100 = 60% [1].
chem12a3-cu-27
State two precautions that should be taken when filling and placing a cuvette in a spectrophotometer to ensure accurate absorbance readings. (2 marks)

Rinse the cuvette with a small amount of the solution to be measured, and avoid air bubbles in the light path [1]. Wipe the clear faces clean and handle only by the frosted sides; place the cuvette in the same orientation each time [1].
chem12a3-cu-28
An aqueous solution of potassium permanganate appears purple. Explain this observation in terms of the light absorbed and transmitted by the solution. (3 marks)

White light contains all visible wavelengths, and the solution absorbs light of some wavelengths (mainly green, around 530 nm) as electrons are promoted to higher energy levels [1]. The remaining wavelengths (red and blue/violet) are transmitted [1]. The transmitted light combines to give the complementary colour, so the solution appears purple [1].
chem12a3-cu-29
State how absorbance depends on the concentration of the analyte and on the path length of the cuvette, for a dilute solution at a fixed wavelength. (2 marks)
Absorbance is directly proportional to the concentration of the absorbing species [1]. Absorbance is also directly proportional to the path length of the cuvette [1].
vce-chem12-greenhouse-gases-and-ocean-ac: Without the natural greenhouse effect, Earth's average surface temperature would be closest to:
Greenhouse gases raise the average from about −18 °C to about 15 °C. 15 °C is the actual present average, not the value without the effect.
The main reason atmospheric CO₂ concentration has risen since the Industrial Revolution is:
a decrease in the Sun's output
combustion of fossil fuels and land clearing
Burning coal, oil and gas and clearing forests release CO₂ faster than natural sinks remove it. Photosynthesis removes CO₂, so more of it would lower, not raise, the concentration.
Methane burns according to CH₄(g) + 2O₂(g) → CO₂(g) + 2H₂O(l). What mass of CO₂ is produced by the complete combustion of 16.0 g of methane? (M(CH₄) = 16.0 g mol⁻¹, M(CO₂) = 44.0 g mol⁻¹)
n(CH₄) = 16.0 ÷ 16.0 = 1.00 mol, the mole ratio is 1 : 1, so n(CO₂) = 1.00 mol and m = 1.00 × 44.0 = 44.0 g. Giving 16.0 g wrongly assumes mass is conserved between methane and CO₂.
Octane burns completely: 2C₈H₁₈(l) + 25O₂(g) → 16CO₂(g) + 18H₂O(l). What mass of CO₂ forms from 57.0 g of octane? (M(C₈H₁₈) = 114.0 g mol⁻¹, M(CO₂) = 44.0 g mol⁻¹)
n(C₈H₁₈) = 57.0 ÷ 114.0 = 0.500 mol; the ratio is 2 : 16, so n(CO₂) = 4.00 mol and m = 4.00 × 44.0 = 176 g. Forgetting the 8 : 1 ratio gives only 0.500 mol of CO₂ (22.0 g).
The surface ocean has a pH of 8.1. What is [H₃O⁺] in this seawater?
[H₃O⁺] = 10⁻⁸·¹ = 7.9 × 10⁻⁹ M. The pH value is a negative logarithm, so it cannot be written directly as the exponent coefficient.
Scientists describe the ocean as undergoing 'acidification' even though its pH is about 8.1. This is because:
the ocean's pH is below 7 and it is already acidic
pH is falling, so seawater is becoming less basic (moving towards neutral)
CO₂ is converted into strong acids in the water
Seawater is still slightly basic (pH above 7), but its pH is decreasing as [H₃O⁺] rises. Dissolved CO₂ forms only a weak acid, and the ocean has not become acidic.
An increase in atmospheric CO₂ partial pressure shifts the equilibrium CO₂(g) ⇌ CO₂(aq) so that:
more CO₂ dissolves in seawater, because the system partly opposes the increase in CO₂(g)
there is no change, because the ocean is very large
By Le Chatelier's principle the system shifts right to consume some added CO₂(g). K depends only on temperature, so it does not change.
Compared with cold polar water, warm tropical surface water can hold less dissolved CO₂. This is because the solubility of a gas in water generally:
depends only on the salt content
Gas solubility falls as temperature rises, so warming oceans can absorb less CO₂. Saying it is independent of temperature ignores the endothermic loss of gas from solution on heating.
Which human activity is a major source of nitrous oxide, N₂O?
Use of nitrogen-based fertilisers on farmland
Microbial processes in soil acting on nitrogen fertilisers release N₂O. Livestock and rice paddies are mainly methane sources, and coal combustion mainly releases CO₂.
As CO₂ dissolves in seawater, the concentration of hydrogencarbonate ions, HCO₃⁻:
decreases, because it is converted to CO₃²⁻
decreases, because it is converted to CO₂ gas
increases, because carbonic acid ionises and carbonate reacts with H₃O⁺
Both H₂CO₃ ionising and CO₃²⁻ reacting with H₃O⁺ produce HCO₃⁻, so [HCO₃⁻] rises while [CO₃²⁻] falls. The shift is in the opposite direction to the carbonate change.
What volume does 22.0 g of CO₂ occupy at SLC (25 °C and 100 kPa, molar volume 24.8 L mol⁻¹)? (M(CO₂) = 44.0 g mol⁻¹)
n = 22.0 ÷ 44.0 = 0.500 mol, so V = 0.500 × 24.8 = 12.4 L. Using 22.0 as the number of litres confuses mass with moles.
Earth's surface radiates mainly infrared rather than visible light because:
greenhouse gases convert visible light to infrared
infrared is the only radiation that reaches Earth
the surface is much cooler than the Sun
the atmosphere absorbs all visible light

The wavelengths emitted by an object depend on its temperature, so the cool Earth emits infrared while the hot Sun emits mostly visible light. Greenhouse gases absorb that infrared rather than creating it.
The global warming potential (GWP) of methane over 100 years is about 28. How many tonnes of CO₂-equivalent are represented by 2.0 tonnes of methane released?
CO₂-e = 2.0 × 28 = 56 t. Dividing by 28 reverses the relationship and gives 0.071 t.
The pH of surface seawater is predicted to fall from 8.2 to 7.9. By what factor does [H₃O⁺] change? (3 marks)
[H₃O⁺] = 10⁻ᵖᴴ, so initial [H₃O⁺] = 10⁻⁸·² = 6.3 × 10⁻⁹ M [1]; final [H₃O⁺] = 10⁻⁷·⁹ = 1.3 × 10⁻⁸ M [1]; the ratio is 10⁰·³ ≈ 2.0, so [H₃O⁺] doubles [1].
Identify one human activity that releases each of the following greenhouse gases: CO₂, CH₄ and N₂O. (3 marks)
CO₂: burning fossil fuels (or land clearing) [1]; CH₄: livestock digestion, landfill or rice paddies (or gas leaks) [1]; N₂O: use of nitrogen-based fertilisers (or some industrial processes) [1].
Propane burns completely in air. Calculate the volume of CO₂ produced at SLC (molar volume 24.8 L mol⁻¹) when 5.00 g of propane, C₃H₈, is burned. (M(C₃H₈) = 44.0 g mol⁻¹) (4 marks)
vce-bio12-cell-theory-and-cell-size: bio12a1-ct-9
In Louis Pasteur's swan-neck flask experiment, broth in a flask with a long curved neck stayed free of microbial growth while the neck remained intact. What did this result support?
Microorganisms arise spontaneously from the nutrient broth itself.
Microorganisms need light to grow in nutrient broth.
Microorganisms in the broth came from pre-existing microorganisms carried into it from the air.
Heating the broth creates new microorganisms within it.

Broth in the intact swan-neck flask stayed sterile while air could still reach it, so the microbes must have come from pre-existing microbes rather than arising spontaneously in the broth. Spontaneous generation is the tempting but incorrect idea that the experiment disproved.
bio12a1-ct-10
Which cube-shaped cell has the highest surface area to volume ratio?
A cube with a side length of 1 µm
A cube with a side length of 5 µm
A cube with a side length of 10 µm
A cube with a side length of 20 µm
For a cube, SA:V = 6 ÷ side length, so the 1 µm cube has 6:1 while the 20 µm cube has only 0.3:1. Choosing the largest cube because it has the most surface area ignores that its volume grows faster.
bio12a1-ct-11
A student claims that doubling the side length of a cube-shaped cell doubles its surface area to volume ratio. Which statement correctly evaluates this claim?
The claim is correct, because the surface area and the volume both double.
The claim is incorrect, because the SA:V ratio halves when the side length doubles.
The claim is incorrect, but only because the shape of the cell has changed.
The claim is incorrect, because the SA:V ratio is multiplied by four when the side length doubles.

For a cube, SA:V = 6 ÷ side length, so doubling the side length halves the ratio. Surface area rises by a factor of four and volume by a factor of eight, so they do not increase together. The shape of the cell stays the same when it is scaled up.
bio12a1-ct-12
A cube-shaped cell has a surface area of 54 µm². What is its surface area to volume ratio?

A surface area of 54 µm² gives 6s² = 54, so the side length is 3 µm and the volume is 27 µm³. Then 54 ÷ 27 = 2:1. A 6:1 ratio is the constant from the surface area formula, 1:2 inverts the ratio, and 3:1 is the side length rather than the ratio.
bio12a1-ct-13
A cube-shaped cell has a volume of 0.125 µm³. What is its surface area to volume ratio?

A volume of 0.125 µm³ gives a side length of 0.5 µm, so the surface area is 6 × 0.5² = 1.5 µm² and 1.5 ÷ 0.125 = 12. The 24:1 result comes from not squaring the side length in the surface area, and 1:12 inverts the ratio.
bio12a1-ct-14
A cube-shaped cell grows in side length from 2 µm to 6 µm while keeping its shape. By what factor does its volume increase?
Volume scales with the cube of the side length, so the increase is (6 ÷ 2)³ = 3³ = 27 times. Multiplying by 9 treats volume as if it scaled with area, while 3 uses only the linear increase in length.
bio12a1-ct-15
Which value is the best estimate of the diameter of a typical animal cell?
100 nm
1 mm
10 cm
Typical eukaryotic cells are around 10–100 µm across, so 10–30 µm is a good estimate. A diameter of 100 nm is about the size of a virus, while 1 mm is large enough to see without a microscope.
bio12a1-ct-16
A cell measures 0.02 mm across. What is its diameter in micrometres?
2 µm
200 µm
20 µm
There are 1000 µm in 1 mm, so 0.02 mm × 1000 = 20 µm. Dividing by 1000 gives 2 µm, leaving the number unchanged gives 0.02 µm, and multiplying by 10 000 gives 200 µm.
bio12a1-ct-17
A rectangular box-shaped cell measures 1 µm × 1 µm × 10 µm. What is its surface area to volume ratio?

The surface area is 2(1 × 1 + 1 × 10 + 1 × 10) = 42 µm² and the volume is 1 × 1 × 10 = 10 µm³, so SA:V = 4.2:1. Counting each pair of faces only once gives 2.1:1, treating the box as a 1 µm cube gives 6:1, and inverting the ratio gives 0.24:1.
bio12a1-ct-18
Which development allowed scientists to see fine internal structures of cells, such as membranes and ribosomes, in detail?
The compound light microscope
The electron microscope
The simple magnifying lens used by van Leeuwenhoek
The X-ray diffraction camera

Light microscopes cannot resolve structures smaller than about 200 nm, which includes membranes and ribosomes, while electron microscopes can. The light microscope was essential for cell theory but cannot show these details, and X-ray diffraction is used to study molecular structure rather than to image cells.
bio12a1-ct-19
Which of these cells is typically the smallest in diameter?
A human egg cell
A human red blood cell
A typical bacterium
A typical plant palisade cell

Typical bacteria are about 1–5 µm across, which is smaller than a human red blood cell (around 7–8 µm) or a plant palisade cell (tens of micrometres). A human egg cell is one of the largest human cells, at about 100 µm in diameter.
bio12a1-ct-20
Which two scientists, working in 1838 and 1839, proposed that plants and animals are both made of cells?
Hooke and van Leeuwenhoek
Redi and Pasteur
Watson and Crick
Schleiden and Schwann

Schleiden studied plants and Schwann studied animals, and together they proposed that living things are made of cells. Hooke and van Leeuwenhoek made the first observations of cells and microorganisms, Redi and Pasteur disproved spontaneous generation, and Watson and Crick described the structure of DNA in 1953.
bio12a1-ct-21
A single cube of side 2 µm and eight separate cubes of side 1 µm have the same total volume. Which statement is correct?
The eight 1 µm cubes have a total surface area of 48 µm² and a combined SA:V of 6:1, twice the 3:1 of the single cube.
The single 2 µm cube has a total surface area of 48 µm² and an SA:V of 6:1, because it is one larger object.
Both arrangements have an SA:V of 3:1, because their total volumes are the same.
The eight 1 µm cubes have a total surface area of 24 µm², the same as the single cube.

Each 1 µm cube has 6 µm² of surface, so the eight cubes have 48 µm², while the single 2 µm cube has 24 µm². Dividing by the shared total volume of 8 µm³ gives 6:1 and 3:1 respectively, so dividing a cell into smaller pieces increases the membrane available per unit of cytoplasm.
bio12a1-ct-22
Which tool is used to calibrate the scale of an eyepiece graticule so that cell dimensions can be measured?
A thermometer
A stage micrometer
A pH meter
A digital balance

A stage micrometer is a slide with a known scale, and comparing it with the eyepiece graticule at each magnification gives the size of each graticule unit. A thermometer, a pH meter and a balance do not measure length under a microscope.
bio12a1-ct-23
Cell P is a cube of side 2 µm. Cell Q is a box measuring 1 µm × 2 µm × 4 µm. Which statement about their surface area to volume ratios is correct?
Cell P has the greater SA:V, because cubes have the highest SA:V of any shape.
The two cells have equal SA:V, because both have a volume of 8 µm³.
Cell Q has the greater SA:V, at 3.5:1 compared with 3:1 for cell P.
Cell P has the greater SA:V, at 3:1 compared with about 2.9:1 for cell Q.

Cell Q has a surface area of 28 µm² against 24 µm² for cell P, while both have a volume of 8 µm³, giving 3.5:1 against 3:1. Equal volumes do not mean equal SA:V ratios, and a cube does not have the highest SA:V of all shapes for a given volume.
bio12a1-ct-24
A rectangular prism-shaped cell measures 2 µm × 3 µm × 5 µm. Calculate its surface area, its volume and its surface area to volume ratio, showing your working. (3 marks)
bio12a1-ct-25
A student claims that a large cell is more efficient at exchanging materials with its surroundings than a small cell because it has more membrane. Evaluate this claim. (2 marks)
The claim is incorrect [1]; the large cell has more total membrane but a lower SA:V, so less membrane is available per unit of cytoplasm to exchange materials [1]
bio12a1-ct-26
Distinguish between the magnification and the resolution of a light microscope. (2 marks)
Magnification is how many times larger the image appears than the specimen [1]; resolution is the smallest distance between two points that can still be seen as separate points [1]
bio12a1-ct-27
A cell measures 60 mm long in a photomicrograph taken at a magnification of ×1500. Calculate the actual length of the cell in µm. (2 marks)
bio12a1-ct-28
Describe the contribution of Rudolf Virchow to cell theory. (2 marks)
Stated that all cells arise only from pre-existing cells, by cell division [1]; this completed cell theory by explaining how new cells, and therefore growth and repair, are produced [1]
bio12a1-ct-29

Cube-shaped cells with side lengths of 1.5 µm, 6 µm, 9 µm and 12 µm have surface area to volume ratios of 4:1, 1:1, 0.67:1 and 0.5:1 respectively. Describe the relationship between side length and SA:V ratio, and explain it using surface area and volume. (3 marks)

As side length increases, the SA:V ratio decreases, so the two are inversely proportional [1]; for a cube, SA:V = 6 ÷ side length [1]; surface area increases with the square of the side length while volume increases with the cube, so volume increases faster [1]
vce-bio12-prokaryotic-and-eukaryotic-cel: bio12a1-pe-9
The cell wall of most bacteria is made mainly of which substance?
cellulose.
chitin.
peptidoglycan.
lignin.

Bacterial cell walls contain peptidoglycan, a polymer of sugars and amino acids. Plant walls are made of cellulose and fungal walls of chitin, while lignin is a strengthening material added to some plant walls rather than a bacterial component.
bio12a1-pe-10
Which of the following structures in a eukaryotic cell contains 70S ribosomes, similar to those of prokaryotes?
Lysosome.
Golgi apparatus.
Plasma membrane.
Mitochondrion.

Mitochondria carry their own 70S ribosomes, consistent with their bacterial origin. The Golgi apparatus, lysosomes and plasma membrane do not contain 70S ribosomes, and the ribosomes in the cytosol are 80S.
bio12a1-pe-11
Which statement best describes the function of plasmids in prokaryotic cells?
They carry the main chromosome that controls cell division.
They carry small extra genes, such as antibiotic resistance, that can be passed between bacteria.
They store glycogen as an energy reserve.
They are the site of aerobic respiration.

Plasmids are small, separate circles of DNA that can carry extra genes, such as antibiotic resistance, and can be transferred between bacteria. The main chromosome is the nucleoid DNA rather than a plasmid, and glycogen storage and aerobic respiration are not plasmid functions.
bio12a1-pe-12
A cell appears 2.5 mm long in a light microscope image taken at ×500 magnification. What is its actual length?
50 µm.
5 µm.

Actual size = image size ÷ magnification. The image is 2.5 mm = 2500 µm, and 2500 ÷ 500 = 5 µm. Leaving the value as 2500 µm ignores the magnification, 50 µm comes from dividing by 50 instead of 500, and 0.005 µm comes from treating 2.5 mm as 2.5 µm.
bio12a1-pe-13
Why can a transmission electron microscope reveal structures such as ribosomes that a light microscope cannot resolve?
Electrons have a much shorter wavelength than visible light, giving much higher resolution.
Electron microscopes use coloured stains that light cannot pass through.
Electron microscopes can view living cells in their natural state.
Electron microscopes magnify only about ×2 but keep the specimen in full colour.

The electron beam has a much shorter wavelength than visible light, so resolution is far higher and tiny structures can be seen. The other options are false: electron micrographs are black and white (or false colour), and specimens are prepared in a vacuum, so living cells cannot be viewed.
bio12a1-pe-14
Which observation provides the strongest evidence for the endosymbiotic theory of the origin of mitochondria?
Mitochondria have their own circular DNA and 70S ribosomes, similar to bacteria.
Mitochondria are found only in animal cells.
Mitochondria contain chlorophyll for photosynthesis.
Mitochondria are surrounded by a single membrane, like lysosomes.

Mitochondria have their own circular DNA and 70S ribosomes, features they share with bacteria. This supports the idea that they were once free-living prokaryotes engulfed by a larger cell. Mitochondria are found in plant and animal cells, have no chlorophyll and are surrounded by a double membrane.
bio12a1-pe-15
Which bacterial structure is a sticky outer layer that can help the bacterium resist attack by the host's immune cells?
Flagellum.
Ribosome.
Nucleoid.
Capsule.

A capsule is a sticky layer of polysaccharide outside the cell wall that can help bacteria evade the immune system and adhere to surfaces. A flagellum is used for movement, ribosomes make proteins and the nucleoid holds the chromosome.
bio12a1-pe-16
Most prokaryotes reproduce by binary fission. Which statement best explains why bacterial populations can grow rapidly?
Meiosis produces four genetically different cells, increasing variation.
Mitosis divides chromosomes within a membrane-bound nucleus to make two identical cells.
Binary fission produces two genetically identical cells, and under favourable conditions this can happen quickly.
Cells fuse together to form one larger cell, so the number of cells shrinks.

Binary fission copies the single chromosome and splits the cell into two genetically identical daughter cells, without mitosis or meiosis. Under favourable conditions it can be very rapid, so populations can double quickly. Fusion would reduce cell numbers rather than increase them.
bio12a1-pe-17
Which of the following organisms is a eukaryote?
Escherichia coli.
Saccharomyces cerevisiae (baker's yeast).
Streptococcus.
Cyanobacteria (blue-green algae).

Yeast is a single-celled fungus with a membrane-bound nucleus and membrane-bound organelles. E. coli, Streptococcus and cyanobacteria are all prokaryotes, even though cyanobacteria are often called blue-green algae.
bio12a1-pe-18
A eukaryotic cell is 40 µm across and a bacterium is 2 µm across. How many bacteria, placed end to end, would span the diameter of the eukaryotic cell?
40 ÷ 2 = 20 bacteria. Subtracting the sizes (38) or multiplying them (80) does not count how many fit along a length, and 2 is simply the bacterium's diameter in µm.
bio12a1-pe-19
Which statement about the cytoplasm of a prokaryotic cell is correct?
It contains membrane-bound organelles such as mitochondria.
It contains free 70S ribosomes and the nucleoid region.
It is enclosed by a nuclear envelope.
It contains no ribosomes.

Prokaryotic cytoplasm holds free 70S ribosomes and the nucleoid, with no membrane-bound organelles. Mitochondria are eukaryotic, the nuclear envelope surrounds a eukaryotic nucleus, and ribosomes are present in all cells.
bio12a1-pe-20
Which organelle is found in plant cells and some protists, but not in animal or fungal cells, and contains its own circular DNA?
Chloroplast.
Lysosome.
Centriole.
Vacuole.

Chloroplasts are photosynthetic organelles with their own circular DNA and 70S ribosomes, and they are absent from animal and fungal cells. Lysosomes and centrioles are found in animal cells, and a vacuole is a membrane-bound sac with no DNA of its own.
bio12a1-pe-21
Penicillin kills bacteria by interfering with the synthesis of their cell walls, but it does not harm human cells. Which statement best explains this?
Human cells have peptidoglycan cell walls that penicillin cannot penetrate.
Human cells do not make peptidoglycan, so penicillin has no target in them.
Penicillin acts only on viruses, which are not cells.
Human cells have 70S ribosomes, which penicillin cannot bind.

Penicillin blocks the cross-linking of peptidoglycan, a compound that human cells do not make, so there is no target in human cells. The option about 70S ribosomes is wrong because human cells have 80S ribosomes, and penicillin does not act on ribosomes.
bio12a1-pe-22
Which structure is found in many prokaryotes, is absent from eukaryotic animal cells, and is used by bacteria to attach to surfaces?
Pili.
Mitochondria.
Nucleus.
Centrioles.

Pili are short, hair-like protein projections on bacteria used for attachment to surfaces, and some are used to transfer DNA between cells. Mitochondria, the nucleus and centrioles are all found in eukaryotic animal cells.
bio12a1-pe-23
A cube-shaped cell with sides of 1 µm has a surface area to volume ratio of 6:1. Which change would give a ratio of 3:1?
Halving the side length to 0.5 µm, which doubles the ratio to 12:1.
Halving the side length to 0.5 µm, which halves the ratio to 3:1.
Doubling the side length to 2 µm, which halves the ratio to 3:1.
Doubling the side length to 2 µm, which doubles the ratio to 12:1.

For a cube, surface area to volume ratio = 6 ÷ side length, so doubling the side length from 1 µm to 2 µm halves the ratio to 3:1. Halving the side length to 0.5 µm doubles the ratio to 12:1, so the options claiming a 3:1 ratio from halving are wrong.
bio12a1-pe-24
State the function of ribosomes in a cell. (1 mark)
Site of protein synthesis (translation) [1]
bio12a1-pe-25
Explain how the large central vacuole of a plant cell helps the cell stay firm. (2 marks)
The vacuole takes up water, creating turgor (internal) pressure [1]; this pushes the plasma membrane against the cellulose cell wall, which resists expansion and keeps the cell firm [1].
bio12a1-pe-26
A bacterium with an actual length of 2 µm appears 10 mm long in a light microscope image. Calculate the magnification. Show your working. (2 marks)
Image size = 10 mm = 10 000 µm [1]; magnification = image size ÷ actual size = 10 000 ÷ 2 = ×5000 [1].
bio12a1-pe-27
Describe the role of the plasma membrane in both prokaryotic and eukaryotic cells. (2 marks)
