Controls the movement of substances into and out of the cell (selectively permeable) [1]; separates the cell's contents from its external environment [1].
bio12a1-pe-28
A cube-shaped cell has sides of 3 µm. Calculate its surface area to volume ratio, and explain how a larger ratio affects the efficiency of exchange of substances with the environment. (3 marks)

Surface area = 6 × 3² = 54 µm² and volume = 3³ = 27 µm³ [1]; ratio = 54 ÷ 27 = 2:1 [1]; a larger ratio gives more membrane per unit volume, so exchange of substances with the environment is more efficient [1].
bio12a1-pe-29

A student uses an eyepiece lens of ×10 and an objective lens of ×40 to view a cell. The image of the cell measures 8 mm across. Calculate the actual diameter of the cell in micrometres. Show your working. (3 marks)
Total magnification = 10 × 40 = ×400 [1]; image size = 8 mm = 8000 µm [1]; actual size = 8000 ÷ 400 = 20 µm [1].
bio12a1-pe-30
Compare a bacterial cell with a human liver cell with respect to: the location of DNA, the size of ribosomes, the presence of membrane-bound organelles, and typical cell size. (4 marks)

DNA: bacterium in a nucleoid (not membrane-bound), liver cell in a membrane-bound nucleus [1]; ribosomes: bacterium 70S, liver cell 80S [1]; membrane-bound organelles: absent in the bacterium, present in the liver cell (e.g. mitochondria, endoplasmic reticulum, Golgi apparatus) [1]; size: bacterium typically 0.1–5 µm, liver cell typically 10–100 µm [1].
bio12a1-pe-31
Explain why offspring produced by binary fission are genetically identical to the parent cell, yet bacterial populations can still show genetic variation. (2 marks)

Binary fission replicates the single circular chromosome and the cell divides, so each daughter receives identical DNA [1]; variation arises from mutations and from the transfer of plasmids between bacteria [1].
bio12a1-pe-32
Describe how plasmids carrying antibiotic resistance genes can spread through a bacterial population during antibiotic treatment. (3 marks)

Plasmids carry genes for antibiotic resistance [1]; plasmids can be transferred from resistant to non-resistant bacteria [1]; bacteria that have received the plasmid survive treatment, reproduce and increase the proportion of resistant bacteria in the population [1].
vce-bio12-organelles-and-their-functions: bio12a1-or-9
A plant cell is placed in pure water and becomes firm. What is the main reason?
The cell wall absorbs water and swells until it stretches
The central vacuole takes up water, pressing the cytoplasm against the cell wall
The chloroplasts absorb water and swell
The lysosomes release water into the cytosol

Water enters the central vacuole by osmosis, creating turgor pressure against the rigid cell wall, which keeps the cell firm. The cell wall does not swell, and chloroplasts and lysosomes do not store water.
bio12a1-or-10
Which structure is present in plant cells but absent from animal cells?
A nucleus
A cell membrane
A cell wall made mainly of cellulose
Ribosomes
Plant cells have a rigid cell wall of cellulose outside the cell membrane, which animal cells lack. Nuclei, cell membranes and ribosomes are found in both cell types.
bio12a1-or-11
Centrioles are most directly involved in which process?
Photosynthesis
Storage of starch
Digestion of bacteria
Organising spindle fibres during cell division

Centrioles, found in animal cells, help organise the spindle fibres that separate chromosomes during mitosis. Photosynthesis, starch storage and digestion of bacteria are not centriole functions; the last is a lysosome function.
bio12a1-or-12
Which function is performed by the Golgi apparatus but not by the rough endoplasmic reticulum?
Sorting, modifying and packaging proteins into vesicles
Synthesising polypeptides on attached ribosomes
Breaking down hydrogen peroxide
Producing ATP by aerobic respiration

The Golgi apparatus modifies, sorts and packages proteins into vesicles, while the rough ER synthesises polypeptides on its ribosomes. Hydrogen peroxide is broken down in peroxisomes and ATP is made in mitochondria.
bio12a1-or-13
Which structure gives an animal cell its shape and moves organelles through the cytoplasm?
Cell wall
Cytoskeleton
Nuclear envelope
Central vacuole

The cytoskeleton is a network of protein fibres that supports cell shape and moves organelles and vesicles. Animal cells have no cell wall, the nuclear envelope surrounds the nucleus, and the large central vacuole is a plant cell feature.
bio12a1-or-14
What distinguishes rough endoplasmic reticulum from smooth endoplasmic reticulum?
It contains chlorophyll
It is surrounded by a double membrane
It has ribosomes attached to its outer surface
It is the main site of lipid synthesis

Rough ER has ribosomes attached to its surface, which is why it is the main site of protein synthesis for export. Smooth ER lacks ribosomes and is the site of lipid synthesis, while chlorophyll is found in chloroplasts.
bio12a1-or-15
A white blood cell engulfs a bacterium and fuses the resulting vesicle with an organelle containing digestive enzymes. Which organelle is this?
Ribosome
Chloroplast
Nucleolus
Lysosome
Lysosomes contain hydrolytic enzymes that digest engulfed material such as bacteria. Ribosomes make proteins, chloroplasts carry out photosynthesis, and the nucleolus makes ribosomal subunits.
bio12a1-or-16
What is the main advantage of the inner mitochondrial membrane being folded into cristae?
It increases the surface area for electron transport chain proteins and ATP synthase
It stores the mitochondrion's genetic material
It allows glycogen to be stored for later use
It prevents oxygen from entering the matrix

Folding increases the membrane surface area, so more electron transport chain proteins and ATP synthase can be packed in, increasing ATP production. The other options describe functions that do not relate to cristae.
bio12a1-or-17
In which region of the chloroplast do the light-independent reactions of photosynthesis take place?
Thylakoid membranes
Stroma
Outer membrane
Cristae

The light-independent reactions (Calvin cycle) occur in the fluid stroma, using ATP and NADPH made in the light-dependent reactions. Thylakoid membranes are where the light-dependent reactions occur, and cristae are found in mitochondria.
bio12a1-or-18
What are the main components of chromosomes in a eukaryotic cell?
RNA and lipid
Glucose polymers and ribosomes
ATP and phospholipids
DNA wound around histone proteins
Chromosomes are DNA bound to histone proteins, which package the DNA within the nucleus. RNA, lipids, glucose polymers, ribosomes and ATP are not the main components of chromosomes.
bio12a1-or-19
Which statement about both mitochondria and chloroplasts is correct?
Both contain their own DNA and ribosomes
Both are surrounded by a single membrane
Both produce oxygen as a by-product
Both are found only in animal cells

Both organelles contain their own DNA and ribosomes, which is consistent with the endosymbiotic theory. Both have a double membrane, only chloroplasts release oxygen, and mitochondria occur in plant cells as well as animal cells.
bio12a1-or-20
Lysosomes are formed by vesicles budding off which organelle?
Mitochondrion
Golgi apparatus
Chloroplast
Nucleolus
Lysosomes form from vesicles that bud off the Golgi apparatus. Mitochondria and chloroplasts do not give rise to lysosomes, and the nucleolus is located inside the nucleus.
bio12a1-or-21
State the function of ribosomes. (1 mark)
Site of protein synthesis (translation of mRNA into a polypeptide) [1]
bio12a1-or-22
State the function of the nucleolus. (1 mark)
Production of ribosomal subunits, including synthesis of ribosomal RNA [1]
bio12a1-or-23
Mature mammalian red blood cells lack a nucleus and mitochondria. Explain how this is an advantage for their function in transporting oxygen. (2 marks)

Lack of a nucleus leaves more space for haemoglobin, so more oxygen can be carried per cell [1]; without mitochondria the cell does not use oxygen for its own respiration, so more oxygen is delivered to the tissues [1]
bio12a1-or-24
Explain how the cell wall prevents a plant cell from bursting when it takes in large amounts of water. (2 marks)
The cell wall is rigid and strong, made of cellulose [1]; it resists the outward pressure (turgor pressure) generated by the vacuole and cytoplasm, so the cell does not burst [1]
bio12a1-or-25
Describe the structure and function of lysosomes. (3 marks)

Membrane-bound sacs (vesicles) containing hydrolytic (digestive) enzymes [1]; the enzymes break down materials taken into the cell, such as food particles [1]; they also digest worn-out organelles so their components can be recycled [1]
bio12a1-or-26
Describe the structure of a mitochondrion, naming three parts. (3 marks)
Double membrane: a smooth outer membrane and an inner membrane [1]; the inner membrane is folded into cristae [1]; a fluid matrix containing enzymes, mitochondrial DNA and ribosomes [1]
bio12a1-or-27
A drug stops the nuclear pores from functioning. Explain the likely effect on protein synthesis in the cytoplasm. (4 marks)

mRNA is made in the nucleus by transcription of DNA [1]; mRNA cannot pass through the nuclear pores into the cytoplasm [1]; ribosomes in the cytoplasm cannot receive the mRNA template for translation [1]; so fewer proteins (including enzymes) are made, disrupting cell activities [1]
bio12a1-or-28
Compare the structure and function of the chloroplast and the mitochondrion. (4 marks)

Both have a double outer membrane [1]; the chloroplast has thylakoids stacked in grana containing chlorophyll and a stroma, while the mitochondrion has cristae and a matrix [1]; the chloroplast carries out photosynthesis, converting light energy into chemical energy in glucose [1]; the mitochondrion carries out aerobic respiration, releasing energy from glucose to make ATP [1]
bio12a1-or-29
A student claims that all living cells contain a nucleus. Evaluate this claim using one example. (2 marks)
The claim is incorrect [1]; prokaryotic cells such as bacteria have no nucleus, and their DNA lies in a nucleoid region in the cytoplasm [1]
vce-bio12-plasma-membrane-structure: bio12a1-pm-9
The part of a transmembrane protein that passes through the hydrophobic core of the bilayer is made mainly of
nonpolar amino acids whose side chains interact with the fatty acid tails.
amino acids with polar or charged side chains.
phosphate groups.
sugar residues.

Nonpolar side chains interact favourably with the fatty acid tails in the core. Polar or charged residues would be repelled by the core, so they are found at the ends of the protein facing the aqueous fluid.
bio12a1-pm-10
Which of these is a glycolipid's distinguishing feature compared with a phospholipid?
A phosphate group in each fatty acid tail.
No fatty acid tails at all.
A carbohydrate head group in place of a phosphate-containing head group.
A protein chain attached to its head group.

Glycolipids have a sugar head group instead of the phosphate-containing head found in phospholipids, and they are located on the outer surface of the membrane. A protein chain is not part of a glycolipid, which is why the last option is wrong.
bio12a1-pm-11
Phospholipids rarely move from one layer of the bilayer to the other. The main reason is that
the two layers are joined by covalent bonds between their heads.
the phosphate heads would have to pass through the hydrophobic core of the bilayer.
cholesterol binds each phospholipid in one fixed position.
the fatty acid tails are too short to reach the other layer.

Moving a charged, hydrophilic head through the nonpolar core is energetically unfavourable, so flip-flop is rare while sideways movement within one layer is common. The layers are held together by hydrophobic interactions, not covalent bonds, which makes the first option wrong.
bio12a1-pm-12
Which observation best shows that membrane proteins can move laterally within the bilayer?
Proteins are found on both the inner and outer surfaces of the membrane.
Membrane proteins appear as particles when the membrane is viewed by electron microscopy.
Fluorescent markers on proteins of two fused cells spread over the whole combined membrane over time.
The phospholipid tails in one cell are saturated and in another cell they are unsaturated.
Labelled proteins that mix across a fused membrane show that they are free to move sideways in the bilayer. The other options describe the distribution or structure of proteins, not their movement.
bio12a1-pm-13
A channel protein allows Na⁺ ions to cross the membrane. Which feature of the channel is essential for this?
A hydrophilic lining that forms a water-filled pathway through the bilayer, so Na⁺ does not contact the hydrophobic core.
A hydrophobic lining that matches the fatty acid tails, so the ion dissolves in it.
Covalent bonds that attach the channel to the phospholipid tails.
A large cytosolic tail that holds the ion outside the membrane.
Charged ions need a hydrophilic pathway through the membrane, which a water-filled pore provides. A hydrophobic lining would repel the charged ion rather than let it pass.
bio12a1-pm-14
Compared with a membrane made of phospholipids with long fatty acid tails, a membrane made of phospholipids with short fatty acid tails (same degree of saturation) would be
less fluid, because short tails pack more closely together.
more fluid, because short tails form stronger hydrogen bonds with water.
less fluid, because short tails form more hydrogen bonds with each other.
more fluid, because short tails have fewer contacts between neighbouring tails.

Shorter tails have less contact (van der Waals attraction) between neighbouring tails, so they pack less tightly and the membrane is more fluid. The option claiming closer packing is tempting, but it reverses the effect of shorter tails.
bio12a1-pm-15
How does a carrier protein differ from a channel protein?
A carrier protein forms a continuous water-filled pore, while a channel protein changes shape.
A carrier protein binds a specific substance and changes shape to move it across, while a channel protein forms a pore.
A carrier protein is always peripheral, while a channel protein is always inside the cytosol.
A carrier protein always uses ATP, whereas a channel protein never moves substances.

Channel proteins form open pores, whereas carrier proteins bind a specific solute and change shape to move it. Some carriers use ATP but many do not, so the option saying carriers always use ATP is wrong.
bio12a1-pm-16
Which of the following is NOT a component of an animal plasma membrane?
Cholesterol
Cellulose
Glycoproteins
Phospholipids
Cellulose is a structural polysaccharide found in plant cell walls and is absent from animal plasma membranes. Cholesterol, glycoproteins and phospholipids are all found in animal plasma membranes.
bio12a1-pm-17
Membrane fluidity increases as temperature rises. The best explanation is that
cholesterol melts and becomes a liquid between the phospholipids.
the phosphate heads lose their charge, so they pack more tightly.
the phospholipids gain kinetic energy, so they move more and the bilayer becomes looser.
the bilayer absorbs heat and becomes covalently cross-linked.
Higher temperature increases the kinetic energy of the phospholipids, so they move more and pack less tightly. Cholesterol does not melt; it actually reduces fluidity changes at high temperatures.
bio12a1-pm-18
A receptor protein in the membrane responds to one particular hormone and ignores other hormones. The most likely explanation is that its binding site
is made of phospholipid, so it attracts only lipid-soluble molecules.
is located inside the hydrophobic core, away from other molecules.
is the same as the binding site of every other membrane receptor.
has a shape and chemical properties complementary to that hormone.
Specific binding depends on a complementary shape and chemistry, so only the matching hormone fits the site. Receptors are proteins, not phospholipids, which makes the lipid-soluble option wrong.
bio12a1-pm-19
Where in the plasma membrane are cholesterol molecules located?
Dissolved in the cytosol, away from the bilayer.
Among the phospholipid fatty acid tails, with its small hydroxyl group near the phospholipid heads.
Attached covalently to the tips of membrane proteins.
Between the phosphate heads, with its ring structure in the aqueous fluid.

Cholesterol inserts between phospholipids, with its hydroxyl group near the polar heads and its rigid ring and hydrocarbon body among the fatty acid tails. The option placing the ring in the aqueous fluid is wrong because the ring is hydrophobic.
bio12a1-pm-20
Why is membrane fluidity important for vesicle transport?
It allows membranes to bend, fuse and mix their components during vesicle budding and fusion.
It keeps the membrane rigid so that vesicles can hold their shape.
It stops proteins from moving so that receptors stay in place.
It prevents phospholipids from forming a bilayer.

A fluid bilayer lets membranes bend and fuse, and lets lipids and proteins rearrange as vesicles bud from and fuse with membranes. A rigid membrane would make these changes difficult, which is why the rigidity option is wrong.
bio12a1-pm-21
Which statement about the asymmetry of the plasma membrane is correct?
Carbohydrate chains of glycoproteins and glycolipids are found only on the extracellular (outer) surface.
Carbohydrate chains of glycoproteins and glycolipids are found only on the cytosolic (inner) surface.
The inner and outer leaflets of the bilayer have identical lipid and protein composition.
Cholesterol is found only in the inner leaflet of the bilayer.

The plasma membrane is asymmetric, and its carbohydrate chains are always on the outer surface. Cholesterol occurs in both leaflets, and the two leaflets differ in composition, so the other options are wrong.
bio12a1-pm-22
Which of these is the main lipid making up the plasma membrane?
Triglycerides
Cholesterol
Waxes
Phospholipids

Phospholipids form the bilayer and are the most abundant lipid in the membrane. Cholesterol is present but in smaller amounts, and triglycerides are energy-storage lipids that do not form membrane bilayers.
bio12a1-pm-23
Peptide hormones such as insulin cannot pass through the plasma membrane, yet they can still change the activity of a target cell. Explain how. (3 marks)

Peptide hormones are polar and charged, so they cannot pass through the hydrophobic core of the bilayer [1]; they bind to a specific receptor protein on the outer surface of the membrane [1]; the binding causes a change in the receptor that triggers a response inside the cell, such as a second messenger [1].
bio12a1-pm-24
Several enzymes that catalyse consecutive steps of a metabolic pathway are embedded close together in a membrane. Explain how this arrangement can increase the rate of the pathway. (2 marks)
The product of one enzyme is passed directly to the next enzyme in the sequence [1]; this reduces the time for intermediates to diffuse away, so the pathway runs faster [1].
bio12a1-pm-25
A small tear forms in a phospholipid bilayer in an aqueous environment. Explain why the bilayer tends to reseal itself. (2 marks)
Hydrophobic tails exposed at the edges of the tear are unfavourable in water [1]; the phospholipids rearrange so the tails are shielded and the heads face the water, closing the gap [1].
bio12a1-pm-26
A membrane contains 3 200 cholesterol molecules and 12 800 phospholipid molecules. Express the ratio of cholesterol to phospholipid molecules in simplest form. (2 marks)
bio12a1-pm-27

A transmembrane α-helix rises about 0.15 nm per amino acid residue. Calculate the length of a 20-residue transmembrane helix, and state whether it could span a hydrophobic core about 3.0 nm thick. (2 marks)
20 × 0.15 nm = 3.0 nm [1]; this equals the thickness of the hydrophobic core, so the helix can just span the bilayer [1].
bio12a1-pm-28
Beetroot cells were placed in water at 20 °C and in water at 60 °C for 10 minutes. The water at 60 °C turned red, but the water at 20 °C stayed colourless. Explain this result. (3 marks)

The high temperature damages the membranes, disrupting their structure and denaturing their proteins [1]; the membranes lose their selective permeability [1]; the red betalain pigment stored in the cells diffuses out into the water [1].
vce-bio12-passive-transport-across-membr: bio12a1-pt-9
Which molecule is most likely to cross a phospholipid bilayer by simple diffusion?
oxygen (O₂)
glucose
sodium ions (Na⁺)
amino acids

Small non-polar molecules such as O₂ dissolve in the hydrophobic core of the bilayer and diffuse directly. Glucose, charged ions and amino acids are too large or too polar to cross the core without a carrier or channel protein.
bio12a1-pt-10
A cell is placed in an isotonic solution. Which statement is correct?
Water moves rapidly out of the cell, so the cell shrinks.
Water moves in and out at equal rates, so there is no net change in cell volume.
Solute moves out of the cell until the solute concentrations are equal.
The solution has a lower solute concentration than the cytoplasm, so the cell shrinks.

An isotonic solution has the same solute concentration as the cytoplasm, so water moves in and out at equal rates and there is no net change. The option describing lower solute outside the cell describes a hypotonic solution, which makes the cell swell, not shrink.
bio12a1-pt-11
Which factor does NOT directly affect the rate of simple diffusion across a membrane?
the concentration gradient
the surface area of the membrane
the amount of ATP in the cell
the temperature

Simple diffusion is passive, so its rate depends on the concentration gradient, surface area, diffusion distance, temperature and molecular size. ATP is used only in active transport. Temperature is a tempting wrong answer because it does change the kinetic energy of particles.
bio12a1-pt-12
Which of the following is an example of active transport rather than passive transport?
oxygen moving into a respiring cell down its concentration gradient
water entering a root hair cell through aquaporins, down its gradient
carbon dioxide leaving a respiring cell by simple diffusion
sodium ions pumped out of a cell against their gradient by the sodium–potassium pump

Active transport moves substances against their concentration gradient using energy from ATP, as the sodium–potassium pump does. The other three move down a concentration gradient without ATP, so they are passive.
bio12a1-pt-13
A plant cell is placed in a concentrated sucrose solution and its cell membrane pulls away from the cell wall. What is this process called?
plasmolysis
lysis
crenation
turgidity

Plasmolysis occurs when a plant cell loses water to a hypertonic solution and the protoplast shrinks away from the cell wall. Lysis is bursting and crenation is shrinking, both of animal cells; turgidity is the firm state of a plant cell in a hypotonic solution.
bio12a1-pt-14
Which feature of a small cell most helps simple diffusion supply all of its needs?
a low surface area to volume ratio
a high surface area to volume ratio
a thick plasma membrane
a rigid cell wall around the cell

A high surface area to volume ratio means the membrane is large relative to the cell's contents, so diffusion can reach every part of the cell quickly. A low ratio, or a thick membrane that slows diffusion, makes supply harder. A cell wall does not improve diffusion into the cell.
bio12a1-pt-15

A dialysis bag made of partially permeable tubing contains glucose solution and starch solution and is placed in distilled water. After 30 minutes, which substance or substances would be found in the water outside the bag?
starch only
neither glucose nor starch
glucose only
both glucose and starch

Glucose molecules are small enough to pass through the pores of the tubing and diffuse out, while starch molecules are too large and stay inside. The starch-only option reverses the effect of pore size, and the both option ignores the size limit.
bio12a1-pt-16
The rate of glucose uptake by facilitated diffusion levels off as the external glucose concentration keeps increasing. Why does this happen?
glucose molecules begin to repel one another
the concentration gradient reverses
the cell starts to pump glucose out using ATP
all the carrier proteins are occupied, so transport is at its maximum rate

Facilitated diffusion depends on a limited number of carrier proteins. When all are occupied, adding more glucose cannot increase the rate. The gradient still exists and the process stays passive, so reversal and ATP-driven pumping are wrong.
bio12a1-pt-17
Which statement describes a hypotonic solution relative to the cytoplasm of a cell?
It has a lower solute concentration than the cytoplasm, so water tends to move into the cell by osmosis.
It has a higher solute concentration than the cytoplasm, so water tends to move out of the cell.
It has the same solute concentration as the cytoplasm, so there is no tendency for water to move.
It has a lower solute concentration than the cytoplasm, so solute tends to move into the cell by osmosis.

A hypotonic solution has less solute than the cytoplasm, so water moves into the cell by osmosis. The description of higher solute outside the cell is a hypertonic solution. Osmosis moves water, not solute, so the last option is wrong.
bio12a1-pt-18
The concentration of oxygen inside a cell is 0.02 mmol L⁻¹ and outside the cell it is 0.10 mmol L⁻¹. In which direction does oxygen move, and why?
Out of the cell, because the cell has a higher concentration of oxygen.
No net movement, because oxygen is non-polar.
Into the cell, down its concentration gradient from the higher outside concentration.
Into the cell, because active transport moves oxygen against its gradient.

Oxygen is at a higher concentration outside (0.10 mmol L⁻¹) than inside (0.02 mmol L⁻¹), so it diffuses into the cell down the gradient without ATP. Its non-polar nature allows it to cross, so there is net movement, and active transport is not needed for a downhill move.
bio12a1-pt-19
A potato cylinder with an initial mass of 5.00 g gains mass and reaches 5.60 g after 24 hours in pure water. What is the percentage change in mass?
Percentage change = (change in mass ÷ initial mass) × 100 = (0.60 ÷ 5.00) × 100 = 12.0%. Dividing by the final mass gives 10.7%, leaving out the ×100 gives 0.12%, and 0.60% is just the raw mass gain.
bio12a1-pt-20
In an experiment investigating osmosis using potato cylinders in sucrose solutions, which variable is the independent variable?
the sucrose concentration of the solutions
the change in mass of the cylinders
the length of the potato cylinders
the time the cylinders are left in the solution

The independent variable is the one the investigator deliberately changes, here the sucrose concentration. The change in mass is measured, so it is the dependent variable, and length and time are kept constant as controlled variables.
bio12a1-pt-21
Carrier proteins used in facilitated diffusion are specific to particular molecules. What explains this specificity?
they are made of phospholipid, so they only interact with fat-soluble molecules
each binding site has a shape that fits only particular molecules
they use ATP to change shape for each molecule they carry
they transport only water, which then carries other molecules along with it

Specificity comes from the shape of the binding site on the carrier protein, which is complementary to the shape of one type of molecule. Carrier proteins are not made of lipid, and facilitated diffusion does not use ATP. Water is moved by aquaporins, not carried along by carriers.
bio12a1-pt-22
If the thickness of a membrane is doubled, with all other factors kept the same, the rate of simple diffusion of a gas across it will most likely
double
stay the same
approximately halve
increase about four times

The rate of diffusion is inversely proportional to the diffusion distance, so doubling the distance roughly halves the rate. Doubling the rate reverses the relationship, staying the same ignores distance, and a fourfold increase wrongly applies a squared relationship.
bio12a1-pt-23
Define diffusion. (2 marks)
The net movement of particles from a region of higher concentration to a region of lower concentration [1]; down a concentration gradient, without the input of energy (ATP) [1].
bio12a1-pt-24
Explain why heating beetroot tissue in water causes red pigment to leak out into the surrounding water. (2 marks)

Heat denatures the membrane proteins and disrupts the phospholipid bilayer, making the membrane more permeable [1]; so the pigment molecules can diffuse out of the cell down their concentration gradient [1].
bio12a1-pt-25
Compare simple diffusion and facilitated diffusion, giving two similarities and two differences. (4 marks)

Similarity: both are passive and require no ATP [1]; both move substances down a concentration gradient [1]. Difference: simple diffusion needs no membrane protein, whereas facilitated diffusion requires channel or carrier proteins [1]; facilitated diffusion can become saturated when all carriers are occupied, whereas the rate of simple diffusion rises in proportion to the gradient [1].
bio12a1-pt-26

A dialysis bag containing starch solution is placed in a beaker of iodine solution. After 20 minutes the contents of the bag turn blue-black, but no starch is found in the beaker. Explain both observations. (3 marks)

Iodine molecules are small enough to pass through the pores of the dialysis tubing, moving down their concentration gradient into the bag [1]; the iodine reacts with starch to form a blue-black colour [1]; starch molecules are too large to pass through the pores and remain in the bag [1].
bio12a1-pt-27
Describe the role of aquaporins in the movement of water into a cell. (2 marks)
Aquaporins are channel proteins embedded in the membrane [1]; they allow water molecules to cross the membrane rapidly by facilitated diffusion, down the water concentration gradient [1].
bio12a1-pt-28

A patient is given an intravenous drip of 0.9% saline, and their red blood cells keep their normal shape. Explain why. A second patient is given an intravenous drip of distilled water, and their red blood cells burst. Explain why. (4 marks)

Saline is isotonic to the cytoplasm of the red blood cells [1]; so water moves in and out at equal rates, with no net water movement [1]. Distilled water is hypotonic to the cytoplasm (lower solute concentration) [1]; so water moves into the cells by osmosis, causing them to swell and lyse (burst) [1].
bio12a1-pt-29
Explain why the net rate of diffusion decreases as a solution moves towards equilibrium. (3 marks)

The concentration gradient becomes smaller as particles spread out [1]; so there is a smaller difference between the rates of particles moving in each direction, reducing the net movement [1]; at equilibrium particles move in both directions at equal rates, so the net rate is zero [1].
vce-bio12-active-transport-endocytosis-a: bio12a1-at-9
Which molecule is hydrolysed directly to release the energy used by the sodium–potassium pump?
Glucose
Oxygen
Carbon dioxide
ATP

ATP is hydrolysed to ADP and inorganic phosphate, releasing the energy the pump uses to change shape. Glucose and oxygen are used in aerobic respiration to make ATP, so they are not the molecule that directly powers the pump.
bio12a1-at-10
Which is the best example of exocytosis?
Release of a neurotransmitter from a vesicle into the synapse
Entry of Na⁺ into a neurone through an open channel protein
Entry of water into a root hair cell by osmosis
Entry of glucose into a red blood cell by a carrier protein

In exocytosis a vesicle fuses with the plasma membrane and releases its contents outside the cell, as neurotransmitters are released into a synapse. The other options are passive movements through membrane proteins or osmosis, with no vesicle fusing with the membrane.
bio12a1-at-11
A cell takes in droplets of extracellular fluid containing dissolved proteins by forming tiny vesicles at its membrane. This process is called
phagocytosis.
exocytosis.
pinocytosis.
osmosis.

Pinocytosis ('cell drinking') is endocytosis of fluid and dissolved solutes in small vesicles. Phagocytosis takes in large solid particles, exocytosis releases material from the cell, and osmosis is the passive movement of water.
bio12a1-at-12
In one cycle, a sodium–potassium pump moves 3 Na⁺ out and 2 K⁺ in. If 1200 Na⁺ are moved out of a cell, how many K⁺ are moved in?
1200 ÷ 3 = 400 cycles, and each cycle moves 2 K⁺ in, giving 400 × 2 = 800 K⁺. Dividing 1200 by 2 gives 600, which uses the K⁺ number in the wrong place, and 400 counts cycles rather than ions.
bio12a1-at-13
A cell's sodium–potassium pumps move 300 Na⁺ out of the cell. Assuming one ATP is hydrolysed per cycle and each cycle moves 3 Na⁺ out, how many ATP molecules are used?
300 ÷ 3 = 100 cycles, each using one ATP, so 100 ATP molecules are hydrolysed. Using 300 assumes one ATP per ion, and 150 divides by the K⁺ number instead of the Na⁺ number.
bio12a1-at-14
Which organelle fuses with a phagosome (the vesicle containing an engulfed bacterium) to digest its contents?
Lysosome
Ribosome
Centriole
Nucleolus

Lysosomes contain hydrolytic enzymes that fuse with the phagosome and break down the engulfed material. Ribosomes make proteins, centrioles organise microtubules, and the nucleolus makes ribosomal subunits.
bio12a1-at-15
Which feature of the plasma membrane allows vesicles to fuse with it during exocytosis?
Its rigid cellulose layer
Its fluid phospholipid bilayer
Its impermeable protein layer
Its fixed, immobile proteins

The phospholipid bilayer is fluid, so the membrane can deform and merge with a vesicle membrane. Cellulose is a component of plant cell walls, not the plasma membrane, and membrane proteins can move within the bilayer.
bio12a1-at-16
Which description matches receptor-mediated endocytosis?
Random uptake of any fluid as the membrane folds
Engulfment of a bacterium by a white blood cell
Uptake of specific molecules bound to receptors in coated pits
Release of a hormone from a vesicle by fusion with the membrane

In receptor-mediated endocytosis, specific molecules bind to receptor proteins in clathrin-coated pits, which then pinch off as vesicles, making the process selective. Random fluid uptake is pinocytosis, engulfment of particles is phagocytosis, and hormone release is exocytosis.
bio12a1-at-17
Which statement about active transport is NOT correct?
It requires a membrane protein.
It requires energy from ATP.
It moves substances down their concentration gradients.
It can move substances against their concentration gradients.

Active transport moves substances against their concentration gradients using membrane proteins and ATP. Moving substances down a gradient is passive transport, such as diffusion, and does not need ATP.
bio12a1-at-18
What happens to the membrane of a secretory vesicle during exocytosis?
It fuses with the plasma membrane, adding to the cell surface membrane.
It is digested by lysosomes before release.
It pinches off inside the cytoplasm to form a new vesicle.
It is broken down into amino acids.

When the vesicle fuses with the plasma membrane, its membrane becomes part of the cell surface membrane and its contents are released outside. Pinching off inside the cytoplasm describes endocytosis, the opposite process.
bio12a1-at-19
Which statement best distinguishes endocytosis from active transport?
Endocytosis moves individual ions, while active transport moves large droplets.
Endocytosis moves material in bulk inside vesicles, while active transport moves individual molecules or ions through membrane proteins.
Both processes move material only down concentration gradients.
Only endocytosis requires energy from ATP.

Endocytosis is bulk transport of material within membrane-bound vesicles, whereas active transport moves individual molecules or ions through membrane proteins. Both processes need ATP, so the last option is wrong, and active transport moves substances against gradients, not down them.
bio12a1-at-20
Name the organelle that packages proteins into vesicles before they are exported by exocytosis. (1 mark)
Golgi apparatus [1].
bio12a1-at-21
Describe two features of endocytosis that distinguish it from simple diffusion. (2 marks)

Endocytosis requires energy from ATP, whereas simple diffusion is passive [1]; endocytosis moves material in bulk inside a membrane-bound vesicle, whereas diffusion moves individual small molecules directly across the membrane [1].
bio12a1-at-22
Explain why a neutrophil must be able to change the shape of its plasma membrane when engulfing a bacterium. (2 marks)
The membrane must extend outwards to surround the bacterium [1]; the flexible phospholipid bilayer and cytoskeleton allow the membrane to deform and enclose the bacterium in a vesicle [1].
bio12a1-at-23
Describe how the sodium–potassium pump moves three Na⁺ out of the cell and two K⁺ into the cell during one cycle. (3 marks)

Three Na⁺ bind to the pump protein on the inside of the cell [1]; ATP is hydrolysed, the phosphate attaches to the pump and it changes shape, releasing the Na⁺ outside [1]; two K⁺ bind from outside, the phosphate is released and the pump returns to its original shape, releasing the K⁺ inside [1].
bio12a1-at-24
Describe the sequence by which a digestive enzyme made by a pancreatic cell is released from the cell. (3 marks)

The enzyme is synthesised on ribosomes attached to the rough endoplasmic reticulum [1]; it is transported to the Golgi apparatus, where it is packaged into vesicles [1]; the vesicles move to the plasma membrane, fuse with it and release the enzyme outside the cell by exocytosis [1].
bio12a1-at-25
Explain how endocytosis and exocytosis allow a cell to move large molecules across its plasma membrane, and identify one property of the membrane that makes both processes possible. (4 marks)

In endocytosis the membrane folds inwards around material outside the cell and pinches off a vesicle that carries it into the cytoplasm [1]; in exocytosis a vesicle fuses with the plasma membrane and releases its contents outside [1]; both processes require energy from ATP [1]; the fluid phospholipid bilayer allows the membrane to deform and fuse with vesicle membranes [1].
vce-bio12-binary-fission: bio12a1-bf-9
Plasmids are:
linear chromosomes that carry the cell's essential genes
small, circular DNA molecules separate from the main chromosome that can replicate independently
protein filaments that form the septum
ribosomes that synthesise the cell wall

Plasmids are small circles of DNA found in many bacteria, often carrying non-essential genes such as antibiotic resistance. Linear chromosomes are a eukaryotic feature, so that option wrongly applies eukaryotic structure to bacteria.
bio12a1-bf-10
How many generations of binary fission are needed for one bacterial cell to produce 4096 cells?
Each generation doubles the number of cells, so 2ⁿ = 4096 gives n = 12, because 2¹² = 4096. Choosing 4096 confuses the number of cells with the number of generations.
bio12a1-bf-11
Before dividing by binary fission, a bacterial cell typically grows to:
about half its original size
the same size as before, since it does not need to grow
about ten times its original size
about twice its original size
The cell must roughly double its size so that each daughter cell reaches a normal size after division. Halving the size describes the daughter cells, not the parent before it divides.
bio12a1-bf-12
How many chromosomes does a typical Escherichia coli cell contain?
1 circular chromosome
2 circular chromosomes
23 pairs of linear chromosomes
46 linear chromosomes
E. coli has one circular chromosome, which is replicated before division; two copies exist only briefly during replication. The 23 pairs and 46 options describe the human karyotype, not a bacterium.
bio12a1-bf-13
Which processes can introduce genetic variation into a bacterial population?
crossing over during meiosis
mutation and transfer of DNA between cells, such as plasmid exchange
independent assortment of chromosomes in meiosis I
fertilisation between two gametes

Bacteria do not undergo meiosis or fertilisation, so their variation comes from mutation and from transfer of DNA such as plasmids between cells. The other three options occur only in the sexual reproduction of eukaryotes.
bio12a1-bf-14
Mitochondria reproduce by a process most similar to:
mitosis
meiosis
binary fission
budding

Mitochondria contain their own circular DNA and divide in a way similar to binary fission, which supports the endosymbiotic theory. Mitosis is the nuclear division of eukaryotic cells, which mitochondria do not undergo.
bio12a1-bf-15
A bacterial culture doubles every 15 minutes. How many minutes does it take for one cell to produce 256 cells?
256 = 2⁸, so 8 generations are needed, and 8 × 15 = 120 minutes. The answer 240 comes from doubling the time again, while 90 comes from counting only 6 generations.
bio12a1-bf-16
Generation time for a bacterial population is best defined as:
the time taken for the population to double in number
the time taken for the chromosome to be copied
the time between formation of the septum and cell separation
the time a population spends in the lag phase

Generation time is the time the population takes to double, which under given conditions equals one cycle of binary fission. The other options describe single steps or phases rather than the doubling time.
bio12a1-bf-17
A bacterial population has unlimited nutrients and space. On a graph of cell number against time, with an arithmetic scale, its growth is best shown as:
a flat horizontal line
a J-shaped curve that becomes steeper over time
a straight line with a constant gradient
an S-shaped curve that falls after a peak

Each generation doubles the population, so each time interval adds more cells than the one before, making the curve steeper. A straight line would mean the same number of cells is added in every interval.
bio12a1-bf-18
A bacterial culture is kept at 10 °C instead of its optimum of 37 °C. The rate of binary fission falls mainly because:
the circular chromosome becomes linear at low temperature
plasmids are lost from the cell
enzymes involved in DNA replication and cell division work more slowly
the cell switches to meiosis to conserve energy
Binary fission depends on enzymes, and their rate falls as temperature drops below the optimum. The chromosome does not change shape with temperature, and bacteria do not undergo meiosis.
bio12a1-bf-19
Where does the septum form during binary fission?
in the middle of the cell, between the two chromosome copies
at both ends of the cell, close to each chromosome
at the outer surface of the cell wall
only after the daughter cells have separated
The membrane pinches inward and a new wall forms at the midpoint, between the separated chromosome copies. The septum forms before the daughter cells separate, so the last option is wrong.
bio12a1-bf-20

A single bacterium at 37 °C has a generation time of 20 minutes, and at 25 °C it has a generation time of 60 minutes. Both populations start from one cell. After 2 hours, the population at 25 °C compared with the population at 37 °C is:
four times larger
one-sixteenth the size
the same size
16 times larger
At 37 °C there are 2⁶ = 64 cells after 2 hours, and at 25 °C there are 2² = 4 cells, and 4 ÷ 64 = 1/16. Describing the population as 16 times larger inverts the ratio.
bio12a1-bf-21
A bacterial cell contains one circular chromosome and two plasmids. How many separate circular DNA molecules does it contain?
One chromosome plus two plasmids gives three separate circular DNA molecules. An answer of 1 ignores the plasmids, and an answer of 2 ignores the chromosome.
bio12a1-bf-22
A student states that after binary fission each daughter cell contains only half the DNA of the parent cell. Explain why this is incorrect. (2 marks)
The chromosome is replicated before division, so the parent has two copies of its DNA [1]; each daughter receives one complete copy, the same amount of DNA as the original parent cell [1].
bio12a1-bf-23
A bacterial culture grows from 250 to 8000 cells in 3 hours. Calculate the generation time, in minutes. (3 marks)
8000 ÷ 250 = 32 = 2⁵, so 5 generations occurred [1]; 3 hours = 180 minutes [1]; generation time = 180 ÷ 5 = 36 minutes [1].
bio12a1-bf-24
Explain how plasmids can allow a bacterial population to become resistant to an antibiotic within a few generations. (3 marks)

Some bacteria carry plasmids with genes for antibiotic resistance [1]; the plasmid can be transferred to other bacteria, spreading the resistance genes [1]; the surviving resistant cells divide by binary fission, so the resistant population grows rapidly [1].
bio12a1-bf-25
Compare binary fission in prokaryotes with mitosis in eukaryotes. Identify two similarities and two differences. (4 marks)

Similarity: the DNA is replicated before the cell divides [1]; similarity: both produce two genetically identical daughter cells [1]; difference: binary fission does not use a spindle of microtubules, whereas mitosis does [1]; difference: a prokaryote has one circular chromosome not enclosed in a nucleus, whereas a eukaryote has multiple linear chromosomes enclosed in a nucleus [1].
bio12a1-bf-26
Explain why the chromosome must be fully replicated before the two copies separate during binary fission. (2 marks)
Each daughter cell must receive one complete copy of the chromosome [1]; separating before replication is complete would leave a cell with incomplete genetic information [1].
vce-bio12-the-eukaryotic-cell-cycle-and-: bio12a1-cc-9
Which of the following gives the correct order of the stages of the cell cycle?
G1, S, G2, M
S, G1, M, G2
M, G1, S, G2
G1, M, S, G2
The cell cycle runs G1, S (DNA replication), G2 and then M (mitosis). Orders that put M before S misplace DNA replication, which must be completed before division.
bio12a1-cc-10
A cell at the start of metaphase has 8 chromosomes, each made of two sister chromatids. How many chromatids are present in the cell?
Eight chromosomes with two sister chromatids each gives 8 × 2 = 16 chromatids. Answering 8 counts chromosomes instead of chromatids, and 32 doubles the correct count again.
bio12a1-cc-11
Which statement about the centromere is correct?
It is the region of the chromosome that codes for spindle proteins.
It is a membrane-bound organelle that organises microtubules.
It is the region where sister chromatids are joined and where spindle fibres attach.
It is the site where the nuclear envelope reforms in telophase.
The centromere holds sister chromatids together and is the point where spindle fibres attach during mitosis. The structure that organises microtubules is the centrosome, which is not membrane-bound.
bio12a1-cc-12
Which event occurs during telophase?
Chromosomes line up along the metaphase plate.
Sister chromatids separate at their centromeres.
Chromosomes condense and become visible under the microscope.
Nuclear envelopes reform around each set of chromosomes at the poles.
In telophase the chromosomes reach the poles and decondense, and a nuclear envelope reforms around each set. Lining up is metaphase, centromere splitting is anaphase, and condensation is prophase.
bio12a1-cc-13
What is the role of the centrosomes in an animal cell during mitosis?
They organise the spindle microtubules that pull sister chromatids apart.
They produce the ATP needed to replicate DNA.
They attach sister chromatids to each other before replication.
They form the cell plate that divides the cytoplasm.

The centrosomes duplicate in interphase, move to opposite poles and nucleate the spindle microtubules. Mitochondria make ATP, and a cell plate is a plant cytokinesis structure rather than a centrosome role.
bio12a1-cc-14
What type of protein do spindle fibres consist of?
Actin
Tubulin
Collagen
Keratin
Spindle fibres are microtubules built from tubulin. Actin forms the contractile ring in animal cytokinesis, while collagen and keratin are structural proteins that are not part of the spindle.
bio12a1-cc-15
What is the function of cyclins in the cell cycle?
They are structural proteins that form the spindle fibres.
They are enzymes that cut DNA at the centromere.
They bind cyclin-dependent kinases (CDKs) and regulate progression through the cell cycle.
They attach sister chromatids to the nuclear envelope.
Cyclins rise and fall in concentration through the cycle and activate cyclin-dependent kinases, which drive transitions between phases. Spindle fibres are made of tubulin, not cyclins.
bio12a1-cc-16
The mitotic index of a tissue sample is calculated as:
the number of cells in mitosis divided by the total number of cells observed
the total number of cells observed divided by the number in mitosis
the number of cells in interphase divided by the number in mitosis
the number of chromosomes divided by the number of cells observed
The mitotic index is the proportion of cells that are in mitosis, so the number in mitosis is divided by the total. Inverting the division gives a value above 1, which cannot be a proportion.
bio12a1-cc-17
Which statement correctly distinguishes mitosis from cytokinesis?
Mitosis divides the cytoplasm, while cytokinesis divides the nucleus.
Mitosis divides the nucleus, while cytokinesis divides the cytoplasm to form two cells.
Mitosis produces four haploid cells, while cytokinesis produces two diploid cells.
Mitosis occurs in G1, while cytokinesis occurs during S phase.

Mitosis separates the duplicated chromosomes into two nuclei, and cytokinesis divides the cytoplasm to form two cells. The reversed option swaps the two processes, and the four-cell option describes meiosis, not mitosis.
bio12a1-cc-18
Which statement best describes the time a typical dividing cell spends in interphase compared with mitosis?
Mitosis occupies most of the cell cycle because cells divide continuously.
Interphase and mitosis last the same length of time in most cells.
Interphase lasts only a few minutes, as the cell spends most of its time dividing.
Interphase occupies most of the cell cycle, while mitosis is comparatively brief.
In most cells interphase (G1, S and G2) makes up the majority of the cycle, while mitosis is short. The options that make mitosis dominant or equal reverse the actual proportions.
bio12a1-cc-19
Why are the two sister chromatids of a replicated chromosome genetically identical?
They are copies made by DNA replication of the same chromosome.
They are the products of crossing over during prophase.
They were inherited from two different parents.
They are the same as the homologous chromosome of the pair.
S phase replicates each chromosome exactly, so sister chromatids carry identical DNA sequences. Crossing over, homologous pairing and parental origin relate to meiosis, not to sister chromatids.
bio12a1-cc-20
A cell in metaphase has one chromosome that is not yet attached to a spindle fibre. What happens at the spindle checkpoint?
The cell skips metaphase and moves straight into telophase.
Anaphase is delayed until all chromosomes are correctly attached to spindle fibres.
The cell proceeds to cytokinesis, producing a daughter cell with an extra chromosome.
The chromosomes replicate again during G2.

The checkpoint holds the cell at metaphase until every chromosome is attached, so sister chromatids separate only when correctly aligned. Proceeding early would be the tempting error, risking daughter cells with missing or extra chromosomes.
bio12a1-cc-21
A single cell undergoes three consecutive rounds of mitosis with no cell death. How many daughter cells are produced?

Each round of mitosis doubles the number of cells, so 2 × 2 × 2 = 8. Six assumes each round adds two cells, and nine is 3 squared, which multiplies the number of rounds rather than doubling the cells.
bio12a1-cc-22
Name the structure that forms in an animal cell during cytokinesis to pinch the cytoplasm into two cells. (1 mark)
Cleavage furrow (formed by a contractile ring of actin filaments) [1]
bio12a1-cc-23
Define interphase. (1 mark)
The period of the cell cycle between divisions in which the cell grows, replicates its DNA and prepares for mitosis [1]
bio12a1-cc-24
Distinguish between a chromosome and a chromatid in a cell after S phase. (2 marks)
A chromosome consists of two sister chromatids joined at the centromere after S phase [1]; a chromatid is one of the two identical copies of DNA that make up a replicated chromosome [1]
bio12a1-cc-25
Describe the events of telophase and cytokinesis in an animal cell. (3 marks)

Telophase: the chromosomes reach the poles and decondense [1]; a nuclear envelope reforms around each set of chromosomes [1]; cytokinesis: a cleavage furrow forms and pinches the cytoplasm into two separate daughter cells [1]
bio12a1-cc-26
Describe the key events of G1, S and G2 of interphase. (3 marks)

G1: the cell grows and makes proteins and organelles [1]; S: DNA is replicated so that each chromosome has two sister chromatids [1]; G2: the cell continues to grow, checks the replicated DNA and makes proteins needed for division, such as tubulin for spindle fibres [1]
bio12a1-cc-27
A student writes: 'Mitosis produces four daughter cells, each with half the chromosome number of the parent cell.' Identify the two errors in this statement and correct them. (2 marks)
Mitosis produces two daughter cells, not four [1]; each daughter cell has the same (diploid) chromosome number as the parent, not half [1]
bio12a1-cc-28
Explain why a sample of rapidly growing embryonic tissue would have a higher mitotic index than a sample of mature liver tissue. (4 marks)

Embryonic cells divide rapidly to produce the cells needed for growth [1]; so a greater proportion of cells are in mitosis at any one time [1]; cells in mature liver tissue divide only rarely, so few are in mitosis [1]; the mitotic index is the proportion of cells in mitosis, so it is higher in the embryo [1]
bio12a1-cc-29
A cell cycle lasts 18 hours. G1 lasts 8 hours, S phase lasts 7 hours and G2 lasts 2 hours. Calculate the time spent in mitosis, and the percentage of the cycle spent in interphase. (3 marks)
Time in mitosis = 18 − (8 + 7 + 2) = 1 hour [1]; time in interphase = 8 + 7 + 2 = 17 hours [1]; 17 ÷ 18 × 100 = 94.4% (about 94%) of the cycle [1]
vce-bio12-apoptosis-and-cancer: bio12a1-ap-9
Tumour suppressor genes normally code for proteins that
stimulate cells to divide whenever growth factors are present.
inhibit cell division or trigger apoptosis when a cell is damaged.
break down the extracellular matrix so that cells can move.
form the spindle fibres that separate chromosomes in mitosis.

Tumour suppressors such as p53 slow division or trigger apoptosis when needed, so losing them removes a brake on growth. Stimulating division describes the normal role of proto-oncogenes, and spindle fibres are structures rather than regulatory proteins.
bio12a1-ap-10
During apoptosis, what change to the plasma membrane signals phagocytes to engulf the cell?
Phosphatidylserine moves to the outer surface of the membrane.
Glucose transporters are removed from the membrane.
The membrane ruptures and releases cytoplasm.
The membrane becomes completely impermeable to all molecules.

Exposed phosphatidylserine acts as an 'eat me' signal that phagocytes recognise, so apoptotic cells are cleared without spilling their contents. Rupture and release of cytoplasm happens in necrosis, not apoptosis.
bio12a1-ap-11
Cytotoxic T cells destroy virus-infected body cells mainly by
releasing viral particles to be neutralised by antibodies.
causing the infected cell to undergo necrosis and burst.
stimulating the infected cell to undergo mitosis more often.
triggering apoptosis in the infected cell.

Cytotoxic T cells trigger apoptosis in the infected cell, which removes it without releasing viral particles or causing inflammation. Bursting by necrosis would release virus into the tissue, so it is the wrong mechanism.
bio12a1-ap-12
Which of the following is a chemical carcinogen?
X-rays
Benzene in tobacco smoke
Ultraviolet-B radiation
Gamma rays from a radioactive source
Benzene is a chemical that damages DNA and is present in tobacco smoke. X-rays, UV-B and gamma rays are physical agents, so they are not chemical carcinogens.
bio12a1-ap-13
Why does the risk of many cancers increase with age?
Older cells divide less often, so fewer mutations are made.
Cells accumulate more mutations over time from repeated DNA copying and environmental exposure.
Caspases become more active in older tissues.
Older tissues produce fewer stem cells, so tumours cannot form.

Mutations build up with each cell division and each exposure to mutagens, and several are usually needed for cancer, so risk rises over decades. The option saying older cells divide less is wrong because many adult tissues keep dividing throughout life.
bio12a1-ap-14
A tumour starts with 500 cells and the cell number doubles every 2 days. If all cells keep dividing, how many cells are present after 6 days?
Three doublings occur in 6 days: 500 → 1 000 → 2 000 → 4 000. Adding 500 cells every 2 days gives 2 000, while 8 000 counts four doublings instead of three.
bio12a1-ap-15
A mutagen is best defined as an agent that
increases the rate of change in the base sequence of DNA.
kills cells by necrosis and causes inflammation.
activates caspases directly in healthy cells.
increases the rate of mitosis without affecting DNA.
A mutagen raises the rate of DNA mutation, which may or may not lead to cancer. Necrosis, caspase activation and faster mitosis are not defining features of a mutagen.
bio12a1-ap-16
Angiogenesis, which growing tumours stimulate, is the
breakdown of blood vessels by caspases during apoptosis.
division of blood cells in the bone marrow.
release of cytochrome c from mitochondria.
formation of new blood vessels that supply nutrients and oxygen to the tumour.

A tumour larger than a few millimetres needs its own blood supply, so it stimulates new vessel growth. The other options describe apoptosis, blood-cell production and the intrinsic apoptosis pathway rather than angiogenesis.
bio12a1-ap-17
Which statement correctly compares mitosis and apoptosis?
Apoptosis produces two daughter cells, whereas mitosis destroys the nucleus.
Both processes are triggered by the release of caspases from mitochondria.
Mitosis is a form of cell death, whereas apoptosis increases the number of cells.
Mitosis produces two genetically identical daughter cells, whereas apoptosis is a controlled way for a cell to die.

Mitosis makes two genetically identical daughter cells, whereas apoptosis is a controlled way for a cell to die. The other options swap these roles or misattribute caspase activity and changes in cell number.
bio12a1-ap-18
Radiotherapy kills cancer cells mainly by
causing DNA damage that cells cannot repair, leading to cell death.
stimulating angiogenesis so that the tumour grows faster.
increasing the rate of mitosis so cells divide more quickly.
heating the tumour above 100 °C to denature its proteins.

Radiation breaks DNA strands, and cancer cells that cannot repair the damage stop dividing or undergo apoptosis. Increasing mitosis or angiogenesis would worsen the cancer, and radiotherapy does not work by boiling tissue.
bio12a1-ap-19
Which is a common cause of necrosis?
A programmed signal that activates caspases
Removal of the cells between developing fingers
Loss of blood supply to a tissue, so its cells run out of oxygen and ATP
Normal replacement of old cells in the stomach lining
Loss of oxygen and ATP makes cells swell and burst, releasing contents that trigger inflammation. The other options describe programmed, controlled cell death, which is apoptosis.
bio12a1-ap-20
Which cell is most likely to be removed by apoptosis?
A healthy skin cell that is functioning normally
A muscle cell that is actively contracting
A cell with DNA damage that cannot be repaired
A liver cell that has just been formed by mitosis
Apoptosis removes cells whose DNA damage cannot be repaired, which stops them passing mutations to daughter cells. The other cells are healthy and functioning, so the body keeps them.
bio12a1-ap-21
Which of the following best describes a tumour?
An abnormal mass of cells formed by uncontrolled cell division.
A group of cells that have been removed by apoptosis.
A cluster of phagocytes that have engulfed dead cells.
A mass of red blood cells that has formed in the bone marrow.
A tumour is an abnormal growth of cells, which may be benign or malignant. Apoptotic cells and phagocyte clusters are removed by the body, and red blood cells do not form tumours.
bio12a1-ap-22
Explain why a benign tumour is usually less dangerous than a malignant tumour. (2 marks)
A benign tumour stays in one place and does not invade surrounding tissue [1]; a malignant tumour invades nearby tissue and can spread to other parts of the body, disrupting organ function [1].
bio12a1-ap-23
Explain why chemotherapy drugs that target rapidly dividing cells also cause hair loss and nausea. (3 marks)

The drugs damage DNA or block mitosis, killing cells that divide rapidly [1]; hair follicle cells and the cells lining the digestive tract also divide rapidly [1]; so these healthy cells are damaged too, causing side effects [1].
bio12a1-ap-24

A tissue produces 12 000 new cells per day by mitosis and loses 9 500 cells per day by apoptosis. Calculate the net change in cell number per day and state whether the tissue is growing or shrinking. (2 marks)
12 000 − 9 500 = 2 500 cells gained per day [1]; the tissue is growing, as its cell number is increasing [1].
bio12a1-ap-25
In a biopsy of a tumour, 21 of 350 cells counted were in mitosis. Calculate the mitotic index as a percentage. (2 marks)
bio12a1-ap-26
Explain how exposure to ultraviolet radiation can lead to skin cancer. (3 marks)

UV radiation is absorbed by DNA, forming thymine dimers that distort the DNA [1]; if these are not repaired correctly, the DNA base sequence is changed (a mutation) [1]; mutations in genes controlling the cell cycle or apoptosis can cause cells to divide uncontrollably and form a tumour [1].
bio12a1-ap-27
Explain why a tumour can become more aggressive over time as further mutations accumulate. (3 marks)

Cells in a tumour continue to acquire mutations as they divide [1]; cells with mutations that increase division or help them escape apoptosis have a growth advantage and out-compete other cells [1]; this produces a more aggressive population that may spread to other tissues [1].
bio12a1-ap-28
Explain why cancer cells that have lost contact inhibition continue to divide when they touch neighbouring cells. (2 marks)
Normal cells receive a signal from neighbouring cells that halts division [1]; cancer cells do not respond to this signal, so they keep dividing and form a mass [1].
bio12a1-ap-29
Explain why a mutation in a gene that codes for a DNA repair enzyme can increase cancer risk. (2 marks)
Without a working enzyme, DNA errors and damage are not corrected [1]; mutations then accumulate in genes controlling cell division, increasing the likelihood of cancer [1].
bio12a1-ap-30
Describe how cancer cells spread from a primary tumour to form secondary tumours elsewhere in the body. (3 marks)

Cancer cells detach from the primary tumour and invade the surrounding tissue [1]; they enter the blood or lymphatic system [1]; they travel to a distant site, where they settle and divide to form a secondary tumour [1].
vce-bio12-stem-cells-and-specialisation: bio12a1-sc-9
Plant growth continues throughout life in regions called meristems, such as the root and shoot tips. The cells in these regions are best described as
stem cells that keep dividing and can differentiate into specialised plant cells.
fully differentiated cells that have lost the ability to divide.
gametes that fuse during fertilisation to form a new plant.
cells that have lost their genes during differentiation.

Meristem cells are stem cells that divide by mitosis and differentiate, so plants can keep growing. Fully differentiated cells have generally lost the ability to divide, and gametes do not form plant tissue in a meristem.
bio12a1-sc-10
Which feature of a root hair cell most directly increases the rate at which it absorbs water and mineral ions from the soil?
A thick, lignified cell wall.
A long, thin extension that greatly increases surface area.
Many chloroplasts that supply energy for water uptake.
A large central vacuole that fills most of the cell.

The long extension increases the surface area to volume ratio, speeding up absorption. A thick lignified wall would be rigid and slow movement of water, and chloroplasts are of little use in roots that are underground.
bio12a1-sc-11
Mature xylem vessel elements transport water up a plant. Which combination of features is characteristic of them?
Living cells with an intact nucleus and end walls.
Thin walls with cytoplasmic strands and no lignin.
Hollow, dead cells with lignified walls and no end walls.
Cells with flagella that push water upwards.

At maturity, xylem vessels are dead hollow tubes with lignin-strengthened walls, and their end walls have broken down to form a continuous channel. The option describing living cells with nuclei does not match xylem vessels.
bio12a1-sc-12
Motor neurons carry impulses over long distances, such as from the spinal cord to the leg muscles. Which feature is an adaptation for this function?
A very short axon, so impulses travel quickly.
Many chloroplasts in the cell body.
A membrane that is freely permeable to all ions.
A long axon, often insulated by a myelin sheath.

A long axon covered in myelin allows fast conduction over long distances, as the impulse jumps between the gaps in the sheath. Animal neurons do not contain chloroplasts, and a freely permeable membrane could not maintain the ion gradients needed for an impulse.
bio12a1-sc-13
Skeletal muscle fibres are long cells that contain many nuclei. This feature is an advantage because the nuclei
store energy as ATP for the whole fibre.
stop the cell from dividing during contraction.
together direct the large amount of protein synthesis needed for contraction.
allow the fibre to exchange gases more rapidly.

Each nucleus controls a region of the cytoplasm, so many nuclei support the high rate of protein synthesis needed for contraction. Nuclei do not store energy, and the number of nuclei does not change how quickly gases diffuse.
bio12a1-sc-14
The epithelial cells lining the small intestine have microvilli on their surface. What is the main function of this feature?
To secrete mucus that protects the intestinal wall.
To make the cells contract so food is pushed along the gut.
To pump oxygen into the blood.
To increase surface area for absorption of digested nutrients.

Microvilli greatly increase the surface area of the cell membrane, speeding up the absorption of digested food. Mucus is made by other cells, and the cells lining the intestine do not contract to move food along.
bio12a1-sc-15
Guard cells surround each stoma in a leaf. When guard cells take in water and become turgid, the stoma
opens, allowing carbon dioxide to enter the leaf.
closes, reducing water loss from the leaf.
stays the same size, because water does not move into guard cells.
closes permanently and stops all gas exchange.

When guard cells take in water and become turgid, they bend apart and open the stoma, letting carbon dioxide in for photosynthesis. The stoma closes when guard cells lose water, so the option describing closure on turgidity has the direction reversed.
bio12a1-sc-16
The trachea is lined with ciliated epithelial cells. What is the function of the cilia?
To produce surfactant that reduces surface tension in the alveoli.
To sweep mucus and trapped particles up towards the throat.
To absorb oxygen from the air into the cell.
To contract and push air into the lungs.
Cilia beat in a coordinated wave to move mucus, with trapped dust and microbes, up and away from the lungs. Surfactant is made by other cells in the alveoli, and cilia do not contract to move air.
bio12a1-sc-17

In therapeutic cloning, the nucleus of a patient's body cell is placed into an egg cell whose nucleus has been removed, and stem cells are harvested from the resulting embryo. What is the main advantage of this approach?
The stem cells will be totipotent, so they can form a placenta.
The stem cells will be identical to the egg donor, so they cannot be rejected.
The stem cells are genetically matched to the patient, which reduces the risk of immune rejection.
No embryo is created, so the procedure raises no ethical concerns.

The nucleus comes from the patient's own cell, so the stem cells are a genetic match and are less likely to be rejected. The stem cells are pluripotent rather than totipotent, and the method does create an embryo, which is why it is ethically contested.
bio12a1-sc-18
Adult skin cells can be reprogrammed to become induced pluripotent stem cells (iPSCs). Which property do iPSCs share with embryonic stem cells?
They can form extra-embryonic tissues such as the placenta.
They are totipotent and can form a whole organism on their own.
They are fully specialised and can no longer divide.
They can differentiate into all the cell types of the body.

iPSCs are pluripotent, like embryonic stem cells, so they can form all body cell types but not extra-embryonic tissue. Totipotency is a feature of very early embryonic cells, and iPSCs are not specialised.
bio12a1-sc-19
Companion cells are closely associated with phloem sieve tubes. Why do companion cells contain many mitochondria?
They produce ATP to power active transport of sugars into the sieve tubes.
They store the water needed by the xylem vessels.
They synthesise lignin to strengthen the sieve tubes.
They carry out photosynthesis to supply energy to the sieve tubes.

Companion cells respire aerobically to make ATP, which powers the active loading of sugars into the sieve tubes. Lignin is found in xylem rather than phloem, and storing water is not a role of companion cells.
bio12a1-sc-20
Palisade mesophyll cells in a leaf are packed with chloroplasts and lie just beneath the upper epidermis. This arrangement is an adaptation for
storing starch for the plant's roots.
absorbing light energy for photosynthesis.
transporting water from the roots to the leaf.
reducing gas exchange with the atmosphere.

Palisade cells sit near the leaf surface and contain many chloroplasts, so they capture the most light for photosynthesis. Starch storage occurs in other tissues, water is carried by xylem rather than palisade cells, and gas exchange is needed for photosynthesis.
bio12a1-sc-21
Name the process by which a cell becomes structurally and functionally specialised for a particular role. (1 mark)
Differentiation [1]
bio12a1-sc-22
Give one advantage of collecting stem cells from umbilical cord blood rather than from bone marrow. (1 mark)
Collection is non-invasive, so the donor does not need surgery or experience pain [1].
bio12a1-sc-23
Explain why multicellular organisms contain specialised cells rather than every cell performing all functions. (2 marks)

Division of labour means each cell type can be structurally and functionally adapted to carry out one role efficiently [1]; cells can be grouped into tissues and organs that perform complex tasks no single cell could carry out [1].
bio12a1-sc-24
Explain why embryonic stem cells are more potent than adult stem cells. Refer to the stage of development at which each is found. (3 marks)

Embryonic stem cells come from the early embryo, before cells have committed to a lineage, so they can form all body cell types (pluripotent) [1]; adult stem cells are found in mature tissues and have become restricted to forming the cell types of that tissue (multipotent) [1]; as development proceeds, the genes for other cell types are progressively switched off [1].
bio12a1-sc-25
Explain how the lining of the small intestine is continually replaced, using the terms 'stem cell' and 'differentiation'. (3 marks)

Stem cells at the base of intestinal crypts divide by mitosis to produce new daughter cells [1]; some daughter cells differentiate into specialised cells, such as absorptive cells, by switching on particular genes [1]; older cells move up to the tip of the villus, where they are shed, so the lining is replaced about every few days [1].
bio12a1-sc-26
Explain how a small piece of plant tissue can be used to grow many genetically identical plants. Refer to undifferentiated cells in your answer. (3 marks)

Cells in the tissue are undifferentiated, stem-like cells that can still divide and form new tissues [1]; hormones in the growth medium stimulate them to divide, forming an undifferentiated mass called a callus [1]; cells in the callus then differentiate into roots and shoots, producing genetically identical plants (clones) [1].
vce-bio12-plant-transport-systems: bio12a1-pl-9
Stomata open in the light mainly because guard cells take up potassium ions (K⁺). This causes
water to enter the guard cells by osmosis, increasing turgor and bowing the cells apart.
water to leave the guard cells, making them flaccid and opening the pore.
the guard cells to lose their chloroplasts and collapse inwards.
the xylem to pull the guard cells apart by cohesion.

Active uptake of K⁺ lowers the water potential inside the guard cells, so water enters by osmosis, the cells become turgid and the pore opens. Water leaving the cells would make them flaccid and close the pore.
bio12a1-pl-10
Guttation, the loss of drops of liquid water from the leaf margins of some plants, usually occurs at night because
transpiration is at its highest rate, forcing water out of the hydathodes.
root pressure pushes xylem sap out through hydathodes when transpiration is low and humidity is high.
phloem sieve tubes leak sugar solution onto the leaf surface.
stomata are fully open, so water is forced out through them.

Root pressure builds when transpiration is low, such as on humid nights, and pushes xylem sap out through hydathodes. Guttation is not caused by high transpiration, and the liquid is xylem sap, not phloem sap.
bio12a1-pl-11
Water moving through the cell walls and intercellular spaces of the root cortex, without crossing a plasma membrane, is following which pathway?
Symplast pathway, through the cytoplasm linked by plasmodesmata.
Transpiration pathway, through the stomata of the leaf.
Apoplast pathway, through cell walls and intercellular spaces.
Phloem loading pathway, driven by active transport of sucrose.

The apoplast pathway moves water through non-living cell walls and spaces. The symplast pathway passes through cytoplasm via plasmodesmata, and the Casparian strip at the endodermis forces water into the symplast before it reaches the xylem.
bio12a1-pl-12
Which set of conditions gives the fastest rate of transpiration?
Cool, humid, still and dark.
Cool, dry, still and dark.
Warm, humid, still and dark.
Warm, dry, windy and bright.

Warmth, low humidity, wind and light all increase transpiration, because they speed evaporation, steepen the water vapour gradient and keep stomata open. Each of the other sets includes at least one factor that slows transpiration.
bio12a1-pl-13
Sucrose is moved into sieve tube elements at a leaf (the source). This loading is usually done by
active transport, with companion cells using ATP.
diffusion down a concentration gradient from the xylem.
osmosis into the xylem vessels, pulled upward by transpiration.
root pressure forcing sugar into the phloem.

Companion cells use ATP to pump sucrose into sieve tube elements against a concentration gradient. Xylem and the transpiration pull are not involved in loading phloem, and root pressure acts on xylem sap, not on phloem loading.
bio12a1-pl-14
In the pressure flow hypothesis, sap moves through phloem from a source to a sink because
transpiration pulls sap up the sieve tubes from the roots.
loading sucrose at the source lowers water potential, water enters by osmosis and pressure rises; unloading at the sink lowers the pressure, so sap flows down the gradient.
sieve plates act as pumps, moving sap in both directions.
sucrose diffuses passively from the sink to the source.

Water entering by osmosis at the source raises hydrostatic pressure, while unloading at the sink lowers it. This pressure gradient moves sap by mass flow. Transpiration drives the xylem, not the phloem, and sieve plates are not pumps.
bio12a1-pl-15
Which feature allows water to move sideways between neighbouring xylem vessels?
Sieve plates at the ends of the vessels.
Plasmodesmata linking companion cells.
Pits in the lignified walls, where the wall is thin and unlignified.
Living cytoplasm lining the vessel walls.
Pits are thin, unlignified areas of the vessel walls that let water pass sideways between vessels. Sieve plates belong to phloem, and xylem vessels have no living cytoplasm.
bio12a1-pl-16
A plant cell is placed in a solution with a lower water potential than the cell sap. The cell will
gain water and become more turgid.
stay the same, because water potential does not affect movement of water.
gain solutes from the solution, increasing its water potential.
lose water and become flaccid.

Water moves by osmosis from higher to lower water potential, so the cell loses water, loses turgor and becomes flaccid. The cell would gain water only if the solution had a higher water potential than the cell sap.
bio12a1-pl-17
A leafy shoot takes up 4.5 mL of water in 3 hours. What is the average rate of water uptake?
1.5 mL h⁻¹
7.5 mL h⁻¹
13.5 mL h⁻¹
0.67 mL h⁻¹
Rate = volume ÷ time = 4.5 mL ÷ 3 h = 1.5 mL h⁻¹. Adding the numbers gives 7.5, multiplying gives 13.5, and dividing time by volume gives about 0.67, so these are all wrong.
bio12a1-pl-18
Which feature of root hair cells increases the rate at which they absorb water?
Thick, lignified walls.
A large surface area from many long, thin extensions.
Many chloroplasts for photosynthesis.
A waxy cuticle over the cell surface.

Root hairs are long, thin extensions of epidermal cells, which give a large surface area for absorbing water and ions. Lignified walls and a waxy cuticle would restrict uptake, and root cells generally lack chloroplasts.
bio12a1-pl-19
Most water lost from a leaf on a typical sunny day is lost through
the cuticle, as liquid water droplets.
lenticels in the stem.
root hairs.
stomata, as water vapour.

Stomata account for most transpiration because they are open to the air and are numerous. The cuticle is waterproof and loses little water, lenticels are minor in stems, and root hairs take in water rather than losing it.
bio12a1-pl-20
Stomata usually close at night because
without light, guard cells stop actively taking in K⁺, so water leaves them and they lose turgor.
the xylem stops transporting water at night.
guard cells absorb sucrose and become rigid.
the leaf temperature rises sharply at night.

Light drives ATP production in guard cells that powers K⁺ uptake. Without light, guard cells lose K⁺ and turgor, so the pore closes. Xylem transport does not simply stop at night, and leaf temperature usually falls.
bio12a1-pl-21
Which sequence correctly shows the pathway of water from the soil to the atmosphere?
Soil → xylem → root hair → stomata → atmosphere.
Soil → root hair → root cortex → endodermis → xylem → leaf mesophyll → air spaces → stomata → atmosphere.
Soil → root hair → phloem → leaf mesophyll → stomata → atmosphere.
Soil → root cortex → phloem → xylem → stomata → atmosphere.
