Any gamete from one parent can fuse with any gamete from the other, so each zygote combines a random gamete from each parent [1]; each gamete carries a random mix of maternal and paternal chromosomes from independent assortment, so each parent produces 2ⁿ different gametes [1]; the number of possible zygotes is therefore (2ⁿ) × (2ⁿ), a very large number of different combinations [1].
bio12a3-sex-27
State the number of chromatids that each chromosome contains at the start of anaphase I. (1 mark)
Two sister chromatids, joined at the centromere [1].
bio12a3-sex-28
Describe how the sex chromosomes determine the sex of a human offspring. (2 marks)

Females have two X chromosomes (XX) and males have one X and one Y chromosome (XY) [1]; each ovum carries an X chromosome, and the sex of the offspring depends on whether the sperm that fertilises it carries an X (female) or a Y (male) [1].
vce-bio12-reproductive-cloning: bio12a3-clone-9
In somatic cell nuclear transfer (SCNT), the mitochondrial DNA of the cloned embryo comes from which source?
the somatic cell donor, because mitochondria are found in the nucleus
the surrogate mother's uterus
the cytoplasm of the egg donor, which is not removed when the egg nucleus is removed
the sperm donor, because fertilisation takes place

Mitochondria sit in the cytoplasm, not the nucleus, so they stay in the egg when its nucleus is removed. The clone's nuclear DNA matches the body cell donor, but its mitochondrial DNA does not. The surrogate and any sperm donor contribute no genetic material in SCNT.
bio12a3-clone-10
After a donor nucleus is placed in an enucleated egg, the reconstructed cell is given an electric pulse or chemicals. What is the purpose of this step?
to activate the reconstructed egg so that it starts dividing as an embryo
to remove the donor nucleus from the egg
to cause meiosis so that the chromosome number is halved
to fuse the egg with a sperm cell so that it is fertilised

The pulse or chemicals mimic fertilisation and trigger the cell to divide and form an embryo. SCNT uses no sperm, so fertilising the egg would give a mixed-parent embryo, and meiosis would halve the donor's chromosome number.
bio12a3-clone-11
In SCNT, the donor nucleus must be reprogrammed. What does this mean?
the donor DNA is permanently mutated to match the egg's DNA
the donor nucleus is replaced by a sperm nucleus
the donor cell's chromosomes are halved by meiosis before transfer
the egg cytoplasm switches on genes that were silenced during differentiation, so the nucleus can direct development of a whole organism

A nucleus from a specialised cell has most of its genes switched off, and reprogramming switches the needed ones back on. Reprogramming changes which genes are active, not the DNA sequence itself, so the mutation option is wrong.
bio12a3-clone-12
Which statement correctly compares embryo splitting with somatic cell nuclear transfer (SCNT)?
both produce offspring that are genetically identical to the parent that donated the nucleus
embryo splitting produces offspring that are identical to each other, whereas SCNT produces offspring with the nuclear DNA of the body cell donor
embryo splitting requires an enucleated egg, whereas SCNT does not
both produce offspring that are genetically identical to the surrogate mother

Embryo splitting divides the cells of one early embryo, so the offspring match each other but not either parent. SCNT copies the nuclear DNA of a single adult body cell. The option saying both copy a parent is wrong, because embryo splitting begins with fertilisation.
bio12a3-clone-13
Which plant tissue is most often used as the explant in micropropagation, and why?
meristem tissue, because its cells divide actively and are often free of viruses
mature xylem, because it is fully differentiated and stable
pollen grains, because they are haploid and easy to sterilise
root hairs, because they live for a long time

Meristem cells are actively dividing, undifferentiated cells, and the growing tip is often virus-free. Mature xylem cells are dead and cannot divide to form new plants. Plants grown from haploid pollen would not be clones of the parent.
bio12a3-clone-14
In plant tissue culture, a medium with a high cytokinin to auxin ratio tends to promote which outcome?
root formation
shoot formation
seed formation
leaf abscission

A high cytokinin to auxin ratio favours shoot growth, while a high auxin to cytokinin ratio favours root formation. Root formation is the result of the opposite ratio, which makes it a tempting mistake.
bio12a3-clone-15
Most attempts at SCNT fail or produce abnormal embryos. What is the most likely biological reason?
the donor nucleus is too large to fit inside the egg cell
the surrogate's immune system destroys every embryo on contact
all the donor cell's chromosomes carry faulty alleles from the egg
the donor nucleus is not fully reprogrammed, so development is abnormal or stops early

Many transferred nuclei do not switch on the full set of genes needed for normal development, which is a main reason for the low success rate of SCNT. A nucleus is small enough to fit in the egg, and the enucleated egg supplies no chromosomes that could add faulty alleles.
bio12a3-clone-16
A bull is cloned by SCNT, using a body cell from the bull and an enucleated egg from a different cow. Which statement about the sex of the clone is correct?
the clone's sex is random, as in sexual reproduction
the clone's sex is determined by the surrogate mother
the clone's sex matches the nucleus donor, because the sex chromosomes are in the nucleus
the clone's sex matches the egg donor, because the egg determines sex

Sex chromosomes are part of the nuclear DNA, so the clone is male, like the bull. The egg donor contributes only cytoplasm, and in mammals the sperm, not the egg, carries the sex chromosome that determines sex.
bio12a3-clone-17

Each explant produces 3 new plantlets in each subculture cycle, and every plantlet is subcultured in the next cycle. Starting with 1 explant, how many plantlets are produced after 4 subculture cycles?
The number is multiplied by 3 each cycle, so 3 × 3 × 3 × 3 = 81. The answer 27 is the result after only three cycles, and 12 comes from 3 × 4, which ignores that the number multiplies each cycle.
bio12a3-clone-18
Which is a disadvantage of plant tissue culture for producing many plants?
it cannot produce plants with a desirable trait
it requires pollination and seed formation
it cannot produce more than one plant from a single leaf
repeated subculturing can cause mutations, leading to variation among the plantlets

Repeated subculturing can introduce mutations, a problem known as somaclonal variation. Tissue culture needs no pollination or seeds and can produce many plantlets from a small piece of tissue, so the other options are wrong.
bio12a3-clone-19
Which natural process gives the most similar result to plant tissue culture?
pollination by insects, which mixes genes from two plants
vegetative reproduction, such as by runners or tubers, which gives genetically identical plants by mitosis
wind dispersal of seeds from a flower
meiosis in the anthers, which produces haploid pollen

Runners and tubers produce new plants by mitosis from parts of the parent, just as tissue culture does, so the offspring are clones. Pollination, seed dispersal and meiosis all involve sexual reproduction or new gene combinations.
bio12a3-clone-20
A cow's body cell has 60 chromosomes. How many chromosomes does the embryo produced by SCNT contain?
The donor nucleus supplies a full set of 60 chromosomes, and the enucleated egg contributes none. The answer 30 is the gamete number, and 120 wrongly adds two complete sets together.
bio12a3-clone-21
Explain why cells from an early embryo can be separated to produce several complete embryos. (2 marks)
Early embryo cells are undifferentiated and totipotent, so each can develop into any cell type [1]; each separated group of cells can therefore develop into a complete embryo [1].
bio12a3-clone-22
Explain why explants are grown in sterile conditions in plant tissue culture. (2 marks)
Sterile conditions prevent contamination by bacteria or fungi [1]; contaminants would compete with the explant for nutrients or kill the plant tissue [1].
bio12a3-clone-23
Describe how scientists could confirm that a cloned animal is genetically identical in nuclear DNA to its nucleus donor. (3 marks)

Collect DNA samples (e.g. from tissue or blood) from the clone and the donor [1]; compare DNA profiles or markers, such as microsatellites or sequence data, at several loci [1]; matching results at all loci indicate identical nuclear DNA [1].
bio12a3-clone-24
Explain why embryo splitting can produce only a limited number of viable offspring. (2 marks)

Only the cells of an early, undifferentiated embryo can each form a whole organism, and the embryo has a limited number of cells [1]; splitting it into too many pieces leaves each piece with too few cells to develop successfully [1].
bio12a3-clone-25
Compare micropropagation with SCNT in terms of the cells or tissues used, the conditions for growth, and the genetic outcome. (4 marks)

Micropropagation uses small pieces of plant tissue (explants, often meristem), whereas SCNT uses a body cell nucleus placed in an enucleated egg [1]; micropropagation grows explants on sterile nutrient media with hormones, whereas SCNT embryos are stimulated to divide and then implanted into a surrogate uterus [1]; both produce offspring genetically identical to the source of the nuclear DNA [1]; micropropagation involves no egg or sperm, whereas SCNT uses an egg but no sperm [1].
bio12a3-clone-26
Describe two welfare concerns about reproductive cloning of livestock. (2 marks)
Many cloned embryos fail or die before or soon after birth, so many animals suffer [1]; surviving clones may have health problems such as abnormal organ development or shortened lifespan [1].
bio12a3-clone-27

In a cloning trial, 250 SCNT embryos were transferred into surrogate mothers and 12 calves were born alive. Calculate the percentage of transferred embryos that produced a live calf. Show your working. (2 marks)
Working: 12 ÷ 250 × 100 [1]; answer: 4.8% of transferred embryos produced a live calf [1].
bio12a3-clone-28
Explain why a harmful mutation in the nuclear DNA of a donor cell could affect many individuals if that cell is cloned. (2 marks)

Clones are genetically identical in nuclear DNA, so the same mutation is copied into every clone [1]; if the mutation is harmful, all of the clones are affected, so the problem is repeated across the population [1].
vce-bio12-structural-physiological-and-b: bio12a3-adapt-9
Which of the following is a physiological adaptation?
A koala sleeping for most of the day in the fork of a eucalypt tree
A camel's body temperature rising by several degrees during the day rather than being held constant
Long, narrow leaves covered in a dense layer of hairs
A desert lizard burrowing underground during the hottest hours

A physiological adaptation is an internal regulated process. A camel letting its body temperature rise during the day, so it does not have to sweat to stay cool, is one. Sleeping and burrowing are behaviours, and leaf hairs are a structural feature.
bio12a3-adapt-10
A bird living in a cold alpine environment has feathers that trap a layer of warm air close to its skin. This feature is best classified as
structural
physiological
behavioural
biochemical

Feathers are a physical feature of the body, so the adaptation is structural. A physiological adaptation is an internal process, such as changing blood flow to the skin, while fluffing the feathers up on purpose would be a behaviour.
bio12a3-adapt-11
A meerkat group posts a sentry that gives a warning call when a hawk approaches, while the rest of the group keeps foraging. Which statement about the sentry is correct?
It is a structural adaptation that makes the meerkats harder to see
It is a physiological adaptation that increases the sentry's alertness
It is a behavioural adaptation that reduces the risk of predation for the group
It is a physiological adaptation that releases a chemical warning

Posting a sentry is something the animals do, so it is a behavioural adaptation, and its function is to warn the group and lower each animal's risk. The structural and physiological options mislabel the category, and the chemical warning option describes a mechanism the sentry does not use.
bio12a3-adapt-12
Two cube-shaped models of an animal have sides of 2 cm and 4 cm. Which statement about surface area to volume ratio is correct?
The 2 cm cube has the smaller ratio, because its surface area is smaller
Both cubes have the same ratio, because both have the same shape
The 2 cm cube has a ratio of 1.5 cm⁻¹ and the 4 cm cube has a ratio of 3 cm⁻¹
The 4 cm cube has the smaller ratio, at 1.5 cm⁻¹, which is half the 3 cm⁻¹ of the 2 cm cube

The 2 cm cube has 24 cm² of surface and 8 cm³ of volume, a ratio of 3 cm⁻¹, while the 4 cm cube has 96 cm² and 64 cm³, a ratio of 1.5 cm⁻¹. A larger body has a smaller ratio, so the common mistake is to compare absolute surface areas instead of the ratio.
bio12a3-adapt-13
Which statement correctly describes the function of the thick, corky bark of a eucalypt trunk?
It stores water that the tree can draw on during drought
It insulates the living cambium beneath, protecting it from heat during bushfires
It absorbs carbon dioxide for photosynthesis
It produces hormones that control the timing of flowering

Thick bark is a structural adaptation that insulates the living tissue beneath it, so a bushfire heats the cambium more slowly. Bark does not store water or absorb carbon dioxide, since photosynthesis happens mainly in the leaves, and hormone production is a physiological process rather than a function of bark.
bio12a3-adapt-14
Desert mammals lose a large amount of water in exhaled breath. Which structural feature helps reduce this loss?
Convoluted nasal passages that cool exhaled air, so water vapour condenses and is returned to the body
Rapid, shallow panting that increases evaporation from the tongue
Large lungs with a high breathing rate to take in more oxygen
Sweat glands spread over the whole body surface

Convoluted nasal passages cool exhaled air so that water vapour condenses on them and is recovered, which is a structural feature that reduces water loss. Panting, a high breathing rate and sweating all increase water loss, so they are wrong even though they help with cooling.
bio12a3-adapt-15
Mangroves growing in waterlogged, low-oxygen mud produce aerial roots called pneumatophores. What is their main function?
They anchor the tree in soft mud and stop it being uprooted by tides
They excrete excess salt from the plant into the surrounding mud
They project above the mud and take in oxygen for the submerged roots
They absorb water from the mud only at night

Pneumatophores are structural adaptations that project above the mud and take in air, supplying oxygen to the buried root tissues. Anchoring is the role of other root types, and salt removal is a physiological process rather than the function of these roots.
bio12a3-adapt-16
Many desert birds move long distances to areas where rain has recently fallen, because rainfall in these regions is unpredictable. This movement is best classified as
physiological
structural
reproductive
behavioural

Moving to follow unpredictable rain is an action taken by the animal, so it is behavioural. The structural and physiological options describe body features or internal processes, and reproductive describes a different biological function.
bio12a3-adapt-17
A seed-eating bird has a short, thick, cone-shaped beak. Which statement about this feature is correct?
It is a physiological adaptation that increases the bird's production of digestive enzymes
It is a behavioural adaptation that makes the bird choose seeds over insects
It is a structural adaptation that lets the bird crack and husk hard seeds
It is a structural adaptation that stores water for use during dry periods

A short, thick beak is a physical feature, so it is structural, and its shape lets the bird crack and husk hard seeds. The digestive, diet-choice and water-storage options either mislabel the category or describe a function the beak does not have.
bio12a3-adapt-18
Which of the following is a physiological adaptation to cold?
Shivering, which generates heat through rapid muscle contractions
Sheltering in a shaded thicket during the hottest part of the day
Growing a dense, insulating coat of fur
Migrating to a warmer latitude in autumn

Shivering is an internal process that generates heat through muscle contraction, so it is physiological. Sheltering from the heat and migrating are behaviours, and a dense coat is a structural feature.
bio12a3-adapt-19
Seabirds drink seawater and must remove the excess salt. Which feature achieves this?
Thick plumage that keeps seawater away from the skin
Salt glands near the eyes that secrete a concentrated salt solution
Feeding only on prey that contains no salt
A large stomach that stores seawater for later use

Salt glands are a physiological adaptation: they actively excrete concentrated salt, which lets the bird drink seawater safely. Plumage is a structural feature and diet choice is behavioural, and neither removes salt from the body; storing seawater in the stomach would add to the salt load.
bio12a3-adapt-20
A small nocturnal rodent in an arid zone restricts its foraging to the hours after sunset, when the air is cooler. This is best described as
a physiological adaptation that lowers its metabolic rate
a structural adaptation that reduces its surface area
a physiological adaptation that increases its tolerance of heat
a behavioural adaptation that reduces heat stress

Choosing when to forage is an action the animal carries out, so it is behavioural, and it reduces heat stress. The other options name the wrong category, or describe a feature that the timing of foraging does not change.
bio12a3-adapt-21
During drought, many eucalypts close their stomata around midday to reduce water loss. This response is best classified as
structural, because the stomata are a physical feature of the leaf
behavioural, because the plant moves its leaves to shade them
physiological, because it is a regulated internal process
reproductive, because it limits flowering during drought

Closing stomata is a regulated internal response that reduces transpiration, which makes it physiological. Stomata are structures, so calling the response structural confuses the feature with the process it carries out.
bio12a3-adapt-22
A bird living in a dry environment excretes uric acid, a paste-like waste, instead of urea. A student calls this a structural adaptation. Which correction is best?
It is a physiological adaptation, because it is an internal metabolic process that conserves water
It is a behavioural adaptation, because the bird chooses a diet that produces less waste
It is still structural, because the kidneys are body organs
It is not an adaptation, because it does not involve any physical feature

Excreting uric acid is an internal process that saves water, so it is physiological. Calling it structural confuses an organ with the process it carries out, which is the common mistake in this question.
bio12a3-adapt-23
Define a behavioural adaptation and give one example from an Australian animal. (2 marks)
An action or behaviour carried out by an organism [1] that improves its chance of survival or reproduction, e.g. an echidna curling into a ball with its spines facing outwards when threatened [1].
bio12a3-adapt-24
Classify the thick, hard exoskeleton of a crab as a structural or physiological adaptation. (1 mark)
Structural [1].
bio12a3-adapt-25
Explain how a pale, reflective coat helps a desert mammal reduce heat gain from the environment. (3 marks)

Pale colours reflect a greater proportion of incoming solar radiation [1]; less radiant energy is absorbed by the skin [1]; so less heat is gained from the environment, and less evaporative cooling and water loss is needed [1].
bio12a3-adapt-26
Describe two physiological adaptations that help a small mammal in an alpine environment conserve body heat, and explain how each works. (4 marks)

Vasoconstriction: blood vessels in the skin narrow [1], reducing blood flow to the surface so less heat is lost to the air [1]; shivering: rapid, involuntary muscle contractions [1] release heat from the metabolism of the muscles [1].
bio12a3-adapt-27
Explain how sweating cools the human body, using the idea of latent heat. (2 marks)
Water evaporates from the skin surface [1], and the energy needed to change it from liquid to vapour (latent heat) is taken from the skin and blood, cooling the body [1].
bio12a3-adapt-28
Describe two behavioural adaptations that help a small mammal survive a cold winter, and explain how each works. (4 marks)

Huddling with other individuals [1], which reduces the surface area exposed to cold air per animal and so reduces heat loss [1]; sheltering in a nest or burrow lined with insulating material [1], which traps warm air and reduces exposure to wind and cold [1].
bio12a3-adapt-29
Explain why a leaf from a plant in a shaded rainforest understorey is typically larger and thinner than a leaf from a plant in an exposed, dry habitat. (3 marks)

Larger leaves provide more surface area for light capture in low light [1]; thin leaves shorten the diffusion path for CO₂ to reach the chloroplasts [1]; exposed, dry habitats favour smaller, thicker leaves, which reduce the surface area for water loss [1].
bio12a3-adapt-30
Give one example of a physiological adaptation that a marine fish uses to maintain its salt balance. (1 mark)
Chloride cells in the gills actively pump excess salt out of the body [1].
vce-bio12-adaptations-to-australian-envi: bio12a3-aus-9
The platypus hunts for invertebrates on river beds with its eyes, ears and nostrils closed. It locates its prey mainly using
electroreceptors in its bill that detect the weak electric fields produced by prey
echolocation clicks produced by its tongue
a lateral line of sensory organs along its body
smell through its nostrils, which stay open underwater

The platypus bill contains thousands of electroreceptors that detect the weak electrical signals produced by prey muscles. Echolocation is not used by platypuses, and a lateral line belongs to fish; the nostrils close underwater, so smell is not the main sense used there.
bio12a3-aus-10
Grey mangroves (Avicennia marina) grow in salty tidal mud, where salt builds up in their tissues. They get rid of excess salt mainly by
pumping salt into aerial roots (pneumatophores), which release it into the air
keeping their roots completely waterproof so that no salt can enter
secreting salt through salt glands on their leaves, where it crystallises and is shed
opening their stomata only at night so that salt cannot enter

Grey mangroves have salt glands on their leaves that secrete excess salt, which then crystallises on the leaf surface and can be shed. Pneumatophores take in oxygen in waterlogged mud and do not remove salt, and the roots are not waterproof, so some salt is taken up.
bio12a3-aus-11
The water-holding frog (Cyclorana platycephala) survives long dry periods in inland Australia. The water it needs during this time is stored in its
lungs
stomach
gall bladder
urinary bladder
The water-holding frog stores large volumes of water in its urinary bladder, which it draws on during dry periods. The gall bladder stores bile, and the lungs and stomach do not act as water stores.
bio12a3-aus-12
Many annual wildflowers in the arid interior survive dry years as dormant seeds, germinating only after heavy rain. The main advantage of this strategy is that
seeds germinate in the dry season, when temperatures are lower and competition is lower
seedlings germinate only when there is enough water to grow, flower and set seed before the soil dries out
the adult plants store water in their seed coats, which then germinate when needed
seeds are dispersed by wind during drought, when the ground is bare

Germinating after heavy rain gives seedlings enough moisture to complete their short life cycle before drought returns. Germinating in the dry season would usually lead to death, and seed coats do not store water for the adult plant.
bio12a3-aus-13
Cushion plants in the alpine areas of the Australian Alps grow as low, dense mounds close to the ground. Compared with taller plants nearby, the cushion is most likely to be
exposed to higher wind speeds, which increase its rate of photosynthesis
more likely to lose water through its leaves because it is closer to the ground
warmer and less windy, which reduces heat loss and water loss
dispersed further from the parent plant by strong winds

A dense, low cushion creates a warmer, more sheltered microclimate, reducing heat loss and drying out. Higher winds increase water loss and do not improve photosynthesis, and the cushion shape does not help disperse seeds further.
bio12a3-aus-14
Many leaves of Australian rainforest trees have a pointed tip, called a drip tip. The function of this tip is to
trap water on the leaf so it can be absorbed through the surface
increase the leaf's ability to absorb light in the shaded understorey
close the stomata at the tip, reducing transpiration
shed rainwater quickly, so the leaf dries and fungi and algae cannot grow on it

Drip tips channel water off the leaf quickly, so leaves dry faster and epiphylls (fungi and algae) are less likely to grow. Leaves do not absorb water through their upper surface, and the tip does not change light absorption much.
bio12a3-aus-15
The Queensland lungfish (Neoceratodus forsteri) lives in slow, shallow waterholes that can become low in dissolved oxygen. It can survive these conditions because it
gulps air at the surface and takes up oxygen through a single lung
burrows into dry mud and stays dormant until the next wet season
extracts oxygen from air through its gills while out of the water
stores oxygen in its swim bladder for later use

Queensland lungfish have a single lung-like organ and gulp air at the surface when dissolved oxygen falls. Burrowing into mud is a trait of African lungfish, not this species, and gills cannot extract oxygen from air.
bio12a3-aus-16
Bearded dragons are reptiles that live in arid central Australia. Each morning they bask on rocks to warm their bodies before becoming active. Basking is best classified as
a structural adaptation that improves heat absorption
a physiological adaptation that conserves water
a behavioural adaptation for regulating body temperature
a reproductive adaptation that increases mating success
Basking is an action the lizard performs to raise its body temperature, so it is behavioural. Structural adaptations are physical body features, and basking does not conserve water.
bio12a3-aus-17
Echidnas are covered in sharp, pointed spines. These spines are best described as
modified hairs
modified scales, like those of reptiles
modified feathers, like those of birds
modified claws that have grown along the back
Echidna spines are modified hairs made of keratin that protect the animal from predators. Scales and feathers are different structures found in reptiles and birds, and the spines are not claws.
bio12a3-aus-18
Many Australian native legumes, such as wattles (Acacia), grow in nitrogen-poor soils. Their roots form nodules containing bacteria that allow the plant to
dissolve phosphate from rock particles so it can be absorbed
store nitrate in the root cells as a reserve of water
produce nitrogen gas that the plant uses to make chlorophyll
convert nitrogen gas (N₂) from the air into ammonia that the plant can use

Rhizobia bacteria in root nodules fix atmospheric nitrogen into ammonia, which the plant uses to make proteins and other compounds. The bacteria do not dissolve phosphate, nitrate in roots is not a water store, and nitrogen gas is not used directly to make chlorophyll.
bio12a3-aus-19
Bogong moths migrate each spring from inland plains to cool caves in the Australian Alps, where they rest through the hot summer. The main advantage of this behaviour is that the moths
can feed on abundant nectar in the caves while they rest
avoid the high temperatures and dry conditions of the lowland plains, saving water and energy
grow faster in the cool conditions, so they reach adult size sooner
avoid predators that are active only in winter

Bogong moths rest in cool caves over summer, which avoids the heat and drought of the lowlands and saves energy and water. The moths are already adults when they migrate, so the caves do not promote growth.
bio12a3-aus-20
A small desert rodent is 5 cm long and a larger rodent of the same body shape is 15 cm long. Compared with the larger rodent, the small rodent has a surface area to volume ratio that is
three times greater
nine times greater
one-third as great
27 times greater

For similar shapes, surface area scales with length squared and volume with length cubed, so the ratio falls as length increases; here it is 15 ÷ 5 = 3 times greater for the small rodent. Squaring the length ratio (nine times) or cubing it (27 times) gives the wrong answer.
bio12a3-aus-21

Koalas feed almost entirely on eucalyptus leaves, which are low in energy and protein and contain toxic compounds. Describe one structural and one behavioural adaptation that help koalas cope with this diet. (2 marks)

Structural: a very long caecum (around 2 m) that houses microbes which ferment cellulose and help break down toxic compounds [1]; behavioural: sleeps for around 18 hours or more each day, which reduces energy use on a low-energy diet [1].
bio12a3-aus-22

Classify each of the following as structural, physiological or behavioural: (i) the nomadic movement of emus to areas that have recently received rain; (ii) the dense, waterproof fur of the platypus. (2 marks)
(i) behavioural: an action the emu performs to find food and water [1]; (ii) structural: a physical feature of the body covering [1].
bio12a3-aus-23

The sugar glider is a nocturnal marsupial of eucalypt forests with a gliding membrane (patagium) stretched between its front and back legs. Explain how gliding helps the sugar glider find food in forests where food resources are patchy. (3 marks)

Gliding lets it cross between widely spaced trees with much less energy than travelling along the ground [1]; this allows it to reach scattered feeding sites, such as flowering eucalypts and trees with sap or insects, more quickly [1]; it avoids ground predators during travel, so more time and energy go into finding food [1].
bio12a3-aus-24

Some Australian skinks that live in cold alpine regions give birth to live young instead of laying eggs. Explain how this reproductive strategy helps the young survive in a cold environment. (2 marks)

The mother can bask and move between sunny and shaded sites to keep herself and her developing embryos warmer than the cold surroundings [1]; the young develop inside the mother, so they are protected from frost and cold, and are born early enough in the season to feed and grow before winter [1].
bio12a3-aus-25
Define the term ectotherm. (1 mark)
An animal whose body temperature depends mainly on external sources of heat, such as the sun, rather than on heat produced by its own metabolism [1].
bio12a3-aus-26

Describe three adaptations of the saltwater crocodile (Crocodylus porosus) that help it survive in tropical northern Australian wetlands and coasts, and classify each as structural, physiological or behavioural. (3 marks)

Structural: tough, armoured skin of bony plates (scutes) that reduces water loss and protects against injury [1]; behavioural: basks on riverbanks in the morning to warm up before hunting [1]; behavioural: builds mound nests from vegetation whose decomposition generates heat for the eggs [1].
bio12a3-aus-27

Pigface (Carpobrotus) is a succulent groundcover that grows on sand dunes along the Australian coast. Describe four features of pigface that help it survive in hot, dry, windy coastal conditions. (4 marks)

Fleshy leaves store water and have a thick cuticle that reduces water loss [1]; a low, trailing growth habit reduces exposure to wind and heat [1]; stems root at the nodes, so the plant anchors itself in shifting sand [1]; it spreads vegetatively along the ground, allowing it to colonise and hold dune sand after disturbance [1].
bio12a3-aus-28
Describe how the water-holding frog's cocoon helps it survive a long dry period in inland Australia. (2 marks)

The frog sheds layers of skin that harden into a cocoon around its body while it sits in mud [1]; the cocoon reduces evaporative water loss from the skin, so the water stored in its body lasts longer [1].
vce-bio12-interdependencies-and-keystone: bio12a3-inter-9
Barnacles attach to the skin of a whale and filter plankton from the water that passes the whale. The whale is neither helped nor harmed by the barnacles. This relationship is best described as
parasitism
commensalism
mutualism
competition
The barnacles benefit while the whale is unaffected, which is commensalism (+/0). Mutualism would require the whale to benefit too, and parasitism would require the whale to be harmed.
bio12a3-inter-10

A eucalypt releases chemicals from its leaves that stop seeds of other plant species from germinating in the soil beneath it. The eucalypt gains nothing and is not affected by this. The relationship is an example of
mutualism
parasitism
amensalism
commensalism
One species is harmed while the other is unaffected, which is amensalism (−/0). Commensalism is the reverse pattern, where one species benefits and the other is unaffected (+/0).
bio12a3-inter-11

Lichens are made of a fungus and an alga living closely together. The fungus supplies water and minerals, and the alga supplies sugars made by photosynthesis. Both partners gain from the relationship. This relationship is best described as
parasitism
commensalism
competition
mutualism
Both partners benefit (+/+), which is mutualism. Parasitism would mean one partner benefits at the other's expense, and commensalism would mean only one partner benefits.
bio12a3-inter-12

A fan-tailed cuckoo lays its eggs in the nest of a thornbill. The cuckoo chick is raised by the thornbill parents, who feed it at the expense of their own young. This relationship is best described as
parasitism
competition
commensalism
mutualism

The cuckoo benefits at the thornbill's expense (+/−), which is brood parasitism, a form of parasitism. Competition would involve both species using the same limited resource, which is not the main pattern here.
bio12a3-inter-13
A powerful owl hunts and eats ringtail possums, killing each one it catches. The relationship between the owl and the possum is best described as
commensalism
predation
mutualism
parasitism
The owl kills and eats the possum, so the owl benefits and the possum is harmed (+/−), which is predation. Parasitism involves a parasite living on or in a host that is usually not killed quickly.
bio12a3-inter-14
Which statement best distinguishes an indicator species from a keystone species?
An indicator species is always rare, while a keystone species is always common
An indicator species is a predator, while a keystone species is a producer
The presence or absence of an indicator species reflects environmental conditions, while a keystone species has a large effect on community structure relative to its abundance
An indicator species can live in only one ecosystem, while a keystone species is found in many

An indicator species shows the condition of an environment, such as lichens reflecting air quality, but removing it does not usually reshape the community. The other statements wrongly link these terms to abundance, feeding role or range.
bio12a3-inter-15
Which example best describes an ecosystem engineer?
a koala that feeds on eucalypt leaves
a dingo that hunts kangaroos
a fig tree that is the most abundant plant in a rainforest
a wombat whose burrows provide shelter for many other species

Ecosystem engineers physically change the habitat, and the wombat's burrows create shelter used by many other species. Feeding on leaves or hunting does not change the habitat, and abundance alone does not make a species an ecosystem engineer.
bio12a3-inter-16
Which organism is a decomposer?
a fungus breaking down a fallen eucalypt log
a green turtle grazing on seagrass
a koala feeding on eucalypt leaves
a dingo hunting a kangaroo
Decomposers such as fungi and bacteria break down dead organic matter and return nutrients to the soil. The turtle, koala and dingo all eat living organisms, so they are consumers.
bio12a3-inter-17
The competitive exclusion principle predicts that two species with identical niches
will always evolve to use different niches
will both increase in population as resources become more available
cannot coexist indefinitely in the same place, and one is eventually eliminated
will coexist in equal numbers

Two species using exactly the same resources compete directly, so the less competitive species is eventually eliminated. Niche partitioning, which evolves over time, is how species avoid exclusion, so it is not the prediction of the principle.
bio12a3-inter-18

Two bird species feed on the same insect prey in a eucalypt woodland. Over time they are observed feeding in different parts of the trees, with one feeding on the bark and the other in the canopy. This most likely reflects
interspecific competition that has caused one species to become extinct
mutualism between the two species
a trophic cascade caused by a predator
reduced competition through resource partitioning

Feeding in different parts of the trees reduces the overlap in the resource used, which is resource partitioning, and this lowers competition. Extinction is not described, the birds are not benefiting each other, and no predator is changing lower trophic levels.
bio12a3-inter-19

In a grassland, grass captures 20 000 kJ of energy. Grasshoppers eat the grass, and lizards eat the grasshoppers. Using the 10% energy transfer rule between each trophic level, how much energy is available to the lizards?
200 kJ
20 kJ

About 10% is passed on at each level, so 20 000 kJ becomes 2 000 kJ for the grasshoppers and then 200 kJ for the lizards. The value of 2 000 kJ is only one transfer, and 20 kJ wrongly applies a third 10% transfer.
bio12a3-inter-20
A rainbow lorikeet feeds on nectar and pollen from flowering eucalypts. In the food chain eucalypt → rainbow lorikeet, the lorikeet is best classified as a
producer
primary consumer
secondary consumer
decomposer

A primary consumer eats producers, so a bird that feeds on plant nectar and pollen is a primary consumer. Producers make their own food, secondary consumers eat other animals, and decomposers break down dead matter.
bio12a3-inter-21
In the notation used for species interactions, a relationship shown as (+/0) means
one species benefits and the other is harmed
both species are harmed
one species benefits and the other is unaffected
both species benefit

The + shows that one species gains a benefit and the 0 shows that the other is unaffected, which is commensalism. A (+/−) pattern means one species benefits while the other is harmed, and a (+/+) pattern means both benefit.
bio12a3-inter-22
Define the term trophic level. (1 mark)
The position an organism occupies in a food chain or food web, based on its feeding relationship and source of energy [1]
bio12a3-inter-23
Explain why food chains rarely have more than four or five trophic levels. (2 marks)

At each trophic level about 90% of the energy is lost, mainly as heat from respiration, and so is not passed on to the next level [1]; by the top level too little energy remains to support a viable population of consumers [1]
bio12a3-inter-24
Describe how mycorrhizal fungi and eucalypts are interdependent. (2 marks)

The fungal hyphae extend the tree's root system, increasing the absorption of water and mineral nutrients such as phosphorus for the tree [1]; in return the tree supplies the fungus with sugars produced by photosynthesis [1]
bio12a3-inter-25
Explain why a common and widespread species is not necessarily a keystone species. (2 marks)

A keystone species has a disproportionately large effect on community structure relative to its abundance, so a common species is only a keystone if its removal causes major changes to the community [1]; many abundant species can be replaced by other species, so their loss would have only small effects on other organisms [1]
bio12a3-inter-26
Explain the difference between predation and parasitism. (2 marks)

In predation, the predator kills and eats its prey, so the prey is harmed immediately [1]; in parasitism, the parasite lives on or in the host and gains nutrients from it while usually not killing it quickly [1]
bio12a3-inter-27
Cane toads have toxic skin secretions. Predict and explain the effect of cane toads on a native predator, the northern quoll, and on a prey species of the quoll. (3 marks)

Quolls that eat cane toads are poisoned and die, so the quoll population declines [1]; with fewer quolls, predation pressure on the quoll's prey, such as insects and small vertebrates, is reduced, so prey numbers are likely to increase [1]; changes in the prey population may then affect other species that depend on the prey or compete with it [1]
bio12a3-inter-28
Termites build mounds and tunnels in the soil of many Australian ecosystems. Explain how termites can act as ecosystem engineers, and describe one effect this has on other species. (3 marks)

Termites physically change the environment by moving soil and building mounds and tunnels, which alters soil structure, drainage and the distribution of nutrients [1]; these structures create shelter and habitat for other invertebrates and small animals [1]; if termites were removed, these species would lose their shelter and could decline [1]
bio12a3-inter-29

Algae in a pond capture 60 000 kJ of energy. Water fleas eat the algae, small fish eat the water fleas, and a kingfisher eats the small fish. Using the 10% energy transfer rule, calculate the energy available to the kingfisher. Show your working. (3 marks)
Water fleas receive 10% of 60 000 kJ = 6000 kJ [1]; small fish receive 10% of 6000 kJ = 600 kJ [1]; kingfisher receives 10% of 600 kJ = 60 kJ [1]
bio12a3-inter-30

A disease kills most of the seagrass in a meadow that provides food and shelter for dugongs, green turtles, juvenile fish and prawns. Explain the effects of this loss on at least three populations in the meadow, and describe one flow-on effect on the wider ecosystem. (4 marks)

Dugongs and green turtles lose their main food source, so their survival and reproduction decline [1]; juvenile fish and prawns lose their shelter and nursery habitat, so their numbers fall [1]; larger predators of these fish and prawns lose prey and may also decline [1]; reduced seagrass means less sediment is trapped and stabilised, increasing turbidity and harming other organisms such as filter feeders and corals [1]
vce-bio12-aboriginal-and-torres-strait-i: bio12a3-ik-9
Traditional Ecological Knowledge held by Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander peoples is best described as
knowledge built over many generations through close observation of particular places and passed on through language, stories and practice
a set of general scientific principles developed in universities and then applied to Country
knowledge limited to spiritual beliefs, with no practical ecological content
a fixed list of plant and animal names recorded by early European explorers

Traditional Ecological Knowledge is cumulative and place-based, built up over many generations and transmitted through language, stories and practice. The idea that it is purely spiritual ignores its detailed, practical information about species and seasons, and it is not a fixed list recorded by early explorers.
bio12a3-ik-10
Many savanna Traditional Owners burn early in the dry season rather than late in it, mainly because early, cooler burns
produce the hottest fires, which clear the ground most thoroughly
reduce the fuel that would otherwise feed larger, hotter late-season wildfires and their greenhouse gas emissions
are the only type of fire that will spread through dry grass
allow fire to spread into closed forest so that new growth appears

Early dry season fires are cooler and patchy, so they leave less fuel for the hotter, larger wildfires that tend to occur late in the season. The idea that the hottest fires clear ground best is a common mistake, because intense fire damages habitat and is not the goal of cultural burning.
bio12a3-ik-11
Some cycad seeds are toxic if eaten raw. Aboriginal peoples in northern Australia prepared them by soaking or leaching the seeds in water before eating them. The main purpose of this step was to
ferment the sugars so the seeds taste sweeter
soften the seed so it could be cracked more easily
remove water-soluble toxins before the seed was eaten
reduce the protein content so the seed would store for longer

The toxins in cycad seeds dissolve in water, so leaching removes them and makes the seed safe to eat. Fermentation and softening can be part of other food preparation, but neither removes the toxins, which is why they are not the purpose here.
bio12a3-ik-12
An Indigenous Protected Area is best described as
land that the federal government leases to Traditional Owners for grazing
a national park in which all human use, including cultural burning, is banned
a commercial fishing zone that Aboriginal people may use only for ceremonies
land or sea country that Traditional Owners have voluntarily dedicated for conservation, managed under their own plans and knowledge

Indigenous Protected Areas are voluntarily dedicated by Indigenous landowners and managed for conservation and culture, often in partnership with governments. The national park option is wrong because these areas actively include cultural land management such as cultural burning.
bio12a3-ik-13
When gathering seed from a native grass or bush food, Traditional Owners often leave some of the seed on the plant. Why does this practice support sustainable use?
the remaining seed allows the plant population to regenerate and still feeds wildlife
plants cannot be harmed by any harvest, so the amount taken does not matter
seed left on the plant always rots, so harvesting everything prevents waste
harvested plants produce more seed each year because of the damage

Leaving seed lets plants regenerate and provides food for birds and other animals. The claims that plants cannot be harmed, or that damage boosts seed production, are not sound grounds for sustainable harvest.
bio12a3-ik-14
In many Aboriginal kinship systems, particular plants and animals are linked to certain people, which can lead to
a rule that every species must be eaten at least once each year
obligations to care for those species, which can limit when and how much of them is taken
the belief that species can be bought and sold within families
the view that people should never intervene, because species always look after themselves

Kinship and totem relationships can carry responsibilities to care for and protect particular species, so people may limit when and how much they take. The idea that species are bought and sold describes a commercial system that is not part of traditional management.
bio12a3-ik-15
Some Aboriginal groups managed food plants such as yams not only by collecting them but by tending the plots. Which practice best illustrates this?
digging up every tuber in a patch and leaving no plant material behind
avoiding a patch entirely so that the plants are never disturbed
replanting parts of the tuber and returning later, so the patch can supply food in future seasons
importing non-native crops to replace the native yams

Tending a patch by replanting and returning to it increases future harvests and keeps the food supply sustainable. Clearing a patch completely undermines future yield, and importing non-native crops is not part of traditional management.
bio12a3-ik-16
Many Australian plants have seeds or buds that respond to fire. How can a patchy, cool burn increase the abundance of such species?
fire kills every seed in the soil, so the species must regrow only from roots
fire makes the soil acidic, which these species require to grow
fire permanently removes all competing plants, so the species never face competition again
heat and smoke can trigger germination or resprouting, and reduced competition gives these species room to grow

Smoke and heat can break seed dormancy or stimulate resprouting in many fire-adapted species, and reduced competition helps seedlings establish. The claims that fire kills all seeds or changes soil acidity are common misconceptions and do not describe how these species respond.
bio12a3-ik-17
Why do many Traditional Owners keep fire out of rainforest margins during burning?
rainforest is fire-resistant and benefits from hot, intense fire
hot fire can kill fire-sensitive rainforest plants and the animals that depend on them
rainforest plants produce oils that make fire spread faster into the forest
rainforest trees need fire to open their seed pods

Rainforest edges contain many fire-sensitive species, so a hot fire can destroy them and the animals that rely on them. The idea that rainforest is fire-resistant is a common mistake, because its margins are often damaged by fire.
bio12a3-ik-18
In arid Australia, people can locate water by observing seed-eating birds such as finches and pigeons. Why is this an effective indicator?
the birds store water in their crops and release it near the surface
these birds must drink daily, so they fly to water in the early morning and late afternoon along predictable paths
the birds only nest near water, so any nest reveals a nearby spring
the birds feed only on water plants that grow in standing water

Many seed-eating birds need to drink every day, so their flights to water at dawn and dusk show the direction and distance to water. The claims about storing water in crops, or nesting only near water, are not supported as reasons for this method.
bio12a3-ik-19
Traditional Owners can find the nest of a native stingless bee (sugarbag) in a hollow tree by
listening for buzzing from inside tree trunks, mainly at night
searching for the largest flowering eucalypt in the area and cutting into it
watching the foraging bees and following their flight lines back to the hollow
assuming the nest is in the closest tree to the nearest flower

Foraging worker bees fly in fairly direct lines between flowers and their nest, so following their flight paths can lead to the hollow. Cutting into trees harms the colony, and the other options are guesses that do not track the bees.
bio12a3-ik-20
A tracker wants to judge how recently an animal passed through sandy ground. Which evidence is most useful?
whether the edges of the print are sharp or crumbled, and whether wind, rain or dew has altered it
the exact length of the animal's stride, which shows its age
the colour of the soil inside the print
the total number of tracks in the area, since more tracks always mean a more recent visit

Sharp, unweathered edges and an undisturbed surface suggest a recent track, while wind, rain or dew soften and fill it in over time. Stride length mainly indicates the animal's size and gait, not its age, and the number of tracks says nothing about when a single track was made.
bio12a3-ik-21
When scientists want to publish Aboriginal or Torres Strait Islander knowledge about a species, why is consent from the knowledge holders important?
the knowledge belongs to the people who hold it, and some may be culturally restricted or sacred
knowledge is only protected when it is written down in a government report
scientific journals will not publish any knowledge that comes from oral sources
consent is needed only for knowledge about animals, not plants

Traditional Owners hold cultural and intellectual property rights over their knowledge, and some of it may be restricted by cultural law. The idea that knowledge is protected only when written down is a misconception, since much traditional knowledge is oral and still belongs to its holders.
bio12a3-ik-22
Coastal Aboriginal communities often plan shellfish gathering around the lowest tides. What is the main ecological reason for this?
high tides push shellfish into shallow water where they are easily caught
the sea is calmer at low tide, so shellfish stop moving and can be collected
shellfish only breed during high tides, so low tides are the safe time to harvest them
the lowest tides expose intertidal shellfish that are otherwise underwater and hard to reach

Low tides expose intertidal shellfish, making them accessible and reducing the effort needed to collect them. The claims about high tides pushing shellfish into shallow water, or about breeding timing, are misconceptions about how shellfish behave.
bio12a3-ik-23
Define the term 'Caring for Country' in the context of Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander land management. (1 mark)
The ongoing responsibility of Traditional Owners to look after land, sea, plants, animals and cultural places, using their knowledge, law and practices [1].
bio12a3-ik-24
Explain why ecological knowledge built up over many generations in one place can be valuable for managing that place. (2 marks)

It is based on long-term, direct observation of changes in species, seasons and water that short-term records would miss [1]; it captures local species interactions and environmental cues, so management can be tailored to that specific area [1].
bio12a3-ik-25

A ranger team plans to reintroduce cultural burning on a property where dense shrubs have built up after decades without fire. Outline three steps the team could take to plan the burns safely and sustainably. (3 marks)

Consult the Traditional Owners and use their knowledge of timing, weather and seasonal indicators to choose when to burn [1]; assess fuel loads, wind and humidity, prepare firebreaks, then burn cool and in small patches [1]; monitor the results and plan a mosaic of burns of different ages over time to maintain habitat diversity [1].
bio12a3-ik-26
Explain why the Sea Country approach involves Torres Strait Islander and Aboriginal people in marine management rather than relying only on scientists. (2 marks)

Sea Country includes the reefs, waters and animals that are part of people's culture and identity, so people hold detailed local knowledge of changes [1]; involving them gives management a basis in their rights, responsibilities and long-term care, which supports compliance and continuity [1].
bio12a3-ik-27
Discuss how cultural burning can help reduce greenhouse gas emissions from northern Australian savannas. (4 marks)

Early dry season burns are cooler and patchy, so they reduce the fuel available for later fires [1]; this reduces the area burnt by late-season wildfires, which are hotter and more extensive and release more greenhouse gases in total [1]; savanna burning projects led by Traditional Owners can earn Australian Carbon Credit Units under the Emissions Reduction Fund for emissions avoided [1]; patchy burning also protects large trees and other vegetation that store carbon, so less carbon is lost [1].
vce-psych12-approaches-to-understanding-: psych12a1-appr-9
Paul Broca's patient 'Tan' could understand speech well but could produce only the one word 'tan'. After the patient's death, post-mortem examination found damage to which region?
the left frontal lobe
the right temporal lobe
the left occipital lobe
the cerebellum

Tan's damage was in the left frontal region linked to speech production, while understanding was relatively preserved. Right temporal damage is not the typical cause of this pattern, and the occipital lobe and cerebellum are not associated with fluent speech.
psych12a1-appr-10
A limitation of lesion analysis in human patients with brain damage is that
the damage cannot be seen on any scan
the results always contradict those from animal studies
researchers cannot control the location or extent of the damage
participants cannot give informed consent

Damage from stroke or injury occurs naturally, so researchers cannot choose its location or size, and it may spread across several regions. Damage can usually be seen on CT or MRI, and the other options are not general features of lesion analysis.
psych12a1-appr-11
A patient arrives at an emergency department with a sudden severe headache and possible bleeding in the brain. Which technique is most appropriate for a quick check of the bleed?
electroencephalography (EEG)
functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI)
positron emission tomography (PET)
computed tomography (CT)

CT is fast and readily shows bleeding and skull fractures, which makes it suited to emergencies. EEG and fMRI measure activity rather than giving a quick structural picture, and PET is slower and requires a radioactive tracer.
psych12a1-appr-12
Positron emission tomography (PET) produces images by detecting
changes in blood oxygen levels in the brain
the uptake of a radioactive tracer that indicates metabolic activity
electrical signals from the scalp
the absorption of X-rays passing through the head

PET tracks a radioactive tracer, such as a glucose analogue, to show where metabolic activity is high. Blood oxygen changes describe fMRI, scalp electrical signals describe EEG, and X-ray absorption describes CT.
psych12a1-appr-13
Compared with CT, structural MRI has the advantage that it
gives more detailed soft-tissue images without ionising radiation
is cheaper and faster to perform
measures electrical activity in neurons
uses a radioactive tracer to show blood flow

MRI uses magnetic fields and radio waves, so it avoids ionising radiation and shows soft tissue in more detail than CT. MRI is generally slower and more costly than CT, while electrical activity and radioactive tracers belong to EEG and PET.
psych12a1-appr-14
In fMRI studies, researchers often subtract the brain activity recorded during a control task from that recorded during an experimental task. The purpose of this is to
remove the need for a control group
increase the temporal resolution of the scan
isolate activity linked to the cognitive process of interest
measure electrical activity that the BOLD signal cannot show

Both tasks share general visual and motor demands, so subtraction leaves activity specific to the process being studied. Subtraction does not change temporal resolution, which remains limited by the slow BOLD response.
psych12a1-appr-15
A split-brain participant holds a familiar object in their right hand, out of sight, and can usually say what it is. This is because
the corpus callosum carries touch information from the right hand to the right hemisphere
touch is processed equally by both hemispheres
the right hand is controlled by the right hemisphere, which can name objects
touch from the right hand is processed by the left hemisphere, which controls speech

Touch from each hand is sent to the opposite hemisphere, so input from the right hand reaches the left hemisphere, where language is usually produced. This input does not need to cross the corpus callosum, so it can be named.
psych12a1-appr-16
Lateralisation of brain function refers to the idea that
each hemisphere performs identical functions
some functions are mainly controlled by one hemisphere rather than the other
functions are spread evenly across the whole cortex
the lateral (outer) areas of the brain control all sensory input
Lateralisation describes specialised functions, such as language production in the left hemisphere for most people. The other options describe equal distribution of function or misread the term.
psych12a1-appr-17
A researcher lesions the hippocampus of some rats and leaves others intact, then compares maze performance between the two groups. This is best described as
a correlational study, because brain structure and behaviour are measured
a case study, because individual rats are studied in depth
an experiment, because the researcher manipulates the lesion (the independent variable)
a longitudinal study, because the rats are observed over time

The researcher controls which rats receive the lesion and compares them with a control group, which defines an experiment. Correlational designs measure existing variables without manipulating them, and this study compares groups rather than in-depth single cases.
psych12a1-appr-18
Before an MRI scan, people with metal implants (such as some surgical devices) are screened because the strong magnetic field can
absorb X-rays and hide the brain's structure
move or heat metal objects in the body
block the radio waves needed to make an image
expose the person to ionising radiation
The strong magnet can pull on ferromagnetic implants and heat some metals, creating a serious safety risk. MRI does not use X-rays or ionising radiation, and absorbing X-rays describes CT.
psych12a1-appr-19
The electrical signals recorded by EEG mainly reflect
the firing of single neurons in the brainstem
changes in blood flow to deep brain structures
the synchronised activity of large groups of cortical neurons
the decay of a radioactive tracer

EEG electrodes on the scalp detect summed activity from large populations of cortical neurons firing together. Single deep neurons are too far from the scalp to be recorded, and blood flow and tracer decay are measured by fMRI and PET.
psych12a1-appr-20
A key limitation of animal lesion studies is that
results may not generalise to humans because of species differences in brain structure and function
the lesions can never be precisely placed
they cannot provide any information about brain function
they are always conducted without ethical approval

Animal lesion studies allow controlled placement of damage, but the brains of rats or monkeys differ from the human brain, so findings must be applied to humans cautiously. Lesions in animals can often be placed precisely, and these studies do yield information about brain function.
psych12a1-appr-21
Which of the following is an example of a naturally occurring lesion used in case study research?
an electrode placed deliberately in the visual cortex of a rat
a surgeon's removal of the hippocampus to test memory
a deliberate electrical lesion made in a rat's cortex
a stroke that damages the left frontal lobe

Strokes, injuries and disease produce damage without researchers' intervention, which is what makes them natural lesions studied in case studies. Deliberate surgical or electrical lesions are made by researchers for experimental purposes.
psych12a1-appr-22
The BOLD signal measured in fMRI is best described as
a direct record of electrical firing from individual neurons
an indirect measure of neural activity, based on changes in oxygenated blood flow
a measure of the amount of radioactive glucose used by cells
an image of the brain's structure showing fibre pathways

Active neurons increase demand for oxygen, and the local blood flow response changes the ratio of oxygenated to deoxygenated haemoglobin, which fMRI detects. The other options describe EEG, PET and structural imaging respectively.
psych12a1-appr-23
Many fMRI studies use small samples. The main practical reason for this is that
the BOLD signal can only be detected in very small numbers of people
ethics committees set a standard limit of ten participants
scanning is expensive and time-consuming, which limits the number of participants
participants cannot be scanned more than once

fMRI equipment is costly and each session takes time, so sample sizes are often limited for practical reasons. There is no standard ethical limit of ten participants, and fMRI participants can often be scanned repeatedly, which is a strength over PET.
psych12a1-appr-24
In a healthy brain, the main role of the corpus callosum is to
transfer information between the two cerebral hemispheres
control the body's voluntary movements directly
store long-term memories in the frontal lobe
send visual information from the eyes to the occipital lobe

The corpus callosum is a large bundle of nerve fibres connecting the two hemispheres, so it lets them share information. The other options describe the motor cortex, memory systems and visual pathways rather than this structure.
psych12a1-appr-25
Describe the difference between a case study and an experiment as approaches to understanding the brain. (2 marks)

Case study: an in-depth investigation of one person or a small group with naturally occurring brain damage or a condition, in which the researcher does not manipulate variables [1]; Experiment: the researcher manipulates an independent variable under controlled conditions, usually with a control group, to establish cause and effect [1].
psych12a1-appr-26
Identify one ethical consideration when researching people with brain damage, and explain why it is important. (2 marks)

Informed consent: participants, or a legally recognised substitute if their capacity is impaired, must understand and agree to take part [1]; this is important because people with brain injuries may have reduced ability to make decisions, so their rights must be protected [1].
psych12a1-appr-27

A researcher wants to (a) find which brain areas are active while participants complete a memory task, and (b) check participants for structural abnormalities before the study. For each purpose, recommend a suitable technique and justify your choice. (4 marks)

(a) fMRI [1], as it detects changes in blood oxygenation that indicate which regions are active during the task, with good spatial resolution [1]; (b) MRI (or CT) [1], as it shows the brain's structure in detail so abnormalities can be identified, and MRI does not use ionising radiation [1].
psych12a1-appr-28
Name the neuroimaging technique that builds cross-sectional images of the brain from X-rays taken at many angles. (1 mark)
Computed tomography (CT) [1].
psych12a1-appr-29
Penfield used electrical stimulation of the cortex during surgery. Outline how this technique was used to identify brain function, and state one limitation of the approach. (2 marks)

Stimulating a specific area and recording the movement or sensation the patient reported links that area to a function [1]; limitation: it is only possible in the small number of patients undergoing surgery, so the sample is limited and may not be representative [1].
psych12a1-appr-30
A neuroimaging study finds that a region is more active when participants perform a task. Explain why this finding does not, on its own, show that the region is necessary for the task. (2 marks)

The finding is correlational: it shows an association between activity and the task, not cause and effect [1]; the activity could be incidental or a consequence of the task, so evidence such as lesions or stimulation is needed to show necessity [1].
psych12a1-appr-31
State one advantage of fMRI over PET for researching the same participant on several occasions. (1 mark)
fMRI does not use a radioactive tracer, so the participant is not exposed to radiation and can be scanned repeatedly [1].
psych12a1-appr-32

The case of patient H.M., who had his hippocampus removed, suggested a role for the hippocampus in memory. Describe what this case showed, and state one limitation of drawing this conclusion. (2 marks)

After removal of the hippocampus, H.M. could not form new long-term (declarative) memories, suggesting the hippocampus is needed for memory formation [1]; limitation: this is a single case, and the surgical damage extended beyond the hippocampus, so the conclusion may not generalise [1].
psych12a1-appr-33
Explain the difference between structural and functional brain imaging techniques, giving one example of each. (3 marks)

Structural techniques show the anatomy of the brain, such as CT or MRI [1]; functional techniques show activity or processes in the brain, such as fMRI or PET [1]; functional techniques are used to link regions to tasks, whereas structural techniques are used to identify damage or abnormalities [1].
psych12a1-appr-34
Evaluate the use of case studies of brain damage as an approach to understanding brain function. In your answer, refer to one strength and one limitation. (4 marks)

Strength: case studies provide detailed, in-depth information about the effects of specific injuries, which may be rare and cannot be deliberately produced in humans [1]; they can suggest hypotheses about the role of particular regions [1]; limitation: each injury differs in location, extent and the person's prior functioning, so findings may not generalise [1]; the researcher cannot control the damage, so cause and effect cannot be firmly established [1].
vce-psych12-structure-and-function-of-th: The primary visual cortex, which receives information from the eyes, is located in the
The primary visual cortex sits in the occipital lobe at the back of the brain. The temporal lobe is mainly associated with hearing and object recognition, so it is a tempting but incorrect choice.
The primary auditory cortex, which processes sound information from the ears, is located in the
The primary auditory cortex lies in the temporal lobe, on the side of the brain above the ears. The occipital lobe is the visual area, so choosing it confuses hearing with vision.
Which brain structure, at the base of the brainstem, controls automatic functions such as heart rate and breathing?

The medulla oblongata regulates vital automatic functions such as heart rate and breathing. The cerebellum controls balance and coordination, so it is a common confusion because it is also found towards the back of the brain.
Sensory information from the eyes, ears, skin and body (other than smell) is relayed to the cerebral cortex by which structure?

The thalamus acts as a relay station, directing sensory signals to the appropriate areas of the cortex. The hypothalamus regulates hunger, thirst and body temperature, so it is a tempting but incorrect choice.
Which structure, located below the thalamus, regulates body temperature, hunger and thirst?

The hypothalamus sits below the thalamus and maintains homeostasis by regulating hunger, thirst and body temperature. The amygdala is involved in fear and emotion, so it is a tempting but incorrect choice.
A woman with damage to the right parietal lobe tends to ignore objects on her left side, even though her vision is normal. Which function is most affected?
Recognition of the meaning of spoken words
Awareness of space and of the positions of objects around the body
Control of heart rate and breathing

The parietal lobe integrates sensory information to represent space, and right parietal damage often leads to neglect of the left side. Understanding spoken words is linked to Wernicke's area rather than spatial awareness.
Why is the surface of the cerebral cortex folded into ridges and grooves?
It separates the brain into the four lobes
It increases the number of cerebral hemispheres
It increases the surface area available for neurons
Folding packs a large area of neural tissue into the limited space of the skull, so more neurons fit. Folding does not change the number of hemispheres, which is always two.
Which hemisphere is generally more involved in visual-spatial processing, such as judging the layout of a room?
Both hemispheres equally in all people
In most people the right hemisphere is more involved in visual-spatial processing. The left hemisphere is usually dominant for language, so choosing it confuses spatial and language functions.
Which of the following is NOT part of the limbic system?
The medulla is part of the brainstem, not the limbic system, which includes the amygdala, hippocampus and hypothalamus. Each of the other three options is a limbic structure.
Which structure, although only about a tenth of the brain's volume, contains the majority of the brain's neurons?
The cerebellum is small compared with the cerebrum but packs in the majority of the brain's neurons. The cerebral cortex is far larger in volume but contains fewer neurons.
Which structure controls the pituitary gland, which releases hormones into the bloodstream?
The hypothalamus controls the pituitary gland, which in turn regulates hormone release. The hippocampus and amygdala are limbic structures involved in memory and emotion rather than hormone control.
After a stroke, a woman loses vision in the right half of her visual field in both eyes. Which area is most likely damaged?
The left primary visual cortex processes information from the right visual field, so damage there causes loss of right-side vision. Right occipital damage would affect the left visual field instead.
How many lobes does each cerebral hemisphere contain?
Each cerebral hemisphere has four lobes: frontal, parietal, temporal and occipital. Choosing three is a common mistake that overlooks one of these lobes.
Which group of structures forms the link between the spinal cord and the rest of the brain?

The brainstem, which includes the medulla, pons and midbrain, connects the spinal cord to higher brain structures. The limbic system is involved in emotion and memory, and the corpus callosum connects the two cerebral hemispheres.
The corpus callosum is made up mainly of which type of tissue?

The corpus callosum is a bundle of myelinated axons, which is white matter. Grey matter, made of cell bodies and dendrites, is found mainly in the cortex, so choosing it confuses the two tissue types.
In which lobe of the cerebrum is the hippocampus located?

The hippocampus sits deep within the temporal lobe, close to the amygdala. The frontal lobe, at the front of the brain, is mainly involved in movement, planning and decision-making, so it is a common confusion.
Electrical stimulation of the primary visual cortex during brain surgery would most likely produce which experience?
A sensation of touch on the hand
A ringing sound in one ear

Stimulating the primary visual cortex typically produces visual sensations such as flashes of light, because that is where visual signals are processed. Stimulating the somatosensory cortex would produce touch sensations rather than light.
Which groove separates the frontal lobe from the parietal lobe?

The central sulcus separates the frontal lobe from the parietal lobe, with the primary motor cortex lying just in front of it. The longitudinal fissure divides the two hemispheres rather than the lobes, so it is a common mix-up.
The primary motor cortex has a much larger area devoted to the fingers and lips than to the back and legs. What does this suggest about the function of the motor cortex? (1 mark)
Body parts requiring fine, precise movement have a larger representation in the motor cortex [1]
Name the lobe of the cerebral cortex in which Wernicke's area is located. (1 mark)
A stroke damages the right primary motor cortex. Explain why the weakness is seen on the left side of the body. (2 marks)

Motor pathways cross over in the lower brainstem, so each hemisphere controls the opposite side of the body [1]; the right motor cortex therefore controls the left side of the body, so the left side is weakened [1]
Explain how the cerebellum contributes to learning a skill such as riding a bicycle. (2 marks)
The cerebellum fine-tunes movement, coordinating timing and balance as the skill is practised [1]; with repetition, movements become smoother and more automatic [1]
Explain how the hypothalamus contributes to regulating the sleep-wake cycle. (2 marks)

The hypothalamus contains a group of cells (the suprachiasmatic nucleus) that acts as the body's internal clock [1]; it uses light signals from the eyes to regulate daily rhythms of sleepiness and alertness [1]
A person has damage to their left temporal lobe. Explain why they can still hear sounds in both ears. (2 marks)
Auditory pathways are bilateral, so each ear sends signals to both auditory cortices [1]; the right temporal lobe, which is undamaged, still receives input from both ears [1]

A patient whose corpus callosum has been surgically cut is shown the word 'key' only in their left visual field. Describe what they can do with their left hand and what they are unable to say, and explain why. (3 marks)

The left visual field is processed by the right hemisphere [1]; the right hemisphere controls the left hand, so the patient can point to or pick up a key with the left hand [1]; the patient cannot say 'key' aloud because the information cannot cross the severed corpus callosum to the left hemisphere's language areas [1]

Research on London taxi drivers, who must memorise the city's streets, found that their hippocampus was larger than that of comparison participants. Explain what this suggests about the hippocampus. (3 marks)

The hippocampus is involved in spatial memory and navigation [1]; the larger hippocampus suggests that learning and storing detailed spatial maps is associated with changes in its structure [1]; the study is correlational, so it cannot prove that the training caused the enlargement [1]
Explain how myelin increases the speed of messages travelling through the white matter of the brain. (3 marks)

Myelin is a fatty insulating sheath that wraps around axons [1]; it allows the electrical impulse to jump between gaps in the sheath, which is faster than travelling along the whole axon [1]; so messages travel more quickly between brain regions [1]

A patient has damage to the medulla oblongata and to the cerebellum. Describe one function affected by each structure, and explain why damage to the medulla is more likely to be life-threatening. (4 marks)

Medulla oblongata: controls automatic functions such as breathing and heart rate [1]; Cerebellum: coordinates balance and smooth voluntary movement [1]; Damage to the medulla can disrupt breathing and heart rate, which are essential for survival [1]; Cerebellum damage affects coordination but does not directly control vital functions, so it is less immediately life-threatening [1]
Describe how the amygdala and the prefrontal cortex interact when a person perceives a threat, and explain how this interaction can help regulate fear. (4 marks)

The amygdala detects the threat and triggers a rapid fear response [1]; it sends signals that produce physiological arousal and an immediate reaction [1]; the prefrontal cortex evaluates the situation and sends regulatory signals that can dampen the amygdala's response [1]; this allows the person to respond to the threat in a controlled rather than impulsive way [1]
Name each of the four lobes of the cerebral cortex and give one function of each. (4 marks)

Frontal lobe: voluntary movement, planning and decision-making [1]; Parietal lobe: processing touch, pain and temperature [1]; Temporal lobe: auditory processing and object recognition [1]; Occipital lobe: visual processing [1]
vce-psych12-neuroplasticity-and-adolesce: psych12a1-neur-9
Neuroplasticity refers to the brain's ability to
change its structure and function in response to experience
remain the same size whatever a person experiences
replace damaged neurons within days of an injury
keep its neural connections fixed once childhood ends

Neuroplasticity is the capacity of the brain to reorganise its structure and function in response to learning, experience and injury. The idea that connections are fixed after childhood is outdated, and the brain does not rapidly replace large numbers of lost neurons.
psych12a1-neur-10
Myelination during adolescence mainly leads to
a reduction in the total number of synapses across the brain
